9.title: Please watch this in a *REAL* iMax theater
9.content:
How do you compete with the heath Ledger's Joker when you have a mask on your face?

You don't. Bane is a good villain, with a memorable voice and even more memorable lines but his personality and motivation are murky and not as fascinating or understandable as the Jokers'.

With that exception, the overall casting for the movie is the best of the 3 movies. Christopher Nolan must have so much Hollywood Cred by now that he just gets every single on of his first picks, no matter how small a role they have and it is delightful to see.

The cinematography is the best ever. With 72 minutes of iMax footage, you simply need to see this in an iMax theater that supports 70mm film. These are usually round structures with screens 5-stories high unlike most "fake" iMax theaters located inside multiplexes so do your research beforehand!

The pacing and the action scenes are fantastic of course. It is unfortunate that so many key moments were exposed in trailers but such is life. There is plenty left to satisfy.

The question that everybody wants answered is: Is it better than "The Dark Knight Returns" ? My answer is it's on par with it.

9.title: A Stellar Film All Around
9.content:
What a movie. I am not exactly sure why some people are giving this movie such low reviews, perhaps there are just some people who cannot be pleased. I have always been a fan of Batman, but this movie brought it to a whole new level. As a Batman movie, it's unbelievable; everything a fan could ask for. As a motion picture, it's phenomenal, with great plot, character development, and a breath-taking score for the ages. Christopher Nolan has truly created an unparalleled superhero movie, to which composer Hans Zimmer has crafted an ingenious and compelling score.

The acting is truly spot on. Christian Bale is great as Bruce Wayne/Batman, and Michael Caine (Alfred) gives one of the most emotional performances I have ever seen. Anne Hathaway does a stellar job as Selena Kyle/Catwoman, and Tom Hardy's Bane is truly a force to be reckoned with. I went into this movie with significantly lower expectations than The Dark Knight (how could even Nolan top that?). Not only was I pleasantly surprised, I was astounded. A fantastic and satisfying ending to an unbelievable trilogy.

9.title: The perfect ending for a perfect trilogy
9.content:
'The Dark Knight Rises' is a brilliant film, the acting is top notch with everyone giving it their all, especially Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Tom Hardy who stood out the most. The films effects are great, creating a realistic Gotham City. The narrative/story is well constructed and produced which includes some twists along the way. The film also ties in some sub-story lines and hints at other things that are known for being in the Batman universe, such as Robin, which is great. The characters are developed brilliantly, making them believable and engaging.

The premise of the film is also great as it focuses on topics such as ethical, social and political issues rather than mindless action and explosions which are usually featured in Superhero films. Terrorism is also a big part of the film, which is portrayed through Bane perfectly. 'The Dark Knight Rises' also focuses more on the character Bruce Wayne rather than his Batman persona, which was surprising but in a good way as it's different to the typical, cliché superhero film.

'The Dark Knight Rises' is overall my favourite film of 2012 so far, it accomplishes everything possible for the Batman universe/franchise even if it was a bit too long. Christopher Nolan and the cast have done a great job at telling the dark side of Batman. I strongly recommend this film! Also if you're wondering I do believe that Heath Ledger's (R.I.P) performance as the Joker is better than Tom Hardy's as Bane, although both are brilliant. I also believe that both films are equally as good as they tell different chapters of Batmans life perfectly.

9.title: Anyone can be a hero. Even a man who put a coat around a young boy's shoulders to let him know the world hadn't ended
9.content:
I'm sorry if that's a spoiler, but I had to highlight one of my favorite moments of the movie. The way Batman reveals to Gordon that he is Bruce Wayne is just full of emotion. I mean, wow, this movie is on par with The Dark Knight and reveals what is for me the perfect and fitting ending to the whole Nolan saga!

The film debuted yesterday, July 27th here in my city, and I'm already feeling compelled to watch it again next week!

What a wonderful conclusion to a trilogy!!

And as for the comic book references, wow! We have Knightfall, we have Frank Miller's Dark Knight Returns, we have lots of key moments from other Batman stories involving characters like Alfred, and... man! We even have a veiled Robin reference in the movie! I won't tell you how the movie brings that up, but I promise you: you'll find it genius! I never imagined that Nolan would be able to work with so much and made it all perfect sense of it!!

I'm serious, 2:45 hours seems little for what is presented to us on screen! This man never ceases to amaze me!!

Thank you Nolan, thank you for another great, wonderful movie!

9.title: A Devastating fall and a heroic Rise
9.content:
As the finest among contemporary visionaries, Christopher Nolan's strength has always been the narration of an intricate story that often tends to tease the mind. From the story of his origins to his sacrifice for a city, Nolan had turned the Batman into the darker hero that DC Comics had portrayed in recent decades. Now, in a conclusion to his epic trilogy, Nolan proves that Bruce Wayne and Gotham need Batman to exist as a storm is set to come in the form of his most powerful enemy, Bane. Nolan takes his time with a plot-heavy narrative that introduces new characters, Bruce Wayne's return from isolation and Bane's unconvincing attempt to become the most threatening villain Gotham has ever seen. These processes make 'The Dark Knight Rises' an epic that isn't necessarily flawless. 'The Dark Knight Rises' is the arduous fall and eventual rise of Gotham's true hero and that journey is through dark introspection.

Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale) has become a recluse, confined in a section of Wayne Manor, limping with a broken body, the burden of Rachel's loss and Batman's sacrifice at the end of the previous saga that tarnished his image among the mob. After an unwarranted affair with investor Miranda Tate (Marion Cotillard), who salvaged the Enterprise's fortunes, Wayne recovers enough only to face Selina Kyle (Anne Hathaway), aka Catwoman, who deceives him by regularly stealing his belongings and warning him about an imminent storm that will overcome Gotham. Batman must return to face this new threat that has its foundation in the sewer network under Gotham but Bane is no ordinary mercenary. His assault on Gotham would bring annihilation and before The Batman can stop him, he will break him.

The essence of the film's story revolves around the need for Batman. The focus remains on The Dark Knight's return after years of self-banishment, then his devastating fall and finally his prolonged, yet epic rise as the hero. Adjacent to this plot-line is the support that develops for him with the Gotham Police Department under Commissioner Gordon(Gary Oldman) and Blake (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), Catwoman, Lucius Fox (Morgan Freeman) and of course, the heart of the film, Alfred (Michael Caine). These supporting characters do take up much of the screen time especially the Police Department, but without them, the Batman could not stand a chance against an enemy as brutal and indefatigable as Bane. Therein, also lies the film's most disappointing aspect. This grand villain for whom all this has built up. The Bane in DC Comic books was a giant compared to Batman. With the serum going into his body through tubes, his muscular bulk was intimidating and it even aided his intelligence greatly. However, Tom Hardy's Bane is merely the size of Batman, is in fact, slower in action and his plans of devastation are grand but we never got into his mind to see the evil developing. Besides, the voice dubbing was just ridiculous. Bane sounded polite and gentlemanly for some odd reason and more high pitched than the explosions he orchestrated. Bane was just Tom Hardy with a mask and a muffled voice. The evil wasn't just evil enough to be Gotham's reckoning and that's also why Heath Ledger's Joker is sorely missed.

Having said that, Christopher Nolan has not compromised in making this Rise an epic to behold. The opening sky-jacking sequence is nothing short of spectacular. The action with Batman is enthralling as he rides the Bat-pod through Gotham's streets with the entire Police Force chasing him, as he dodges an aerial assault while he maneuvers the Bat through Gotham's skyline and even while he fist fights with Bane. Then there are the explosions through the football field and across the city that are equally astounding. We only wish there was more of that rather than a love making scene with Tate.

Christian Bale handles the transition from a recluse to the rising hero with finesse. Bale's Bruce Wayne is flamboyant when rich but quite an introvert otherwise and darker when he is Batman. Gary Oldman as Commissioner Gordon has a chunkier role and has done justice to it. Joseph Gordon-Levitt has frankly had more time on screen than he deserved. Yet, it proves worthy when his future is revealed. Nevertheless, it's difficult to take him seriously as an Officer and a guardian. Anne Hathaway, as the conniving Catwoman or Selina Kyle is impressive. Far more than what Michelle Pfeiffer and Halle Berry were. Hathaway lends some liveliness and naughty charm to an otherwise somber and serious film. Marion Cotillard has a brief role but an important one. The twist in the story revolves around her and transforms her performance considerably. Morgan Freeman continues as Batman's 'Q' while Michael Caine is exemplary as Alfred, the film's subtle, emotional side. Nolan's version of Bane did not allow Tom Hardy to stand out as Batman's villain. Bane's destruction had a greater impact than his presence on screen. With the louder tone in post-production dubbing and an accent that sounds like an anti-villain, Tom Hardy just could not pull it off.

Warner Bros. Will be laughing like the Joker at the end of all this because Christopher Nolan delivered what we expected. Well, almost. The hype was immense, Batman was beaten half the time, the villain was nothing like the Joker and the film went through arduous lengths to conclude an epic trilogy of the Dark Knight. Yet, you will applaud at the end of it because it was quite a cinematic feat to engage the mob in such a spectacular, immersive manner. Nolan is a dream weaver and his work engages the mind tremendously. This may not be his most superior film yet but it's pretty darn close.

8.712 on a scale of 1-10.

9.title: Deh-shay, bah-sah-rah, bah-sah-rah
9.content:
The two years of wait bore fruit when once again we got to experience a magnum opus - The Dark Knight Rises, the final chapter in the greatest trilogy at the hands of undoubtedly the best director in the world right now, Christopher Nolan. I was fortunate enough to get to watch it in the opening weekend and without any spoilers.

To start with, the plot is complete, meticulously articulated and succeeds in keeping even the most seasoned movie-buffs guessing. Considering that there were no plans of making a sequel to TDK until Feb 2010, the flawless connections made to the story-line from previous two movies are appreciable. Each and every thread introduced, is tied into some knot in the end leaving the viewer content. After starting with a brilliant action sequence, the movie may seem a little slow, but its where Nolan weaves the web. It later picks up pace in its untangle and ends with a break-neck speed in a sensational and unprecedented climax. The action scenes are planted and carried out exceptionally well with the introduction of some cool new Bat-gadgets, which was one of the major attractions.

As each installment of the series is defined by the foes the Batman faces, this one is no different. The earlier parts were made memorable by a resolute Ra's al Ghul and the cunning Joker. Though the untimely demise of the legendary actor Heath Ledger and his unmatchable portrayal of the Joker in the previous edition had left a daunting task in front of the TDKR team in the villain department, I must say they have come up with an evil enough and certainly the toughest opponent Batman has ever faced, in Bane who, Unlike Joker, is a man with a plan.

The extent of thinking done in making the movie, be it a scene or the set or the background score is just mind-blowing. Nolan has brainstormed some clever usage of conditions bearing analogy with few of the things from earlier movies which make Bruce reprise the heroics he did when he began donning the hood, which was a masterstroke. Hans Zimmer (due to his and Nolan's chemistry, James Newton Howard refused to do scores for this movie, as he felt like a third wheel) has once again dug deep and brought up a complementing score, specially mentionable the chants for ' the rise '(which has thousands of fan voices recorded into it). Also, the IMAX scenes are a visual treat and ensure that the death of the IMAX camera, that Nolan broke in his experimentation, does not go in vain.

Talking of the actor-character chemistry- Christian Bale gives another stunning performance as Batman and far more mature one as Bruce Wayne. He is the new Mr. Dependable who never fails. And never before in the saga or in any other of the superhero movies, is the emotional battle of the hero in handling his alter ego shown as closely as in TDKR . The movie, as my friend points out, kinda resembles Batman Begins in that aspect. Unlike TDK, where we get vibes of watching the movie in third person. Michael Caine's intense and earnest portrayal of his character Alfred Pennyworth is surely worth every penny; Hats off to him! Gary Oldman (Commissioner Gordon), Morgan Freeman(Fox), Marion Cotillard (Miranda Tate) and Gordon-Levitt (Blake) carry out their job with no hiccups. Christopher Nolan certainly has a Midas touch when it comes to actors. Once an actor undergoes the Nolan treatment, he/she just blossoms through his/her career. We have seen that happen to Tom Hardy, Gordon Levitt and now with Hathaway. The best performers of the movie I think are Anne Hathaway and Tom Hardy for sure. The cat, I opine, is Hathaway's best performance till date. She has swayed the cat as if she owns it. Not only in using her feminine deceptive emoting but also in the kick-ass fight sequences in her stilettos, she seems so believable.

Last but not the least, Tom Hardy has brought to life another epic villain. Working in Nolan's biggest movie, playing the primary villain, and not having your face to act with is the toughest challenge an actor can face. With the script binding his face he had only eye-brows and voice to make do with, and boy! has he done wonders with it. His thunderous voice needs no background score. His physique rivals that of the masked vigilante and has emoted Bane's inspiration (which is one of the pivotal storyline aspect to lookout for) masterfully.

A standing ovation for this one. Go watch it if you haven't already. Nothing more i can say... Deh-shay, bah-sah-rah, bah-sah-rah !!!

9.title: Incredible
9.content:
Wow.

Coming out of the theater that's all I could say.

Just wow.

So many elements of this movie clicked perfectly, and very few missed.

The acting, and writing for the film was about as good as you're going to get. If this is Christian Bale and Christopher Nolan's farewell to Batman, then it's great that they went out with a bang.

The best part of the movie for me, just like in the Dark Knight, was the villain. Tom Hardy as Bane in my mind stole the show. He was the perfect rival to pit against Bruce Wayne. He pushed Wayne to his limits, not only physical but mentally. Anne Hathaway, who I have never been a big fan of, was great as Catwoman. She walked the perfect line of killer and sweetheart. Christian as Batman has once again, done nothing but impress. I still don't understand why Batman talks, scratch that, growls when he's talking to people who know he's Bruce Wayne... Gordon Joseph Levitt as Officer Blake was a great addition to the cast. The rest of the cast, Gary Oldman, Morgan Freeman, and Michael Caine just like in the two movies, were great in their roles. I did find, however, find Marion Cotillard as Miranda, to be an okay addition at best. And for people who saw The World is Not Enough, her role and interactions with certain characters will seem very familiar.

Overall it was one of, if not the, best movies this year. I wouldn't call it better than the Dark Knight, but then again that was one of the best movies of this generation.

I'd recommend this just about anyone.

9.title: Excellent conclusion to an astounding trilogy
9.content:
Having successfully avoided all hype behind this film, not seeing any trailers or reading any articles, I saw The Dark Knight Rises the day I returned from my month-long trip. The film was great. That's no surprise. How great though? Well...

I believe this film to be the weakest of the 3 Nolan Batman films, which is nothing to be ashamed of: it's like being the worst Lord of the Rings film, and I liked this significantly more than The Two Towers. All the Bale films deserve my 9s. But where Batman Begins had character and heart and The Dark Knight transcended the superhero sub-genre with the Joker, Dark Knight Rises is just an epic comic book story that wraps up the arcs and themes established by the trilogy while providing a villain who completely establishes a mood of hopelessness.

Nolan seems to have wanted to go out with a physical bang, and so the epic scale of this film increased. You may like this change to a bigger stage, but personally I didn't. The small hand to hand fights that were so captivating in Batman Begins and the set pieces of The Dark Knight seem small compared to some of the explosive events that occur in Dark Knight Rises, but this makes the smaller scenes in DKR less significant. It also seems that there's less actual Batman in the film: he takes a very long time to show up, then takes an extended break in the middle. This leads to much more support screen time: the new characters make the first 20 minutes tough to understand as many banker characters and police officers are indistinguishable. The new cast members also reduce scenes with favourites like Alfred and Commissioner Gordon. However, some may welcome the change of lead characters.

The story is strong, a complete package. There are slow segments, but the film is very satisfying, especially in its conclusion. As I've mentioned before, there is a relatively low percentage of Batman screen time. I hope you like Joseph Gordon- Levitt, as he has lots to do. The film also has a neat twist, though it doesn't really change much. There are small faults and unexplained actions, but nothing crucial. I'll say it again: the conclusion to the trilogy is remarkable in how it wraps up Bruce's story, while letting the audience make up in their minds what happens next for Gotham.

The acting is excellent. There's no Joker to tentpole performances, (and no one could possibly hope to follow up the Joker) but everyone pulls their weight, especially Bale in his best turn as Batman and Hathaway as Catwoman (though she's never called that). Even more than when I saw it, I'm really liking Bane's treatment, especially his curious voice and menacing mask.

The action and technical work, visual and audio, are supreme. The cinematography is masterful. Nothing else needs to be said about that.

According to Nolan, pain, both physical and mental, is the main idea of the film. I found there to also be a positive message of hope in one fitting word, "rise". I like the positive end to such a dark series, one of the greatest trilogies of all time, the best comic book films of all time developed by one of the greatest movie-making teams of all time.

8.7/10

9.title: Awesome movie but certainly not the best...missed a few tricks!
9.content:
A very difficult movie to pull it off, considering TDK's success and the unbelievable expectations from every1. The movie overall is a masterpiece which keeps pounding your heart with general fear and vulnerability in the air (Thanks to Hans Z). But sadly it is a bit disappointing that after coming this far Nolan gave it away...what could have been truly a legendary movie. Letdown #1 Turning Bane into just a pawn was scripted to pull in a surprise but it down weighed the villain's overall impact. Throughout the movie you have this biggie who seems invincible and all powerful and suddenly you turn him into a mere physical power house working for someone else. Wrong move. Letdown #2 The phenomenon "The Dark Knight Rises" should have been more intensely captured. The building getting lit up with batman symbol was good but more needed to be done - people on the streets, getting inspired and charged up ready to wage the war. I think it was captured at 60-70%. Letdown #3 The biggest letdown was the final action scene. It was supposed to be a War as Batman clearly envisioned, but what turned out to be was a mini battle over a small area. This scene should have been more grand, compelling and hair raising with probably commoners joining them, loads of lives should have been lost and an impossible battle should have been won against all odds. Probably, Nolan was restricted by time or something but it took away the ultimate punch!

Yet, you have a stunning final touch to the trilogy. Thats the beauty of Nolan.

9.title: Because an Epic Film is Epic
9.content:
It felt like I was waiting for this release for a lifetime.. well in real since the time it was announced to come out. I am now a very impatient guy so decided not to rely on my friends to get a ticket to its screening or to wait for a decent print to come out and downloaded a cam rip of it. Sad I know. But it was worth it actually worth more.

But the movie was just plain awesome, no it can't be compared to Heath Ledger's Dark Knight, but truly a matching conclusion to the one of the best series of movies ever made.

From bane's presumably muffled voice to rise of allegedly dry Bruce Wayne, the entire runtime of the film keeps you tied to your seat. Anna Heathway as CatWoman was just a cherry on the top of this delicious cake. In contrast to what other reviews would tell you about plot holes in DKR, there were none. It was made as a movie, it was a movie and it had flaws like a movie should have. People would criticize it for an over-dramatic strike on Gotham's Stock Exchange, Catwoman's lavish lifestyle despite of living in a slum, shady bankruptcy of Bruce Wayne, sudden development of Tate's character etc. But these weren't flaws, these were just speed of a fast paced plot. You can't expect Nolan to show each and every second of every character's life, some you have to develop through your common sense.

If watched in the right frame of mind, DKR truly proves itself to be an inspirational peace. It hits people with a down syndrome as a hope to rise again. Nolan successfully portrays that times are never dark for anyone, forgotten people have their true chance of rise once again provided they find the right motivation. For Bruce Wayne it was a reality slap that his efforts of raising hope in people of Gotham without leaving a successor were shallow and his belief on people to be good were just baseless. Then he rises putting his trust in people who are willing to change, people who are burglars on face and angels at hearts. Sigh I can't put enough words in how inspiring the movie personally was for me.

*Quote* Why do we fall? So that we can learn to pick ourselves up *End Quote*

9.title: "The greatest film of this decade, the greatest action film of all time..."
9.content:
The Dark Knight rises is a perfect ending to an awe-inspiring series that is Batman. The plot line splits into many and comes back together seamlessly, with little plot holes or confusion. The inclusion of Catwoman and Robin makes the series embrace the comics and serves as a fitting ending to the trilogy. This is the best film of the decade, the best action film of all time.

The plot lives up to the film's title, with Batman coming out of retirement and Robin taking his place giving everybody a great sense of closure and stratification to this fantastic trilogy,with all the plot lines closing so there are no questions left to be answered.

A true sense of fear is brought to the film, and the hopelessness to victory was a great watch, conveyed in a longer time, which I always like to see. The hostage of the city was plausible, and the action scenes great.

My hat's off Nolan, already he is becoming one of the greatest directors of all time. Bring on Man of Steel!

9.title: Epic Finale
9.content:
It's tricky to have a thriving trilogy yet Nolan has effectively fulfilled the Batman legend with style.

No one has ever taken super-hero based movies seriously until we got introduced to Batman Begins. Staying true to the origin of the cape crusader Christopher Nolan has taken us deep into the world of Bruce Wayne's fractured life & his reason to fight injustice under the hood of shadowy vigilante. With a fitting foundation we were offered with the next installment which will always remain as the Holy Grail to all batman fans & movie fanatics alike. Even today, The Dark Knight not only stands out as the best graphic novel adaptation but also as a dark intricate notable crime chronicle. It's regrettable to miss prodigy like Heath Ledger whose feat as the Joker has immortalized one of the best screen play villain in recent times.

Plot : It has been eight years since Batman vanished from Gotham City after taking blame for crimes committed by late Two Face/Harvey Dent. When a mystifying cat burglar going with the name Selina Kyle forces herself into Wayne Manor, Bruce senses sinister plot however arrival of a masked radical named Bane & his rebellious army compels Bruce to put on the cape for one last time in order to shield the very city which once branded him an enemy, based on lies engineered by Commissioner Gordon for greater good as we know from last chapter.

It is recommended to be well versed with Batman Begins as lots of reference takes queue to conclude the story arc. Stakes were higher for making this film as the anticipation had built up from past few years hoping for a great grandiose finale. Nolan has accomplished to bring this story to yet another level which very few have tried to gamble. Unlike the 2nd installment The Dark Knight Rises plays heavy on script with various twists & the last half an hour is nothing short of spectacular. It is unreasonable to compare Bane's character next to Joker. Tom Hardy succeeded to flesh out Bane as shear brute where physical intimidation plays a key role. The fight between Bane & Batman is one of the most imposing moments in Rises where it taunts us by showing that even heroes can be bested. Anne Hathaway as Selina Kyle grounded the character not just as grifter but also as a classic movie femme fatale. Keeping true to the rational world of Nolan she delivers a striking show. Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Officer Blake is one of the new additions to this saga & plays an integral part. Christian Bale as Bruce Wayne pulls off yet another marvelous act & does justice to cape crusader's tale. Apart from brilliant performance from other supporting casts the soundtrack set by Hans Zimmer is beyond doubt, epic.

This is a story which showcase us how Batman has affected the society & how Bruce has to deal with new threat & decide whether he shall return to save Gotham. The Dark Knight Rises is a multi layered story with massive amount of action, something which we have experienced in Nolan's other chartbusters. It's really amazing to see how the movie brings everything to full circle. Let's just say, the final installment proves to be a fitting conclusion to one of the greatest trilogy in modern times.

9.title: The weak link of the trilogy, but still an awesome Batman movie.
9.content:
The Dark Knight Rises is the conclusion to Christopher Nolan's trilogy of Batman movies. I absolutely loved the first two, Batman Begins and The Dark Knight. I'd go as far as to call them perfectly done Batman movies. Unfortunately, The Dark Knight in particular set a pretty high standard for itself, and I think from the beginning it was hard for Rises to top it. But after seeing it twice now, Rises is easily my least favorite of the trilogy, and the only one that I actually had problems with.

The Dark Knight Rises takes place a whole eight years after The Dark Knight. Gotham City is in peace time, and has been thriving on the lie that was created for it by Batman. Because of it though, Bruce Wayne hasn't put on the Batman suit in eight years, and has since become a recluse. He's forced to return, however, when a terrorist known as Bane invades Gotham and intends to destroy it.

I will say, before I get into my nitpick problems, that this movie is still definitely awesome. Just because it's not up to the standard of the first two doesn't mean I didn't still love it. There's a lot to enjoy in Rises. There's epic moments, great action, rich character interactions, fitting music, and some really memorable scenes. When characters go through pain, you feel it with them.

The cast didn't disappoint at all either. The returning players delivered everything you'd expect from them. Christian Bale as Bruce Wayne/Batman (possibly his best performance of the trilogy honestly), Michael Caine as Alfred, Gary Oldman as Gordon, and Morgan Freeman as Lucius Fox, all of them were just as great as they were before. The newcomers were just as great. Joseph Gordon-Levitt plays a new cop named John Blake, and he honestly carried the movie by himself at certain times. Tom Hardy plays the villain Bane, and although I wasn't as much of a fan of the character as I expected to be, Hardy's performance was awesome. He has a mask on the whole time, so a lot of his acting is simply done with his eyes, and it's so easy to overlook how great he does it. And finally, Anne Hathaway plays Catwoman...err, Selina Kyle. Her character honestly might have been my favorite in the movie. Hathaway just really delivered and exceeded expectations, and she was just a real treat to watch.

Now, to some of the things I didn't like. These are all minor things, and as such I really didn't have any MAJOR problems with the movie. There were just a collection of minor things that tended to irk me.

For one thing, the movie runs at almost three hours long. Movie length doesn't bother me, it's that even at that long of a runtime the movie still felt slow for the first hour, and then rushed for the rest of it. I just feel like they tried to squeeze way too much plot into one movie, and so if some stuff was cut, I think it would have been beneficial. I think one thing that could have helped that is cutting out a character, Miranda Tate. If I could pick one character that really just wasn't that interesting, it'd be her.

I also feel like they spent too much time explaining some thing, and then not enough explaining others. The movie is very dialogue-heavy, and normally I love dialogue a lot, but it just seemed to be put in the wrong places at some points. Sometimes images speak more than words, and I think that's what this needed at times.

The editing was terrible at times. The movie didn't do well with time lapses, because it actually takes place over the course of about half a year, and it didn't feel like that a lot of the time. And then other time lapses honestly made no sense. There's a scene where a stock market is being attacked (no spoilers, it's in the trailers), and it's day time. It's said in the movie that only eight minutes pass in there, and yet when they leave it's pitch dark night time. That's just lazy editing.

The sound editing bothered me too. There's times when it's hard for characters to be understood. The biggest offender of this is Bane. Since he has a mask on, his voice was created in the sound editing process. There's times when it's hard to understand him, and then there's times where he sounds like he's talking on a microphone, even in the opening scene when he has a bag on his head and his voice should be muffled. I don't blame Tom Hardy for this, I blame the sound editing guys.

Finally, I hated the ending. Not completely, but certain aspects of it. Still, I can't go into details without spoiling it. Basically though, something that goes in hand with that, is that I don't mind when a superhero movie changes the mythology, as long as it's done well. And, I wasn't a fan of how it was done here.

It may seem like there's a lot I hated about the movie, but really there wasn't. These are all just minor complaints, and really a lot of them I didn't notice until I thought about it more later on. It's still an awesome movie, and I do have to say I think it was a fitting conclusion to the Batman trilogy.

9.title: When Gotham is in ashesYou'll have my permission to die.....
9.content:
A few days ago, this is what I said ,"Markets plummet, countries come crashing down, jobs decrease, but 'the dark knight rises', always.."

After watching the movie, I believe that the Dark Knight NEVER EVER disappoints, he always lives upto his image. May His Soul Rest in Peace, but this movie didn't need a Heath Ledger!! Though Joker overshadowed Batman in the 'The Dark Knight', this movie was totally about the Caped Crusader himself.

After watching this movie, I must say 'In Nolan, We Trust'!!! The guy knew he had a huge responsibility towards his fans, and with such amazing prequels such as 'Batman Begins' and 'The Dark Knight', he must be under tremendous pressure to deliver a movie that can equal what he did in his prequels. And I must say, though difficult, he more that succeeded by giving us a movie with high emotional content and super classy effects

Casted as a murderous evil shadow, Bruce Wayne hangs his boots of being the Righteous Henchman (maim, not kill!!) for the City of Gotham and leads a life of a recluse. Gotham itself is complacent about its security as there has been a sharp drop in organized crime. But it is a lull before a storm..

And that storm is BANE (Tom Hardy)

Effective in his loud bass like voice (when he speaks, it's sort of creepy!!), with a hideous protruding gas mask covering his face, awesome fighting prowess- he fights like a bull, carrying along with him the momentum and quick reflexes. The way he takes control of the entire Gotham city is awesome

The clash between Batman and Bane is worth every penny

The female leads of the movie are sexy and svelte. Both Anne Hathaway (Selena or the Bat Girl!!) and Marion Cotillard (as Miranda) did their part extremely well (if I mention anything further, it would be considered as a SPOILER!!)

Gary Oldman (as Commissioner Gordon), Morgan Freeman (as Fox) and Michael Caine (as Alfred) essayed their roles perfectly.

A special mention here of Joseph Gordon-Levitt (as Blake, a.k.a?!!!), watch out for this character- he has larger role to play

But more than anything, it's Christian Bale who takes away the cake as the Batman. This is THE BEST SUPERHERO MOVIE SERIES!!! And Christian Bale has a very large part in making this blockbuster an Epic.

The Batman rules and I ask the other next-door friendly superheroes (Spiderman, Ironman, Hulk, etc.) to take a bow

Christopher Nolan- Respect!!!!! For me- he is in the same league as Steven Spielberg and James Cameron. And I must say, he has consistently given us some extremely good movies (Best of luck for 'Man of Steel')

The Batman series have been a helluva ride.

Saddened by the prospect that it's over

But I sense a new beginning at the horizon, from ash will rise the Phoenix..

Lastly, I have but one thing to say, "When Gotham is in ashesYou'll have my permission to die."

9.title: The Dark Knight Rises...An apt justice to the Title
9.content:
Firstly this is the first time I am writing a review for a movie so please forgive me for my mistakes.

The first thing that attracts me the most after watching this movie is the title of the movie.For me this movie aptly justifies the mere existence of Batman(the man behind the mask).This movie makes you feel that it could well be you who can be behind the mask of Batman.It's more of Bruce Wayne than Batman who dominates the movie for me.Christian bale is Superb as Bruce Wayne.He really shows how good an actor he really is with his understated yet dominant performance in this movie.

Then again the world depicted in the movie is so engaging and made so realistic that everyone would get sucked into it and would never want to get out of it.

The story itself is portrayed wonderfully tying up each and every end with a suitable cause.There are a lot of characters in this movie yet it feels real coz everyone has a single motive either to save or to destroy Gotham city.

I would not go into the details of every character as it would spoil excitement of those who haven't yet watched it.

One small thing which I feel was not fully used was the character of Blake played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt.Yet after watching the movie the only thing that comes to mind is THE DARK KNIGHT RISES...Please go and see this movie this will linger in your mind longer than The Dark Knight(Although The Joker remains the best villain ever portrayed in a movie).

9.title: A Satisfying and Epic conclusion to one of the greatest Trilogies of all time
9.content:
I'm impressed more than ever. This movie was a fun ride all the way. It started off slow, and then lead into the final in a very unique and pleasant way. The movie ran a full circle. Everything was superior from the actors, to acting, action sequences, atmosphere, dialogue, character development, plot, etc.

I loved the plot twists, IMO. There were at least 3 or 4 main plot twists, all which occurred at the end of the film. I was blown away by the final twist. I won't mention anything here, because I don't want to ruin anything for anyone.

Not only that I loved the dialogue. Especially by Alfred in one of his last scenes with Bruce. It was very emotional indeed, and very good. I also loved the atmosphere. The movie was building up the suspense minute after minute. Especially when the movie was approaching the end, that's when the suspense was at its highest level. Everyone was glued to their seats, without saying a word, and without doing anything. My eyes were glued to the screen like never before.

The movie ran a full circle. TDKR was strongly connected to both Batman Begins, and TDK. This movie ran a full circle by revisiting BB, and TDK, and this completed the circle.

When I saw this in IMAX I was blown away. All of the special effects, and action scenes were presented in a very good fashion. I really loved the football explosion scene, as well as the chase scenes.

If I were to compare this with TDK, obviously TDK will win, because of Heath Ledger's flawless performance as the Joker. However the strong points of this movie were Character Development, and Atmosphere. The character development was unbelievable, yet real. It showed how Bruce returned, then fell short of his abilities, and finally got defeated. But then got back up slowly, and won the battle with the help of many others. The atmosphere was very serious. There were no funny parts, and even if there were any then they would be early in the film. It was very thrilling, and kept building the suspense.

The movie started off slowly, then when Batman got captured it was even more slow, however by the time it reached the final act, the movie picked up the speed by a lot. In the final act you were introduced to many plot twists, and that was very thrilling. Some of the twists might have been predictable, but the others were totally unpredictable, IMO.

Overall I would say this movie was very good. It was beyond good, indeed. I will give it a 9/10. One point is off, because of the slow parts, and plot holes. However the ending was the best ending to the best trilogy. Fantastic job Nolan. You presented us the best trilogy with a perfect ending. Bravo!

9.title: Worth seeing in the theaters
9.content: This movie was one of the best movies of the year. It was a fantastic end to The Dark Knight franchise. The theater experience is only a benefit to an already outstanding movie. The plot was well developed and the dialogue was very realistic. Tom Hardy did a fantastic job as Bane> it was very hard to match Heath Ledger's performance of the Joker, but I think Tom did the best job possible. The only reasons that I did not give this movie ten stars is because of two things. 1. It was very difficult to understand Bane through his mask in some parts. He was a very sinister and well played character, but his words don't sound like English when he talks a lot at one time. 2. The way Bane died in the movie was to quick for me. All of a sudden Catwoman comes out of no where and blows a hole in his stomach. Batman should have kicked his ass to death. Otherwise the movie was phenomenal. GO SEE IT TODAY!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

9.title: The best movie I ve watched in a while
9.content:
It has been quite sometime since I 've seen a movie that inspired me enough to write about it. The Dark Knight Rises is one such wonderful movie. It combines great story telling on a huge scale with exceptional acting by some of the finest actors of this generation and a haunting musical score. Usually when something is eagerly expected, it seldom lives up to its expectations. I waited for the release of this movie with fevered anticipation and was not at all disappointed.

Comic book movies are usually imbued with a sense of juvenility, a silliness that asks us not to take them seriously and usually, that makes the movie going experience incredibly fun. The Nolan trilogy, however is dark, grave and almost melancholy. It is serious and appeals more to the intellectual side of the viewer. That is what sets this film and its prequels apart from the myriad comic book inspired movies out there.

Every moment of this film is engrossing and you can t help but get invested emotionally in the story. ( When Michael Caine cries at the grave " I 've failed you , Master Bruce" - did you not get misty eyed ?? ) Christian Bale as Bruce Wayne/Batman is sensational. His acting is restrained and nuanced. Think about it - do you think you could ever feel sorry for a billionaire who has cool gadgets, an awesome crib and coolest cars in the world? - But you genuinely do. Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman and Gary Oldman play their parts like the seasoned veterans they are. Tom Hardy had pretty big shoes to fill as he had to follow Heath Ledger's Joker as the villain in this movie. He does a respectable job as the malevolent Bane but I missed that indescribable something extra that Heath Ledger brought to the Dark Knight. His villainy seemed all the more evil because it had no purpose, no goal, no end game.

Nolan's films work on many different levels. They have all the earmarks of a traditional superhero movie - a city under attack, really cool fights, car ( if i can use the word car ) chases, ridiculously awesome modes of conveyance ( Seriously, how cool were the Bat and the Bat bike ) and good looking women. They also can be viewed as an allegory of the times we live in. The mob taking over the city is eerily reminiscent of the anarchy during the riots in the UK. His films also bring to the fore the inner demons most of us harbour and make them all seem oddly personal.

I see and hear about fans of the Star Wars Franchise who collect memorabilia, attend conventions dressed up as characters in the movie and get married at Star Wars themed weddings. I never understood what made them so attached to the movies. [ Honestly - the movies were probably great when they were first released decades ago but now they seem ( dare I say it ) ...ahem .... lame. Star Wars worshipers please don t kill me. ]. I understand now. This trilogy made me realise that we can genuinely like something so much that we would seem overzealous to others.

I can say with little doubt that this trilogy will become something akin to the Star Wars of this generation, though I seriously doubt if the fans of batman will ever be as crazy as the Star Wars fans. I certainly hope that no blogger, in the future, has the temerity to call these films lame. Only Time will tell.

9.title: A great finish to a great series.
9.content:
The epic conclusion to Nolan's Batman saga was heavy and nimble at the same time. With a runtime of 164 minutes, when the end credits roll, all you're left with is wonder. Is it as good as 'The Dark Knight'? Perhaps not, in terms of performance and wit. But yes, in terms of scale, impact and depth.

'The Dark Knight' was more focused on external entities that challenge Batman. But 'The Dark Knight Rises' is all about Batman himself. The story, as we all know, is about a masked villain (Bane) who threatens to annihilate Gotham with a timed nuclear device. Batman, who was nursing his emotional and physical wounds in quite seclusion following the demise of Rachel Dawes, is forced out of his hiding to tackle Bane. Selina Kyle, who is occasionally mentioned as 'Cat Burglar' (and not Cat Woman), comes to his aide, although in the very end. So does Commissioner Gordon, John Blake (the new guy, a clean and honest cop played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt) and Lucius Fox. Suffice to say, the outline of the story itself is filled with numerous twists and surprises... so much so that it is almost impossible to provide a plot summary without dishing out life threatening spoilers. But... it was a hell of a ride!

I must say that on a few occasion, the character of Selina Kyle serves as a pleasant reminder of our favorite villain-in-a-makeup from TDK. Anne Hathaway, take a bow. However, her character develops very differently towards the end. Nolan hits it out of the stands with the surprise twist he pulls on Marion Cotillard's character. Tom Hardy has a very difficult job portraying a villain from within that mask. I understand it is very difficult to emote/act with just your eyes and forehead exposed, but he manages fine. As some critics had pointed out, Bane did seem a little one dimensional. But we feel that because we take 'Joker' as the precedence... a very unfair comparison! Michael Caine, as Alfred, gets to bring his histrionics out of the bag in this movie. I doubt if the drama was really that necessary! Gary Oldman has some pretty intense moments in this movie. I was rather worried that his acting skills were quite underutilized in the previous Batman movies. But TDKR gets him to perform like the fine actor he is. Joseph Gordon- Levitt and Morgan Freeman are very appropriate with their acting. Marion Cotillard fails to leave a lasting impact in the final few minutes where she could have really made a difference! But I guess that's because Nolan didn't want her to. It has always been his style to downplay the obvious.

The action sequences were good. But when was a Nolan movie all about explosions and martial arts? The real show stopper has always been the screenplay, weaved together by crisp editing and the very involving music of Hans Zimmer. The prevailing metaphor of economic crisis is occasionally stark, particularly so when Oldman delivers the 'help- coming-from-inside-Gotham' speech to Matthew Modine. As expected from Nolan, the story works on different levels to create a host of captivating impressions on the viewers mind.

On a different note, Bruce Wayne's efforts to escape from the prison could have been made a little shorter. That episode seemed to drag a little longer than required (just a personal opinion). But Christian Bale's depiction of Bruce Wayne is the strongest in TDKR. His chemistry with Cotillard was quite fascinating, but that again is subject to the plot twist I will not disclose here. Performance wise, my personal favorite from the entire movie is Anne Hathaway hands down. Unlike 'Inception', Nolan does not end this movie with a question mark. He removes all doubts with the final scene, as if to declare his exeunt from the Batman arena. All said and done, the trilogy does leave scope for extension but I don't think Nolan will be interested.

Now that the series comes to an end, we are left to wonder at the scale of this trilogy. A comic hero movie that gets as acclaimed as 'Godfather', 'Shawshank Redemption' or 'Schindler's List', an action movie series that has moved both critics and younger viewers alike... what a terrific achievement for a director and a screenplay writer! This should win some Oscars, but if it doesn't, no one cares. The Dark Knight did rise in this movie, perhaps above and beyond the altitude of all other super heroes in the history of Hollywood.

(P.S - Unless you talk about the nagging void left by one particular character in the series... miss you Mr. Ledger!)

9.title: The Dark Knight Rises
9.content:
To relaunch a well loved story and do it right is an immense task. To carry the story on and make an even better film in the progress is monumental. To finish that story and do it right is akin to climbing Mount Everest by hopping on one leg.

With "The Dark Knight Trilogy", Christopher Nolan has done all this and more. He has cemented his place in the history books by creating a franchise of intelligent comic book films, adding them to his rostra of intellectual blockbusters. Most importantly, with "The Dark Knight Rises", Nolan has once again made an excellent film to add to an extraordinary canon: "Memento", "Insomnia", "Batman Begins", "The Prestige", "The Dark Knight", "Inception". He is the rightful owner to the title of Greatest Film Maker of the moment; a modern day Scorcese with a traditionally epic view of films such as DeMille would have been proud of.

This is not to say that there aren't problems with the film; the script, though keeping you guessing throughout most of the plot, is let down but not in a traditional sense. More, it is the mythology of the Batman story that hinders it. Such was the problem with the introduction of Harvey Dent in "The Dark Knight"; knowing the story of this tragic character automatically overshadowed him with the spectre of Two Face. Yet Nolan used this to his advantage, making sure the audience weren't treated like idiots because of it, and making the excellent choice to give the Joker no back story whatsoever to counter-balance this. In "The Dark Knight Rises", if you know the mythology, then a few characters appearance will be more obvious than others.

Despite this, once again the story is treated as realistically as if it was a modern-day thriller. Batman as a character is perhaps (at a stretch) one of the most believable comic book heroes; he has no super powers, he is spurred on by his own tragedy, his own darkness. The characters around him, particularly the villains, are influenced and inspired by this darkness; some for good - an aspiring, perhaps slightly naive police officer played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt is excellent support, and Gary Oldman is once again great as Comissioner Gordon.

The ones whose motives are less than desirable are also treated with great care and attention. Tom Hardy's Bane has come under a lot of scrutiny due to the mask the actor wears, but more of his dialogue can be heard clearly than previously reported. Besides, one COULD be cynical and suggest that this is another ploy by Nolan to get you to come and watch the film again just to try and catch every sentence, but that's probably going too far. Hardy gives an unusually restrained performance as this psychopath, his accent unclear as to where he exactly comes from, but a brutal, brooding force who is determined to reach his goal, whatever the cost.

For myself, however, there are three stand out performances; Anne Hathaway as Selina Kyle, who we KNOW is Catwoman yet is never defined as such, gives a sensual, streetwise kick to the character and should play this kind of character more often, not least because she looks stunning in the costume. Michael Caine as Alfred could be forgiven for simply turning up yet manages to bring quite a few tears to the eye as someone watching the closest person he has to a son potentially head to their grave.

But the film belongs to Batman, and that's thanks to Christian Bale. If he was overshadowed by Heath Ledger's excellent performance in "The Dark Knight", here he takes the film back for the vigilante and rises victoriously. In fact, sadly one of the things the film really lacks is a performance like Ledger, such was the power there. Still, Bale growls and grimaces, contemplates and sacrifices. It takes a good forty minutes for Batman to actually appear - a brave decision by Nolan - and the film really examines what it means to fight for good in a corrupt world by mirroring Batman's fight with Bane's more villainous revolution.

The set pieces are stunning, in particular a memorable scene in a football stadium, and its refreshing that Nolan refuses to go down the 3D road. Hans Zimmer's score pounds away with rough, tribal chants and violence. When it comes to the ending, some would argue that Nolan perhaps goes too far. But the important thing to realise is that he has ended this franchise, he has ended this trilogy. The question now is, for Nolan, where the hell does he go from here? 9/10

9.title: Outstanding
9.content:
Just caught the premiere of The Dark Knight Rises in PVR with my brother-in-law last night and I simply stand in awe of what I witnessed. It was one of the most absorbing work of cinema I have ever seen. Chris Nolan has excelled himself as a director. The fact that he is one of the most talented appears from the stats themselves. Nolan uses the acting skills of Christian Bale to perfection when the Batman was man handled by the intimidating figure of Bane. Oldman, Freeman & Caine are crafty as usual. I am a movie freak and cannot stay until I watch at least two movies a day. But I ain't watching any movie for a day or two. I simply want to stay put keeping this movie capture my mind. A must see!

9.title: Is it any good though?
9.content:
You can probably tell by the number of stars I've given it that my answer is yes. But was it an entirely satisfying conclusion? I write this just over 24 hours after I saw the movie in glorious IMAX, and I still can't answer that question. Don't get me wrong, it was epic film-making - the kind of film you don't come out of regretting that you paid good money to go and see it. I could reel off a number of positive descriptive words that have already been used by critics and fans on this site, but that of course would be boring.

I came away from the cinema feeling a little exhausted - partly because Chrisopher Nolan and his colleagues seemed intent on Bane-smashing our senses to a pulp, but also because I couldn't help but feel there was too much going on this film. Not like Spiderman 3, but certainly enough for me to drift off from the film a few times. Now I've read quite a few pieces of criticism from people/critics that say of certain scenes "urgh that's not very realistic" or "he wouldn't heal that quickly" etc etc. I'm not here to wave a big Plot Hole flag at entirely pathetic and minor issues. To paraphrase Nicholson's Joker, in what kind of a world do we live where a man dresses up as a bat?! And to answer, we don't. The Dark Knight Rises is a piece of fiction based on a comic book. It isn't realistic. Nolan's trilogy may be more believable for sure, but I still can't find Gotham on Google Maps if you know what I mean...

What slightly marred the film for me was the flow of it. I would have been quite happy if this film had been 15-20 minutes longer perhaps just so they could take their time with a few of the story arcs and not rush around like they did. I know that it might not have been a popular idea to have a film over 3 hours long. Perhaps the Studio applied pressure to cut down the running time. But on the other hand I also thought there were a few scenes/characters which could have been cut altogether, like Matthew Modine's Deputy Commissioner Foley or Cillian Murphy's Dr Crane. I felt they didn't really add anything to the film.

Also, as much as I like Joseph Gordon-Levitt, his character was given an unnecessary amount of screen-time in my opinion. Some of the characters we had come to know and love were occasionally benched to make way for John Blake. (I understand why they did this for sure - I just didn't like it.)

So was the film any good? Absolutely.

Was it a satisfying end? ...err.....I honestly couldn't tell you. Yes and no?

Does Alfred's performance make a grown man want to have a little weep? Too right! (the only other film I've wept in is Team America, but for significantly different reasons).

Did it follow the age-old Original Star Wars model of a strong opener, better sequel and weak conclusion? I would say yes - but I would go as far as saying the Dark Knight Trilogy is better than the Star Wars Trilogy, and The Dark Knight Rises a great deal better than Return of the Jedi.

Sorry to be boring but The Dark Knight Rises is engrossing, magnificent, and a breath-taking experience. And as for it's flaws - nothing that a Director's Cut wouldn't fix.

9.title: The Batman is back !!
9.content: Great action-packed movie from beginning to end. Enjoyment factor easily surpasses the first two installments of the franchise. Almost all of the familiar characters, portrayed by the original actors, are back and they are all better developed. The Bat Cave is back, the mansion rebuilt (finally) and the gadgets abound. It's engrossing, good dialog, great screenplay, lots of heroics and some good plot twists. 2 hours 40 minutes flew by like it was only 90 minutes and there didn't seem to be any wasted energy or low spots throughout the film. The plot unfolded in a logical and dynamic manner. There have been a number of flaws pointed out by other reviews (haters) at this venue but I don't think that it's fair to over criticize. I enjoyed it for what it is, a decent final chapter to a trilogy which is based on a comic book hero. I saw it on a huge screen featuring the new Sony digital projection and sound system in stadium seating. It was epic and worth the price of admission. Action films don't get much better than this. See it.

9.title: Allows you to say it really is an Awesome Batman Trilogy Sart to Finish
9.content:
The Dark Knight Rises I personally feel didn't have high expectations because of The Dark Knight, even though its possibly one of the best films ever made, but its expectations were set from the third trailer of the film. I have rarely seen a trailer which I can say is possibly better than some complete movies I have seen. It is safe to say that it lived up to these expectations through flying colour's.

The action was immense. Bain strength pushing Batmans, to the limit, both mentally and physically. The Anarchy of The Dark Knight wasn't in Rises, but it never should have been, Bain's approach is completely different. You did feel throughout the film, yourself questioning how far Batman could go to take on the brute strength of Bain without questioning what he stood for himself. The scenes between Bain's Henchmen and Gotham's Police force are some of the best scenes from any hero movie to be created, and there were enough scenes to allow you feeling you were in the thick of the action rather than just watching over it. But is was also great to have some humour mixed in to the bleak times, through the use of catwoman.

But where Rise's was at its best was when it was looking at its characters beliefs and emotions. This was especially true with the major players. Batman's dilemma around how to finish Bain, Catwoman and where her loyalty lies, Bain's belief in what he is doing and what he wants to take from it, Alfred and how he wants his adopted son Bruce, to lead his life. Blake, the list can go on and on, all these and more make The Dark Knight rises stand out when beliefs are confronted and questioned. And all the actors and actresses allow these questions to feel genuine, unlike other action films where your asked to accept straight away who is the villain and who is the hero.

The only things that stop it getting 10/10 are a few minor details. Very very occasionally I felt Bains mask did get in the way of understanding what he was saying, I wished there had been more of a back story to catwoman as there had been to Bain, and maybe they could have used Scarecrow more than how they did.

But to put simply it brings Begins and The Dark Knight, mixes the two up to create an amazing piece of film that takes you on one hell of a journey start to finish. Easily one of the the best 'Super'hero movie and trilogy's ever created. Overall 9/10.

9.title: Loved everything, except for the feminist Bullshit
9.content: CAUTION: CONTAINS SPOILERS Everything in this movie was great except for one thing - the feminist bullshit - and I am not talking about Catwoman. I didn't mind Catwoman's over-the-top-testosterone-male-hating portrayal. The really annoying feminist twist was at the end, when we find out that it was not Bain that escaped from the prison; it was Ra's al Ghul's pathetic daughter. Bain was an amazing villain who clearly had as much spirit and dedication as Bruce Wayne. So why detract from the character by saying Ghul's daughter "made the jump" and not him? Otherwise, women everywhere will become the brainless sex slaves of men. I can't believe Nolan fell for that stupid piece of political correctness.

9.title: The Dark Knight Rises is a splendid finale that had surprised me from beginning to end. Don't Miss It!
9.content: Batman finally returns 8 years after the Joker and Harvey (Two-Face) Dent terrorized Gotham City (4 years to us) in the brilliantly dark "The Dark Knight". Now Christopher Nolan returns to Gotham, bigger and darker than ever with his conclusion of his "Batman" trilogy that began with the incredible "Batman Begins". "The Dark Knight Rises" is a splendid finale that will surprise you and will make you stand up and cheer. In short: It's a crowd-pleaser, however it lacks the edginess and the brilliance of "The Dark Knight", but the brutality and the corruption of power is certainly there. Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman (Christian Bale) has retired from being Batman after the death of Harvey Dent, which forces him to take the blame for that, causing the Gotham City Police to chase after him. But will Batman ever come back? Takes too long for us to figure this out, but it will happen. Anyway, a new terror comes to town: A hulking, face-covered hoodlum known as Bane (a superior Tom Hardy) who comes to watch Gotham crumble down to rubble and nothingness with a deadly force that could destroy the city. Commissioner Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman) and police officer John Blake (a perfectly-cast Joseph Gordon-Levitt) team up to stop Bane and to save Gotham. Also, along for the ride is Selina Kyle, a.k.a Catwoman (The scene-stealing Anne Hathaway), who is a sexy thief dressed in a catsuit with a heart of gold and her sassiness to boot. She teams with the Batman, which will force Bruce Wayne to deal with giving Gotham City a new hero or to remain in the shadows forever. At 165 minutes, "The Dark Knight Rises" focuses more of the character-development and mood, rather than the plot, which is a good one. It's big, explosive and loud, but in the right sense. The brutal violence, the emotional drama and its darker moods are a rather splendid fit and it had surprised me from beginning to its (shocking, but true) conclusion. I think Christopher Nolan is a better action director than Michael Bay, because he doesn't go for mindless action and too much humor. He goes for our hearts and can surprise audiences with its twists and turns without slipping into silliness and I became a fan of what he does as a director, ever since "Memento". He uses IMAX cameras for the action scenes with cinematographer Wally Pfister and they are breathtaking. He gives a lot of support from his excellent all-star cast that also features returning regulars Morgan Freeman as Lucius Fox and Michael Caine in an Oscar-worthy performance as Bruce's personal butler, Alfred. Also, new characters joining into the mix including Oscar-winner Marion Cotillard as Miranda Tate, who helps Bruce out in his time of grief, emotionally and romantically and Matthew Modine is superb as a cop who doesn't let anyone get in his way, especially Blake. See if you can also spot some cameos from two of the villains from "Batman Begins" and learn how it all comes full circle. Bane is a good villain, has a limited sense of humor and his voice is altered down for us, which is easy to understand. (Why? You'll find out soon enough.) But he doesn't have what the Joker had: Maximum horsepower. Since this is the last of Christopher Nolan's "Batman" series, I think it's rare that the third and final installment of a trilogy exceeds expectations for people. "The Dark Knight Rises" is one of those rare ones, joining alongside "The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King". As the movie comes to an end, it gives us one last twist that proves the old adage, "As one story ends, another begins." Don't Miss It!

9.title: A good superhero sequel, but a great conclusion to a trilogy
9.content:
Third installments have a history of letting us down — in the superhero world especially. You won't find a lot of folks who list a movie with a "3" at the end as their favorite of a movie series, and frankly, they don't have a lot to choose from either.

It's extremely tough to find the perfect third, even with all the ground-breaking Christopher Nolan's adored and beloved Batman films have accomplished. "Batman Begins" changed the way Hollywood looked at the characters and properties sitting on its shelves, and "The Dark Knight" changed the way blockbusters are made, period. Both set high bars for filmmaking, and in the process, saddled "The Dark Knight Rises" with astronomical expectations.

Many would argue it's an impossible order, and watching "The Dark Knight Rises," you get a sense Nolan didn't care to meet it. No, it's not about apathy or laziness — he was just more concerned with creating a sense of completeness, with finishing the story arc he dreamed up years ago. In doing so he gives us the first connected and complete original movie trilogy in movie history that doesn't have the name "Star Wars" attached to it.

Conclusiveness: "The Dark Knight Rises" greatest strength and greatest weakness. Nolan's drive to achieve finality gives the film a greater sense of purpose and ultimately a feeling of satisfaction, yet at the same time, the film is slave to it; "Rises" doesn't have its own identity so much as it completes a whole.

The powerful escalation of events in "The Dark Knight" necessitates this, as it should. Batman (Christian Bale) has taken the fall for the corrupted Harvey Dent so that Commissioner Gordon (Gary Oldman) could use Dent's image to continue to clean Gotham of crime — and it worked. The city is at peace eight years later, only our hero Bruce Wayne stays cooped in his rebuilt mansion, nursing his psyche, unconfident that he can affect the same change as Bruce Wayne that he did as Batman.

Yet Bruce's sense of purpose is quickly renewed when he crosses paths with a jewel thief named Selina Kyle (Anne Hathaway) and learns of a new masked rogue named Bane (Tom Hardy) amassing a force deep within Gotham. With some urging from Gordon, Bruce takes up the cowl, unaware that his most grueling mental and physical trials lie before him.

Also new to the mix are other Nolan "Inception" alumni Joseph Gordon-Levitt as bold rookie cop John Blake and Marion Cotillard as Wayne Enterprises board member Miranda Tate. Coupled with Hathaway and Hardy, the talent on screen is palpable, and it eases the juggling of the film's subplots necessitated by their characters' existence.

The new faces are just one of many factors increasing the scale, stage and stakes of "The Dark Knight Rises." Like the previous films, the story is immersive and the action engrossing. What the major sequences lack in ingenuity (except for the excellent opening plane hijacking), the film replaces with more visceral combat, which is in a way much more fitting of the nature of the film (and Bane's scheme). The film is both intensely personal and wildly large, something that becomes easier to appreciate when the chaos has died down and the credits roll.

The personal comes mostly with Bruce's journey, plus the sense of intimacy we have built over the years with characters such as Alfred (Michael Caine) and Lucius Fox (Morgan Freeman). The film hearkens a lot to "Batman Begins," which is no surprise considering the objective is so clearly to unite the three films. What happens in that first film is firmly entrenched in "Rises," so anyone rusty on it would benefit from a refresher course.

To bring the entire trilogy full circle, a lot needs to happen. Critics of "The Dark Knight" and its plot contrivances will find more cause to nitpick the many pieces that seem to fall into place here. The destination of the film — it's final five minutes — is so powerful and satisfying that Nolan must have imagined it from the beginning and determined to construct the film around arriving there. Doing so meant making certain sacrifices to "The Dark Knight Rises" as a singular entity for the benefit of the three-film story.

Yet without "The Dark Knight Rises," the trilogy would be incomplete and unsatisfying. While it is the least perfect piece of Nolan's incredible enterprise, is is unquestionably the most essential. Viewed independently, its faults can seem to pile on top of one another, but viewed within the context of the trilogy, suddenly the themes and ideas begin to expand and grow, and the film's many subplots and characters begin to feel essential.

Why? Because it had to end the way it does. Nolan's Batman is so rich, his vision and purpose for Batman and what he represents is so clear, that all who love it actually understand it as intuitively as Nolan himself. "The Dark Knight Rises" is predictable in this way, though not because Nolan has regressed, rather because we are on the same wavelength. We know, for example, that in any classic story the good guy is going to win, but just because that outcome is foreseeable doesn't mean it's unsatisfying to see it all play out.

In that way, "The Dark Knight Rises" gives us a thrilling swan song for Nolan's Batman. By daring to be a final chapter rather than succumb to the era of four-quels and five-quels in which money necessitates that filmmakers leave the door open for future chapters, "The Dark Knight Rises" accomplishes the seemingly simple yet incredibly obstacle-ridden task of making a great third installment. Like "Batman Begins" and "The Dark Knight," it's an achievement with no equal.

~Steven C

Thanks for reading! Check out moviemusereviews.com

9.title: The Dark Knight Rises as the best Batman movie thus far
9.content:
The movie did totally exceed my expectations. There is a lot of hype surrounding this movie and because of that I didn't expect that TDKR would be as good as it is.

I want to give this a perfect score but I can't. Certain parts dragged and others they rushed. There are a few scenes that could (or should) have been left on the cutting room floor. At one point I thought to myself that the movie must have been going for two hours or so but I was wrong. I was only an hour into it. The movie does pick up steam as goes though.

Christian Bale is an actor who I have always been a fan of however I was a little disappointed in his portrayal of Batman in the first two movies. In this movie he really did sink into the role. And his Bat-voice is not so over the top as it used to be. I always preferred Michael Keaton as Batman before I saw this movie. After seeing TDKR though I like Bale's performance just as much as Keaton's.

Bane's voice wasn't hard for me to understand (though I think there was one line I couldn't follow). Is Hardy's performance better than Heath Ledger's? I would say that they are equal. But the character of Bane was much more compelling than The Joker in my opinion.

Anne Hathaway's Catwoman was great as well.

Bravo Christopher Nolan and team.

9.title: Nolan ends it all with exhilaration, empathy and excellence.
9.content:
Eight years ago, Batman (Christian Bale) took the fall for the murders committed by Harvey Dent in order to preserve the White Knight's legacy as the defender of Gotham. Dent's death has not proved to be in vain, as the city has remained relatively crime-free during Batman's proverbial exile and Bruce Wayne's subsequent life as a recluse. But as new terrorist leader Bane (Tom Hardy) hatches a plot to literally destroy the city from the inside out, Wayne must again don the cape and cowl and finally become the hero his city deserves.

The Dark Knight Rises is not only an incredible piece of cinema in its own right, but its qualities are accentuated given it is the last film of a truly thrilling series from director Christopher Nolan. The film opens by reacquainting the audience with the bat-verse. Each character, new or established, is introduced in meticulous detail, which could be either a good or bad thing depending on how familiar you are with the source material. The plot does meander intermittently during this time, none more so than when a MacGuffin pops up as the unnecessary driver of Selina Kyle's (Anne Hathaway) motives.

But that is arguably the only weak point in a film that seamlessly combines well-rounded characters with exciting set pieces and a masterful conclusion that subverts exactly what it means to be a 'hero.'

Newcomers John Blake (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) and Miranda Tate (Marion Cotillard) are essentially original creations, but they prove to have much more in common with Batman lore than first thought. Hathaway brings a unique dynamism to Catwoman, and each time she and Bale share the screen completely dispels what appeared to be, on paper, the film's biggest setback. Bane is no Joker, and his introduction doesn't quite reach the exhilarating heights of the funnyman's bank heist, but Hardy's performance more than does the mighty mercenary justice.

With this trilogy, and a quiet little side project called Inception along the way, Nolan has carved out a reputation as the saviour of mainstream blockbusters, and his action sequences in Rises are accordingly first-rate. Respect must be given to the sheer effort and co-ordination needed to pull off Bane's takeover of Heinz Field and the enormous battle between the inmates and Gotham's police force, but it is a severely crippled Wayne's attempt to escape his cruel fortress that will have most viewers emitting a silent cheer, and barring that, an audible one.

Of course, visual accomplishments can only take a film as ambitious as this one so far. The final act deals extensively with the emotional toll being Batman has taken on Bruce Wayne versus his innate philanthropic need to constantly be the hero. The mask itself becomes a prominent motif, perhaps representing the personal suffering Wayne has hidden from for so many years. The saga ends on a note of closure and an overwhelming feeling of satisfaction, implying that one legacy cannot begin until another one ends.
