9.title: The spiritually-rich conclusion to an Epic Trilogy
9.content:
A trilogy often invites the structural idea of a Beginning, a Middle, and an Ending. The same can be said for Bruce Wayne's Batman: In Begins, we see him evolve from pre-Batman into the Batman, in Dark Knight we see Bruce struggle under the cowl, and in Rises we see Bruce post-Batman.

Eight Years have past. Bruce's spirit is broken and shattered; overwhelmed with guilt, despair and pain. For eight years he has reclused in his manor, letting those emotions seep into him, killing his soul. The Batman has always been the physical manifestation of Bruce: the external form of the internal nature. There was a perfectly harmonious, and complimentary relationship between both entities, but when Bruce hung up the cowl at the end of The Dark Knight, this relationship of duality had never mended - his physical manifestation: The Batman, was gone, and all Bruce had left was his spirit; but he never mended or tended to his internal side - the side that was crucial to the pursuit of the Batman.

An inevitable evil comes to Gotham: Bane. A well-written antagonist is one that directly attacks the protagonist's weakness, and in this case, Bruce's crucial flaw is the imbalance between himself and his Batman alter-ego: an imperfect balance between internal nature and external form. Bane's intense physicality propels Bruce to dawn the cape to confront him - however, this act doesn't lift Bruce out of the dark; it plunges him further into it.

What Bruce doesn't realise is that what makes Bane so strong is not just his intense physical strength, but he is primarily propelled by a spiritual motivation - a desire to rule Gotham. This fuels his strength; the external form feeding off a fiery internal nature. On the contrary, this is exactly what Bruce is missing: In Begins and Dark Knight, he had a clear motivation of being the Batman - to fight injustice. A perfect harmony of man and spirit: the internal nature fueling his external form. However, what Bruce doesn't realise is that a broken man cannot save a broken city. If he wants to defeat Bane, he has to succeed within himself.

And that is why Bruce falls. When he faces Bane in the sewers, he believes that Bane will be conquered only by his physical strength. While there is certain truth in that statement, he does not realise that the man behind the fists must be spiritually unified in order to succeed over the other. Naturally, he fails. And Bane destroys the one part of Bruce that mattered to him the most: his body.

With his body broken, Bruce finds himself in The Pit. In order to escape, one must clamber up the bricks and to make a seemingly impossible leap. It's specifically designed to make one think that it takes physicality to escape The Pit, regardless of one's spirit. But that's exactly what Bruce needs to learn - the Batman is not about what lies outside of the cape: the gadgets and the muscle, but what lies on the inside. Bruce must make the climb alone, without the Batman.

As Bruce struggles in recovery, Bane taunts him: the TV showing Gotham under his rule. The city which Bruce worked so hard to preserve is being ruined under his eyes, but the worst part is that he is utterly helpless about it. This propels him to make an attempt at making the leap, but he fails. In total despair, he picks himself backs up and prepares for his next attempt. One of the prisoners remarks that his preparation is wrong, but Bruce retaliates: "My soul is as ready to escape as my body"; he still places his utmost faith in his physicality. He is frustrated, desperate to escape. He channels this anger into his next climb, but this time he doesn't even make it to the leap.

His anger turns to despair. He is helpless and hopeless at the thought of watching his city die while he suffers in The Pit. The prisoner states that what holds Bruce back is his fear - he is afraid of the thought of dying without being able to help his city. In Batman Begins, Bruce embraced his fear of Bats, striking that same fear into his enemies. This time, the theme of fear has come full-circle. His fear of dying helplessly has poisoned him, anchoring him to the bottom of The Pit. What he then learns is the same lesson that he did in Begins: embrace your fear. Bruce lets his fear wash over him, fully embracing the possibility of him dying. He accepts this alternative rather than blindly rejecting it - by turning down the rope, he embraces this fear.

In a truly breathtaking scene, Bruce clambers up The Pit, with the cries of "Desri Bashara" below him. With his internal nature clear and defined, he surges forward towards the platform, latching onto it. Bruce Wayne has risen.

He returns to Gotham, as a unified man of soul and flesh. His motivation for returning to the Batman is still the same - to defeat Bane - but a broken man cannot save a broken city, and Bruce has just proved himself to be unbroken. Now, he is truly ready to defeat Bane.

For the first time in the trilogy, the Batman is seen in the light rather than darkness, a figurative representation of Bruce pursuing his city's ascension out of the dark, and into the light.

As a perfected duality of Man and Bat, Bruce conqueres over Bane, but the city is yet to be saved. As the Batman, he makes the ultimate sacrifice, giving his life to save the entire city. The result of this action is that he has solidified the Batman as a symbol - eternal and everlasting. The Batman's arc has been completed, cementing the power of symbols, and how they outlast the physical boundaries of humans. But one specific human has yet to have a completed arc: Bruce Wayne.

He is believed to be dead, but in a turn of events, it is revealed that Bruce has lived. He has moved on, with the Batman behind him. He is able to fully live his life as one Bruce Wayne - no other entities. The resolution he always deserved.

The character of Bruce Wayne was handled so beautifully in this film - without a doubt, it is my favourite character journey in any film. Although, a great Christopher Nolan film is not just populated by nuanced characters, but thought-provoking themes.

The themes in Batman Begins were psychological - there was an intense focus on the psyche of Bruce Wayne and what propelled him pursue the Cowl.

In The Dark Knight, the themes were incredibly intellectual, with an intense focus on society, corruption and morality.

In The Dark Knight Rises, the themes are primarily spiritual: the aforementioned journey of Bruce Wayne demonstrates the duality between one's spirit and body. Moreover, Rises also incorporates themes of hope. There are three particular instances where this theme of hope is conveyed: Firstly, the city of Gotham is in utter ruin, completely devoid of any hope for their future. The city then turns to their symbol of hope - a chalk bat on a wall: The Batman. Secondly, what keeps Bruce going in The Pit is the hope that he can escape and save his city - interestingly however, Bruce escapes The Pit not by latching onto the hope of escape, rather it's the opposite: embracing the fear of death and failure. Thirdly, when Gotham faces the threat of nuclear explosion, Blake tells the kids to stay in the bus. Obviously staying in a bus won't save the kids, but the act represents the bravery of latching on to a meager hope, even in the face of incredible odds.

I wrote earlier about how The Dark Knight Rises was a microcosm of the entire trilogy. It's also a reason why I love the film, and therefore I will write my thoughts on the trilogy as a whole:

I absolutely love this trilogy. It's easily my favourite of all-time, and it is such a joy and privilege to be able to advance through the trilogy, from beginning to end, and to genuinely feel that you've experienced something. You felt the character's pain, suffered their losses. You also felt the magnitude of the epic moments and the awe of the spectacle.

I still can't comprehend that we actually could experience a trilogy like this. You ever hear people have far-fetched wishes that would be so cool but would never happen? "Imagine if Christopher Nolan directed James Bond! I wish The Hobbit was re-made as one 4-Hour film!". The Dark Knight trilogy feels too idyllic, too good to be true. Nolan's re-imagining of The Caped Crusader is everything I have ever wanted in a superhero film and it is a total miracle that this trilogy was made.

The trilogy was revolutionary, enduring and wildly original. It changed the face of comic book films, showing that a film with a superhero could be just as, or even more interesting than a film without one. This genre of films garnered a massive amount of respect due to Nolan's impeccable work, leaving an indelible mark on the film industry. This impact came from one man: The incredible, ambitious and spectacular Christopher Nolan.

9.title: The knight is darkest before the dawn, but I promise you the dawn is coming!
9.content:
Christopher Nolan is the man who not only saved Batman from the dung heap of the Joel Schumacher days, but also elevated him to a new level such that The Dark Knight was able to overthrow The Godfather on IMDb's top 250, if only temporarily! And with The Dark Knight Rises, he delivers on his promise to give a fitting and emotionally satisfying conclusion to the story of Bruce Wayne that began with 2005's Batman Begins.

After 2008's The Dark Knight raised the bar for Hollywood blockbusters, one must wonder how TDKR could ever hope to outdo TDK. It doesn't, but don't let that convince you that this isn't still a good movie - it's just that TDK is near impossible to top, thanks to the superb performances delivered by Heath Ledger and Aaron Eckhart. But TDKR does indeed try, and in place of the Joker and Two-Face, brings us Bane and Catwoman.

Bane in particular had last appeared in 1997's epic failure known as Batman & Robin, where he was reduced to nothing more than a mindless but brutish henchman to the main villains. Here, he is returned to his comic book roots: a towering hulk of muscle and brute strength enhanced by his cunning and personal charisma, all played to a tee by Tom Hardy. Catwoman too receives a top notch performance as a femme fatale by Anne Hathaway, an actress as talented as she is gorgeous. And of course, Gary Oldman, Morgan Freeman, and Michael Caine return as well - I really can't say anything because the three of them are guaranteed to excel in just about any role you could throw at them.

Two more classic Batman characters appear unexpectedly, but I will refrain from naming them for want of avoiding spoilers. However, viewers will be pleasantly surprised by how well Nolan has been able to save one of them from the scrapheap of Batman mythology. I will conclude this review with a solid recommendation, but be warned! TDKR is best enjoyed only at the end of a session of having first seen Batman Begins and TDK - in that way, the viewer can truly better enjoy the conclusion that TDKR delivers, and how well it ties into those other two.

9.title: The Dark Knight Rises (2012)
9.content:
Batman Begins and The Dark Knight were such stellar movies, and there's little to no differing opinions on that. Dark Knight Rises, however, has a lot of criticism its way. So how good is it?

We're re-introduced to Bane (played by Tom Hardy), and I'm just going to say it. THIS is Bane done right. Bane is known for being a wise, threatening squadron leader that's a force to be reckoned with, and this movie's Bane checks all those marks. Yeah, his voice may come off as goofy initially, but Bane in action is the exact opposite, especially when he beats Batman brutally and locks him away. That iconic scene where Bane breaks Batman's back really stuck with me.

Once again, Christian Bale's Batman is at his peak. This Batman isn't as aggressive as the predecessor, but he still retains the character, and has a lot more emotion as Bruce Wayne. Alfred leaving for good almost made me tear up, and Bale's portrayal solidifies the scene's importance.

Catwoman (Anne Hathaway) doesn't have a lot in this movie to do, but her dynamic with Batman is actually decent. I don't have much to say, but I like this performance of Catwoman.

The action is just stellar, the character chemistry is amazing, and the ending was great. The ending made me tear up, even though Wayne lived. I know, people had issue with that, but that doesn't symbolize Wayne dying. It symbolizes Batman dying. That alone makes the ending hit hard.

People hate this movie because they're wrong. 9/10.

9.title: The Dark Knight Rises Review
9.content:
8 years after Batman protected the image of Harvey Dent, crime in Gotham is at a all time low. Bruce has been held up in his mansion avoiding any public interaction, but when Bane threatens Gotham Bruce must once again put on the cape and save the city.

Another incredible Batman film from Nolan, this film much like the other two are across the board technically flawless but sense I've mentioned that in both of my reviews for Batman Begins and TDK I will focus on the differences that I loved.

First and foremost this is Christian Bales best performance as Batman. We see a very beaten and broken version of Bruce which leads to some great character moments which allow Bale to give an incredible performance.

Anne Hathaway was a very nice addition as Catwoman, this version of Selina Kyle was much more comic book accurate in terms of her humour, stealth, fighting, and sexiness. Also her back story added a sympathetic emotional side.

Bane is a menace and Tom Hardy is great as this character. Bane is a get to the point guy, he doesn't mess around he gets things done. I also liked their more realistic take on the character in terms of the use of his mask.

The stakes were much higher in this then they were in the previous films, which made for a very edge of your seat type of watch.

The ending is very satisfying and leaves on a great note, not much more to say about that.

9.5/10.

9.title: That's how you write an ending!
9.content:
The rise of one is the fall of another. This was a great ending to the Batman trilogy and - I think - my favourite of the three movies.

I like that the last villain is related to Ra's Al-Ghul again. I like that Batman's fighting skills are not impenetrable but rather surpassed by the villain Bane. Unlike in the second movie, Batman was actually down for a while: he himself was actually on the brink of defeat, he was not crumbling simply because of some hostages. That made the opposition more formidable for me.

I enjoy the strong female cast, from Catwoman to Miranda. And I really didn't see the Miranda twist coming. Maybe because I barely knew who she was since she didn't appear in the previous movies, so I basically forgot about her character.

The ending was great and left up to interpretation for the viewer which I enjoy. Is Batman dead? Is he now living a peaceful life as Alfred had envisioned? I believe that either ending would be satisfying but letting the viewer imagine it feels even better. Bravo for a superb end to a groundbreaking trilogy.

9.title: A grand and satisfying conclusion
9.content:
"The Dark Knight Rises," directed by Christopher Nolan, serves as a powerful conclusion to his epic Batman trilogy. The film stars Christian Bale, reprising his role as Bruce Wayne/Batman, who faces his greatest challenge yet in the form of the formidable and merciless villain Bane, played by Tom Hardy.

Christian Bale delivers a deeply emotional and complex performance, portraying a hero who must overcome personal demons and physical challenges to save Gotham City. Tom Hardy's Bane is a terrifying antagonist, bringing a sense of impending doom with his physical presence and strategic mind. Anne Hathaway adds a refreshing dynamic as Selina Kyle, balancing charm and agility in her portrayal of the elusive Catwoman.

Nolan's direction is nothing short of spectacular, with breathtaking action sequences and stunning set pieces that elevate the film's grandeur. Hans Zimmer's powerful score adds to the intensity and emotional weight of the narrative. The screenplay, co-written by Nolan and his brother Jonathan, skillfully ties together themes from the previous films while introducing new, compelling elements.

"The Dark Knight Rises" is a grand and satisfying conclusion to Nolan's trilogy, blending action, drama, and character development in a cohesive and impactful way. It is a fitting end to a beloved series, delivering thrills and emotional depth in equal measure.

9.title: The Dark Knight Rises
9.content: he Dark Knight Rises" leaves the fanciful early days of the superhero genre far behind, and moves into a doom-shrouded, apocalyptic future that seems uncomfortably close to today's headlines. As urban terrorism and class warfare envelop Gotham and its infrastructure is ripped apart, Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale) emerges reluctantly from years of seclusion in Wayne Manor and faces a soulless villain as powerful as he is. The film begins slowly with a murky plot and too many new characters, but builds to a sensational climax. The result, in Christopher Nolan's conclusion to his Batman trilogy, is an ambitious superhero movie with two surprises: It isn't very much fun, and it doesn't have very much Batman. I'm thinking of the over-the-top action sequences of the earlier films that had a subcurrent of humor, and the exhilarating performance of Heath Ledger as the Joker. This movie is all serious drama, with a villain named Bane whose Hannibal Lecterish face-muzzle robs him of personality. And although we see a good deal of Bruce Wayne, his alter-ego Batman makes only a few brief appearances before the all-out climax.

9.title: the grand finale

9.title: Visually stunning and a perfect third act
9.content:
This movie, about Batman who is coerced out of exile with the assistance of the mysterious Selina Kyle in order to defend Gotham City from the vicious guerrilla terrorist Bane, is a great ending to The Dark Knight Trilogy (2005-2012)!

It was a pure joy to watch from start to finish, and the third act especially marked itself as the perfect ending to the trilogy. The story can feel slightly simple, but the scenes themselves really get your attention. It was epic and exciting with a lot of cool action, but also with a twist, where it ends with a tragedy; Batman's death. Batman's line "A hero can be anyone. Even a man doing something as simple and reassuring as putting a coat around a young boy's shoulders to let him know that the world hadn't ended." gets me every time. It's the foundation of Batman's symbol, and it's all about taking the initiative to make a change for the better. Batman Begins (2005) was about a hero being born based on fear, but The Dark Knight Rises was about rising after the fall, which is thanks to Bruce's father Thomas Wayne. This movie was an emotional ride, and what I found most emotional was Alfred Pennyworth crying by the Waynes' grave, but also the public, memorial statements about Batman with the beautiful soundtrack in background by composer Hans Zimmer. It felt so heavy to think about the loss of Batman and his sacrifice for Gotham after many years work. Batman was a hero, but also more than a hero. He was a symbol of hope during the darkest times to all kinds of people until the light shined again.

Bane's task was to destroy Gotham without exception and hesitation with the use of pure terror, and he terrified in every way. I think Joker was the most interesting villain in the trilogy, mainly because of his psychology. However, he was brutal, but Bane was brutal on another level. Joker preferred to surprise people with his actions based on his sneaky ideas, but Bane preferred to force people to watch and feel every detail of his actions from start to finish no matter how terrorizing they were. You could actually count how many times he broke a neck, and he even killed his own men without hesitation to get what he wanted. Just his look was terrifying enough. I had mixed thoughts about his voice, but it was very peculiar, which made him even scarier. You recognized him as soon as you heard his voice. The choreography of Bane's fighting is one of the best ones I have ever seen. It was extremely brutal and fast, and his moves weren't just regular movie moves. You could almost feel the pain of every single punch and kick by him.

The technical aspects made this movie cinematically epic. The general cinematography was my favorite technical element, but also the general sound and of course the soundtrack by Zimmer made this experience very enjoyable. The soundtrack in this one has a more terrorizing and brutal style compared to the beautiful and clean melody in the first movie, and the raw, electric guitar sound in The Dark Knight (2008), which helped to make a fantastic conclusion to the trilogy.

This is a fitting conclusion to the trilogy and a cinematic triumph in its own right. Its seemingly simple narrative still captivates, leading to an epic and bittersweet third act Bane's terrorizing presence, different yet brutal, leaves an indelible impression. The movie's technical excellence, from cinematography to the evocative soundtrack, enhances the experience. In the end, this movie greatly weaves action, emotion, and symbolism, securing its place as a remarkable trilogy conclusion and a significant contribution to cinema.

9.title: The second best film in the trilogy and a fitting conclusion
9.content:
I am in the minority here when I say that The Dark Knight Rises is the second best film in the Dark Knight trilogy ahead of Batman Begins. I can see why people have a problem with this film, honestly I can, however I do feel as if this film was harshly criticised for what it tried to accomplish.

Christopher Nolan has given us one of the best trilogies of all time and this film is a fitting conclusion and personally a nice change of pace for the franchise. The character of Batman up until now, and even in this trilogy, had always been on the top of his game. Batman had never met his match on screen whether that be Keaton's or Kilmer's, lets skip Clooney, the character was never in any real danger from being out staged or classed, physically! So Christopher Nolan gave something new and re-refreshing to the character and that was a true physical presence in the form of Bane. I don't think that Nolan gets enough credit for at least change up the game slightly and giving audience something new to see on the big screen. As well as changing up the tone of the character, the directing in this film is top class from start to finish. A perfect mixture of close hand held shots and city landscapes, this film is beautiful to look at, whether it be in day light or night light. Nolan gave us his all in the franchise and I think it shows more in this film than it does in the other two prior, the overall feeling of overcoming something and finishing.

The cast as in everyone of the films in the franchise is spectacular, firstly lets start with the main man himself. Christian Bale is the best Bruce Wayne/Batman that there has been on screen to this date, yes you probably have a good argument for Keaton, Kilmer or Affleck but for me he is the defining one. This film shows Bruce Wayne in a completely different situation both physically and mentally, Bale excels in both of these regards. His performance in both Wayne and Batman shows what both have gone through, whether that be the emotional heart ache of loosing Rachel in the Dark Knight and the physical deterioration of him from all the fighting. Bale gives an out of this world performance that actually makes you feel a great deal of empathy towards the character, similar to when his parents were shot in the first film. The rest of the cast Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman, Tom Hardy, Marion Cotillard, Anne Hathaway, Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Gary Oldman are all brilliant in their varying roles. The returning characters also show the longevity of the series of films and all that has happen prior to this one, whilst the new characters offer something fresh and interest to involve ourselves with.

The story, lets get one thing out of the way, Yes this film does have plot holes. How did Bane know that Bruce Wayne was Batman? How did Bruce get back into Gotham after escaping prison? These and more are examples of where this film is not as well structured as Batman Begins or The Dark Knight. However for some reason every time I watch this film I can easily give them a pass. This is because for me they never have effected the overall film and have never been jarring to a point were it takes be out of the film. Yes call me a DC fanboy or a biased opinion, you might be right but for me this story tried to change the pace and style of the trilogy which I have to commend it for even though it didn't pull it off all the time.

Another positive is the CGI and practical effects which are moulded in this film perfectly, this is especially apparent with The Bat, Tumblers and Bat Pod. All of the CGI and practical effects look so brilliantly made and choreographed.

The final positive the ending, Yes I do think it is a massive positive. This film and franchise perfectly closes of the story of the Batman/Bruce Wayne character as a whole. This is a rare, this is one of the few films that has actually made me cry. I know that's sad but its Batman and I love it. It is heart aching seeing Alfred crying over the graves and the closing will being read out along with the Hans Zimmer score is beautiful. It gets me every time the ending to this film, what a fantastic achievement Nolan to give such an emotional punch.

Negatives, shock horror a Fan boy of this film actually thinks there are negatives! Yeah my main negative of this film is a strange one and nothing to do with the negatives that most people have with this film. Changing Chicago for New York was probably necessary for this film how ever it does stick out for me considering how well the backdrop of Chicago was so good as Gotham in the other two films.

Finally, I love this film and the franchise overall, it made me into the comic book fan I am now. 95% out of 100, Yes call me DC fanboy but I really don't care, there are plot holes in this film I can see them but for me they never stick out that much and can be easily overseen. Christian Bale will go down as one of if not the best Bruce Wayne/Batman there has been, certainly for me he is the best and this film once again backs up that idea. Nolan has achieved greatest in this film and in this franchise and it will never be forgotten, whether that be the realistic, dark portrayal of the character, the fantastic directing and writing or the mesmerising score! The Dark Knight Trilogy is one of the best!

9.title: A Flawed Movie That Rises Above To Shine
9.content: 21 July 2012. The Dark Knight Rises joins There Will Be Blood (2007) as one of the extremely few flawed movies to rise above its slight annoyances to almost completely overshadow any lingering irritating oversights or logical flaws to become by the end a genuinely satisfying and qualitative, substantive action thriller movie, which only speaks to its strengths and integrity. As for the flaws that are sizeable in number, the stolen necklace that is so easily traced and for Catwoman to be so easily caught the second time; Batman's camouflage of his flying Bataeroflighter of flimsy army stock instead of invisible car used in Die Another Day (2002); just leaving Bane of the roof in which of course the whole movie would have ended perhaps; the overly too convenient angle of the road barriers allowing the criminals to just ride over them from their escape of the Stock Market; and even Batman's own escape using a similar ramp he created; the fusion bomb being so easily armed without a failsafe and the more likely decision in reality of doing using one, an almost unlikely mob scene of good and bad fighting sequences (unlike even what would be an even more authentic Civil War battle of hand to hand combat) and the absence of the better direction and choreography of the jumping in the hell hole scene. The martial arts scenes have been vastly improved for their clarity and visual impact since the first of the three movies in Batman Begins (2005). Nevertheless for all these apparently convenient script devices or oversights, The Dark Knight Rises is aptly named and the darker serious thread as well as the humanity both bad and good that arises sometimes in the same character is so riveting and dramatically authentic that it strikes at the universal themes of the lives of almost everyone watching the movie. The more controversial element of the movie is whether one can make a statement about the movie as being an indictment of our existing capitalist system in America or whether it can be a more subtle endorsement of the present system of structure and political law enforcement in our society. It is fascinating that there is some ways a resemblance to themes that can be found in the epic romantic drama Dr. Zhivago (1965) shot against the background of the Russian Revolution where the masses revolted against the rich elite. The Dark Night Rises is edited, even though a few scenes seem too short (except for considering the overall length of the movie) in a nicely timed way, the characters are both hated and loved, quality of the substance of the deeper dialogue of human, existential being is offered up and the energy and tension, keeps increasing and the audience angst and anguish at the pull of good versus evil and martyrdom of many characters both good and and in this movie continues to build until the end which has its own nicely wrapped, enfolded conclusion as if there was any doubt.

9.title: The best Batman film in Nolan's trilogy
9.content:
The Dark Knight Rises in my humble opinion is the best Batman film in the Dark Knight trilogy. It showcased a thrilling plot, an exceptional villain and epic moments throughout it. Watching it is a powerful experience, you are captivated from start to finish.

Bane is an exceptional villain and one who jumps out at you from the screen. While being the most dominant villain Batman has faced to date he is also intelligent and resourceful. His purpose is not to just destroy Batman but Gotham city. He wants to bring fear and terror to the city. Note that while he uses his strength often he does not always use it, he is a calm and calculated villain who uses it when he needs to hence his power. Batman must not only dominate him physically but also take him on in a game of wits.

Bruce/Batman's climb scene when he is in the pit has to be one of the greatest moments in cinema. The camera-work and techniques Nolan uses to build up Batman as he makes the climb so he can escape was a masterstroke and made this scene epic as he climbed the pit to the top. Nolan shows Bruce being attacked from all angles from losing his company, wealth, his batman legacy to a city he fought to protect. It is for these reasons that make Bane his greatest enemy and when he emerges from the pit he is the strongest Batman he has ever been.

The twist was beautifully done and ties in well with the story. We see that perhaps there was another force in the dark behind the biggest and most challenging villain. It was a fitting and satisfying end to a very enjoyable and memorable film series.

9.title: Love it
9.content:
Epic conclusion to Christopher Nolan's Dark Knight trilogy that leaves a lasting impact with its grand storytelling and impressive visuals.

First and foremost, Tom Hardy's portrayal of Bane is an absolute tour de force. His commanding presence, combined with the menacing voice, makes him a truly formidable and memorable villain. While Heath Ledger's Joker set a high standard in The Dark Knight, Bane holds his own as a complex and imposing adversary for Batman.

Christian Bale's return as Batman is as strong as ever, showcasing the depth and complexity of the character. His journey as Bruce Wayne, grappling with the challenges of being a hero and the weight of his actions, is both engaging and emotionally resonant.

The film's narrative is ambitious and well-crafted, tying up loose ends from the previous movies while introducing new elements. It weaves a compelling tale of redemption, sacrifice, and the rise of the hero Gotham needs.

Anne Hathaway's portrayal of Selina Kyle, aka Catwoman, is a standout performance. She brings a fresh and dynamic take on the character, adding wit and charm to the mix while showcasing her badass fighting skills.

The action sequences are nothing short of breathtaking. Christopher Nolan's masterful direction and practical effects bring a sense of realism to the thrilling action scenes, making them a visual spectacle that leaves you in awe.

The film's emotional depth is another highlight. The Dark Knight Rises explores the human side of its characters, delving into their struggles and triumphs. It offers a satisfying conclusion to Bruce Wayne's journey as Batman, and the final act is both powerful and poignant.

Hans Zimmer's score once again elevates the film, creating a powerful and atmospheric soundtrack that adds to the overall cinematic experience.

In conclusion, The Dark Knight Rises is a triumphant and emotionally satisfying conclusion to the Dark Knight trilogy. With stellar performances, epic action, and a compelling narrative, it solidifies Christopher Nolan's legacy as a visionary filmmaker in the superhero genre.

If you're a fan of superhero films that delve into complex themes and deliver thrilling action, The Dark Knight Rises is a must-watch. It's a fitting and powerful end to a remarkable trilogy that cements Batman's status as one of the most iconic and enduring superheroes in cinematic history. So, sit back and enjoy the epic conclusion as the Dark Knight rises to save Gotham once more!

9.title: Battle of will and defeat
9.content:
What I like the most about this film is that it has achieved binding the entire mythology that's been built in the previous films in the series. From resurrecting our memories of characters and tying up their ends with more information of how the new characters are connected with the old. But most importantly "who is Batman?"

In Batman begins a terrorist organization wants to completely annihilate Gotham city because of how corrupted Gotham is, with its mob bosses and corrupted corporations and government. In the dark knight we see the people and the authority of Gotham facing a villain who's only goal seems to be proving the madness within us and destabilizing or exposing order as a lie. The ultimate goal was to see the people turn against each other, A fall of civilization through mass hysteria and paranoia. Throughout the series we see a similar theme- a socio/ political reason for the destruction of society. The dark knight rises presents itself with a temporary actualization of what the previous films were warning us. Unlike the joker who wanted this by making the people go at each other, bane does it by military invasion and a more stable vision. A vision not born of madness but one of ideal and hate. All these villains have one thing in common, they were all unaccepted and in return didn't accept. Every film tests Batman and his ideals. In rises we see him truly broken and literally rising from a metaphorical hell. The one bane calls home. Every good story is adventurous and every good adventure story has something to reveal about the protagonist - a search for identity. In some films the identity search becomes the central theme, and a conscious effort by the characters. In Batman, Wayne seems to be quite clear of who he is though he always carries an air of mystery about him. True we know his secret cosplay shenanigans but the drama and obstacles that happens around him and his response to them reveals to us more about who he is at the core. A film shouldn't be interpreted so much but the dark knight films are very inviting. I think in the final chapter Batman completely dies. The entire pit climbing(the metaphorical yet literal hell)sequence is purely Bruce Wayne. Every last beat of his heart beats for Gotham and Wayne makes the jump like the child. At that very moment, he's reborn. And like an innocent child would trust a snake, the first thing Wayne does is trust someone who betrayed him. And by death Batman becomes immortalized - a statue is built

9.title: Wonderful
9.content:
I saw this movie in theatres 7 years ago when it came out. At the time I think there was so much anticipation, and the memory of The Dark Knight and Heath Ledger's legendary performance as Joker was so fresh that the final instalment had an impossible bar to live up to.

I walked out of that theatre with mixed feelings, thinking the movie was the weakest of the Nolan Trilogy.

This weekend another Marvel movie was released. The 78th one this week. I'm so jaded by current year superhero movies. I loved them 10 years ago but today I can't sit through them. Last night I tried watching the sequel to Guardians of the Galaxy on Netflix and got 45 minutes before I turned it off.

Tonight I put on The Dark Knight Rises and, despite having seen it already and thinking it was the weakest in it's trilogy, I sat through the entire 2 hours and 45 minutes without pausing once, without picking up my laptop, without leaving the edge of my seat once.

Judging the movie on it's own merits - without comparing to Batman Begins or The Dark Knight, without comparing Bane to Joker ... it is a masterpiece of cinema and it is everything that superhero movies should be.

Anne Hathaway is my favourite Catwoman of all time. Every single character has a rich backstory and develops. Bruce Wayne begins the movie a broken man and Alfred wants desperately to save him but doesn't know how. The story is as much Bruce's inner journey as it is fighting the bad guy - which is so important to good story telling. This is what today's movies are lacking. Commissioner Gordon struggles to cope with a morally questionable decision that he has to live with. The villains are relatable and you can understand why they do what they do - which is the test of a good bad guy (the heroes in their own story). And boy do they ever raise the stakes!

Everything about this movie is spot on and I desperately miss superhero movies like this.

9.title: Wraps up the trilogy with a bat-shaped bow
9.content:
In this last instalment, Batman must come out of an 8 year physical and mental rut to fight The League of Shadows' new face - a brooding mercenary called Bane.

A worthy third and final film to cap off a superhero trilogy that has cemented itself as one of the best. I would say this film is my least favourite of the three, but that is by no means saying it is a bad movie - it had ridiculously big expectations following The Dark Knight.

I think Bane is a top tier villain in the Batman universe and especially his depiction in this movie. It really succeeded in portraying him as a menacing freak of nature, a man born in turmoil who has seen the depths of the world and humanity. He gave me chills in many scenes, not just when he's beating down the Dark Knight with ease. I felt his power and presence whenever he was in frame, and was truly convinced this was Batmans most powerful adversary. Side note - he was only ever framed from a low angle, making him appear bigger in the frame, whereas in their scenes batman would be shot from a high angle, really highlighting the size difference. There is some top-tier, epic scale set pieces here, such as the football stadium destruction and stock exchange robbery. There is impactful character moments and dynamics throughout, which give depth and meaning to the action, which has become standard for these films. Once again we get a powerful and character driven story, wrapped up with a bat shaped bow.

I don't think this movie, and in turn this trilogy, could have ended better. Such masterful and intelligent writing by Nolan to tie up all loose ends: Batman flying off with the bomb after a teary powerful reveal to gordon, being witnessed by the world saving Gotham, Alfred seeing Bruce in Florence with Selina, introducing Blake's true name to be robin - It just feels like it couldn't have ended any other way. A full circle, satisfying but incredibly bitter-sweet ending.

The first half of the movie felt a bit too dense to me, introducing a plethora of new faces, motives and storylines in a short time. It was also a slow start, leaving me drifting off here and there as bane kills some businessman in a fancy hotel. Once the characters and motives came together it was an amazing climax and second half, but it took some time to get there. I also wanted more Batman. He honestly felt like a side-character to Bane for most of the movie, which made me disappointed when Bane was revealed to not be the person we thought. A person preference I have which this film missed is nightime and dark scenes. The majority of it is bright, daytime sequences. This may be fine for some, but I think Batman is synonymous with darkness, and I wanted much, much more. Also, it at times felt like a good action movie in a big city, and Batman just happened to be in that city.

Overall, this film wrapped up a phenomenal franchise with a great entry. A menacing new villain in Bane, an intense climax, emotional depth, great characters and a flawless conclusion - a great film.

9.title: An Epic Conclusion to the Dark Knight Saga

9.title: At its best it is the best
9.content:
"The Dark Knight Rises" has some flaws baked into it, but after this re-watch I've concluded that when it is at its best, it's the best of the Christopher Nolan "Dark Knight" trilogy. Thankfully it's at that "best" for the vast majority of its runtime.

Writer/director Christopher Nolan doesn't make movies, he makes films. There's a distinct difference. Unlike Marvel, with its cookie-cutter popcorn sensibilities, Nolan endeavors to tell an actual story. You see, Marvel movies have plots. Again, there's a difference.

Like "The Dark Knight", "Rises" has elements of then current sociopolitical trends. In the former it was the "War on Terror" and the debate surrounding things like the Patriot Act. It also reflected the end of the Bush Presidency and the start of the Obama era. I certainly have my opinion on what Nolan was trying to say here, but I'll leave the interpretation of that up to the viewer. Here it's the Occupy Wall Street movement. Again, what you see here is up to you, and that is part of what makes these films so unique.

Nolan doesn't hammer us over the head with these themes. Unlike so much of what Hollywood churns out these days, he isn't interested in telling you what to think. Instead, he wants you *to* think. Big difference.

All of that aside, this is an incredible film. My criticisms, which I won't spoil for anyone who hasn't actually seen the movie at this point and has dug through several thousand reviews to find mine, do absolutely nothing to detract from it.

Nolan's Batman saga is a masterpiece and should serve as a template for Hollywood. Not just for its "Comic Book" movies, either.

9.title: A wonderful conclusion to a wonderful trilogy.
9.content:
After eight years in seclusion, Batman resurfaces to face Bane, a mastermind bent on destroying Gotham and has ties to Bruce Wayne's past. Christopher Nolan's conclusion to his Dark Knight trilogy should be treated as a wrap up rather than a third installment. Despite many new characters being introduced, even their conflicts and motives are derived from events that occurred in the previous two films. Such an approach could be seen as a weakness, since the conflict could just end up being sort of a rematch rather than moving the story forward; however, Nolan's approach works terrificly. Over an hour is shot in stunning IMAX, but the film is more touching than it is intense and that's its best quality. Hardy steps in as the genius mercenary Bane, who is slightly bigger, slightly stronger and slightly smarter than Batman, thus making him a challenge best suited for the grand finale. The Joker works best as Batman's arch-nemesis since they are polar opposites, with The Joker standing for everything Batman stands against. Two-Face works best as Batman's most tragic enemy because Harvey Dent is very much like Bruce Wayne the only difference is: Dent copes with his tragedy through revenge rather than seeking justice as Wayne did. Bane works best as Batman's most challenging villain because of his physical and mental superiority—forget the Bane you saw in "BATMAN & ROBIN". Nolan carefully chose all his villains in the series wisely and executed them perfectly. Hardy had big shoes to fill following Ledger's posthumous Oscar winning performance; while Bane is no Joker, Hardy does a satisfying job and should not be compared to Ledger's performance as they are completely different roles. It is Michael Caine, however, that delivers the most memorable and touching performance of the entire film. A wonderful conclusion to a wonderful trilogy.

**** (out of four)
