This is in my opinion a bit of a selfish film on the part of the director. The conclusion was the beginning, all Nolan wanted to do was to pack the punch of the 'death' of Bruce Wayne. Which I'm up for. Just do it in a more coherent and competent fashion.

6.title: Insults your intelligence
6.content:
Didn't love it.

Don't want my money back, I bought the LARGE popcorn so it averages out a little better. Don't want 3 hours of my life back, it's not THAT (Time Machine) bad. Just expected better.

Christopher Nolan - a director who usually doesn't mess up on this scale, seems to have phoned it in, starting with the shooting script.

Camera, makeup, sets, lighting, sound, music , action sequence choreographers - all delivered. Exceeded expectations in fact.

Anne Hathaway was ass-kicking eye candy - totally great. Christian Bale was perfection. Michael Caine underplayed it also to perfection.

Edit/Directorial FAILs include Oldman and Freeman who were only allowed to deliver workmanlike performances this outing. TWO towering talents - used as wallpaper. Sigh. Oldman sizzled in the first two movies. Here his character looked into the abyss and compromised, yet we barely see his pain until it's all over. Freeman's "Lucius Fox" had a lot to be proud of and then a lot to worry about. We don't really /need/ Freeman to give us "the look" that says "the asteroid is coming," but we kinda expect it. He does it so well in a single beat. Those three to five missed "beats" didn't hurt the story, but two mega-talents were already on set and already paid. Editing/direction failed to let them connect with the audience as only they can. Expectations *not* met.

My knowledge of the world and science is often bruised by movies, but this time I felt insulted. Usually this is just engineering stuff (a jet can't actually do "that") but this time we've added geographic impossibilities and more.

A twin turboprop at cruise flies 250-366 MPH. You're gonna put bad guys on ropes to snatch a scientist from inside it while it's flying? Not a chance in the world, but Hollywood does this kind of crap so much, we're used to it by now.

Minion's willing to die for their leader - the antagonist - in large quantities - sure. Wait, there's no Islamic type faith involved? ah, not so likely.

Photographing an English country estate for Wayne Mansion ... well OK, but there are a bunch of former robber baron mansions in Cape Cod that are public parks nowadays - they could REALLY use the location fees to help their maintenance budgets.

Taking VERY WELL KNOWN (and frequently photographed in NatGeo etc.) interiors and exteriors in India and suggest they're a few minutes outside of Pittsburgh - err Gotham; err, NYC; err... Sigh. Suspension of disbelief shattered past point of recovery.

Antagonist in a mask? Check. But why exactly? Constant drip of pain meds, don't ya know. Ah... No. That's not the way pain management works.

10,000 cops trapped in a tunnel for weeks/months fed by care packages? Ah... no. They wouldn't emerge from the tunnel after weeks/months all in starched uniforms and battle ready either.

Terrorist antagonist spouting "we are the 99%" type balderdash at New Yorkers or Pennsylvanians (err, Gothamites) well, OK. BUT A LOT OF THEM BUY INTO IT? Ah...

A 6-figure to 7-figure super car in the garage without Bruce Wayne knowing it is there? No. A Prius or a Suburban sure, but past about $50k, there's a lot of ego in car selection - even for the super rich. They do have a few grins with it though.

Bruce Wayne really needs a cane to walk, then decides to become Batman in a very few days? Only in Hollywierd.

Some Pitsburgh Steelers playing themselves on the gridiron - unless they worked for SEG scale, that's spraying money, not telling a story.

Bat-Transport cycle and 'copter are 100% impossible, but they did look good so that part I can forgive.

Bat-'copter dodging half a dozen surface-to-air missiles by flying between sky-scrapers? Ya know, that's been done so many times, I won't object, other than to simply yawn at what should have been a high tension scene.

Good ride. Lots of wonderful moments. As a whole, it fails to delight. Good opening weekend, if otherwise newsy; but I doubt it breaks $1Bn or even $600m.

6.title: Still can't beat Christopher Reeve's Superman..........
6.content:
I am not in a mood to pit this movie against any other but i was made to think of Superman of the old and then i realized why that film is still superior and still the best comic book film ever made.This film also revolves around the same Superman 2 essence where the villain from the past returns and forms allegiance with a new villain ,Bane in this case to destroy the main character.

The films ending particularly for me is anti-comic book genre and more TV soapie type where there is a twist in the tale.Instead of ending the film with Talia Al'Ghul's revelation the film could have ended with Bane's death.He simply dragged the film for a grand finale.

The film has ended with Robin now taking the charge(probably)....i wonder if the series continues........

6.title: Very disappointing, poor writing, was made to cash-in
6.content:
Being a fan of Christopher Nolan, I was super disappointed in his newest installment. This movie was clearly made to cash-in, no passion. The movie was chock full of one-liners (some with terrible timing) and generally poor scripting.

It felt like a rehash of the previous two movies but executed in a gimmicky way. Almost every dynamic in the story-line was taken from Batman Begins, The Dark Knight, or Inception. It is so weird that Nolan cast actors from Inception in roles that are uncannily similar to the roles they played in Inception. Without getting into spoilers, I thought that every story element had already been executed by Nolan in almost the exact same way in his previous movies. Sure Bane was kinda interesting, but the sound editing for his voice was terrible and amateur. It was as if his voice was omnidirectional (Nolan probably thought this added presence), it was unbearable, as if a overly enthusiastic narrator was reading Bane's lines with a sinister voice.

I felt bad for Anne Hathaway. That girl worked hard for this movie and if the script was written better, she probably could have added a little more personality to the character. (Plus Michelle Pfeiffer is THE catwoman, she dominated that role)

In summary, it was a terrible, poorly written story that resulted in a lengthy, only moderately entertaining flick. I don't recommend this movie if you are expecting to see quality storytelling.

6.title: Better than The Dark Knight ..still far from perfect.
6.content:
I was one who walked out the previous two Nolan Batman films thinking they were...simply okay. Batman Begins was interesting until the plot kicked in and then it was a lot like Tim Burton's Batman replete with a gas attack that didn't carry any weight or importance in the film, despite thousands of people getting gassed. And actually Dark Knight frustrated me because it seemed like a cop movie but it was actually a bit dull and full of comic book ish implausibility (the sonar cell tracker that Batman builds for that one day where he knows he'll have to catch the Joker who will have made a bunch of hostages look like terrorists-- and he just knows Lucius Fox will have to destroy the device when it's all over-- hunh?!) that everyone was raving about, "best movie ever" as good as The Godfather!" etc. etc. Not a chance.

Plus, the problem with Dark Knight was that it was so stark and serious and seemingly grounded in the real world of cops and robbers that it made Batman seem stupid and secondary to the plot. When Batman was standing around the wreckage in the nod to 9-11, my initial response was, "Who's the dork in the costume?" So, you know, I didn't like the movie all that much and preferred say, Iron Man which was a lot of fun and made you believe the on-goings by the sheer charm of its lead actor.

Anyway, Dark Knight Rises is still full of comic book-ish conveniences and leaps of logic but it has a grand, almost operatic outlandishness that makes it a bit more involving and more fun than its predecessor. And it has Catwoman, in a small and underdeveloped part, but still, I love Catwoman as a character and when she's on screen, the movie comes alive. I actually don't understand why both Tim Burton and Christopher Nolan shied away from the Catwoman character and crammed their movies with other villains and needless subplots when the Batman/Catwoman storyline was by far the best thing about their respective movies. Women love romance, right? As long as there's some action guys would be happy. Why not an epic tragic romance centered about Batman and Catwoman?

Going back to the film that is, I have to say I was entertained by its epic, sort of nonsensical plot this time around. And it felt more like a serious Batman comic, centered around Batman -- as opposed to Dark Knight which felt like a big sprawling crime movie with a guy named Batman running around on the periphery. I agree with the criticisms of 'Rises', but what critics seem to be missing about previous Dark Knight is that the tone was all wrong and it makes Batman seem like an afterthought. Rises, while a bit awkward in the details, gets the tone just right. And it's a movie about Batman. Good enough for me.

But yeah, how does a guy with a broken spine come back to full health in two weeks and out punch a big strong steroid fueled powerhouse? Though even the comics had that problem. (I still think Knightfall as written, was a more interesting story)

Okay, enough nerding out.

6.title: Disappointing.
6.content:
Disappointing. Clearly the worst of the three BATMAN movies. Not even close to the BATMAN BEGINS, which surprisingly has always been so underrated.

BANE was pathetic as the villain of an epic franchise ( miss JOKER. RIP Heath Ledger ). BATMAN got no screen time, he wasn't even portrayed as a Superhero in the movie. CATWOMAN couldn't do much. Full points to Freeman, Oldman, Caine and Joseph Gordon though.

Below average action scenes and special effects. Emotions and drama were a stretch.

And seriously , 9.2? Should just be the hype surrounding the BATMAN finale. Expected much better from Nolan. The fans certainly deserved much more.

6.title: The Dark Knight Rises (U/A)-------------Rating: 3/5
6.content:
The Dark Knight Rises (U/A)-------------Rating: 3/5

It is an complete action-thriller....

*Cast and their performances stuns the story to end well.... *BGM was awesome which helps in fastening the screenplay in the second half...... *Direction and cinematography was good and this may lead them to success....

-Story contains to many flashbacks that leads to the complication of script.... -The movie is large must have been little smaller..

6.title: How to be Batman
6.content:
Although I thoroughly enjoyed the performance of many, (Alfred, Cat Woman, Robin) I was utterly confused by the hype surrounding Rises, so I wrote this guide to dissect the caped crusader without ligaments in his knee.

How to be Batman (The Dark Knight)

Be charming, capable, convincing billionaire playboy.

Dump on villains in clever ways, including:

Extraditing a crime boss by attaching him to a plane

Save some idiot by suavely blocking a truck with Lambo

Mysteriously delve in and out of the shadows, juxtaposed to a phenomenal Joker performance.

Defeat the greatest villain of all time by tapping into every cell phone in city.

Sacrifice lifelong love interest for beloved city.

Become martyr for said city.

Alfred is sometimes sad, but mostly proud.

- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -


Batman for Dummies (The Dark Knight Rises)

Do very little for very long time with cane,

get stuck in prison with NO LIGAMENTS in knee and dislocated..vertebra. Yes, vertebra.

Jump (only way to escape the symbolism laden prison, despite being unqualified to ski or even walk)

Somehow find way back into city under complete lock down (unexplained)

Deliver all lines loudly and in plain sight, omitting mysterious and shadowy persona of Batman entirely.

Ask Cat Woman for help (who seems to be doing everything)

Ask Gordon to do the obvious.

Repeat for Lucius

Meanwhile, time is running out

Fly "The Bat", free policemen, then take 5 minutes to dodge 1 volley of missiles between shooting at nothing.

Punch (very prevalent)

Despite a ticking clock and a tendency towards highly intuitive, sophisticated gadgets, more punching.

Get stabbed, despite a valiant punching effort.

Luckily, villains are clueless without the Joker, and decide to wait 5 months for a bomb to self detonate despite very little symbolism and relevance.

Meanwhile, thousands of policeman walk headfirst into heavily fortified line of automatic weapons.

Luckily, villains have never committed a crime and run forward into crowd holding guns, thereby negating any strategic advantage.

Punchfest in town square.

Meanwhile, with no instruction, Cat Woman + Bat Bike is busy doing the hard but simple work of taking out Batman's ENTIRE SOPHISTICATED ARMORY.

After waiting 5 months, Bain decides he can't wait 11 more minutes and tries to shoot you.

Try to recover from numerous plot holes, get into "The Bat"

Swallow clichés and fly neutron bomb off into sunset.

Die in emotionally charged explosion.

Alfred, a highly logical man, is mostly sad, and sometimes confused, but happy to see world renowned "dead" billionaire sitting in plain sight, undisguised, in crowded eatery with Cat Woman.

The End.

The man had no. ligaments.

Even to bypass that by saying his little mechanical knee was powered by some Ironman-like device, there were just too many inconsistencies for me to love this movie.

If nothing else, batman completely disregarded his presence, best served from the shadows. Looking at him in full sight every scene at poorly shot camera angles, delivering his lines just made him and his armor look.. a little ridiculous.

I can't fathom why critics are touting this movie as a worthy successor when it had none of the cold, dark, perverse, morality-driven themes that define Batman. There was no satisfying sense of choice or sacrifice in this movie. Instead, the plot looks like: I should climb out of prison, lets save the city, there's a bomb, I'll sacrifice myself, oh wait, turns out I'm alive. CUE CREDITS

Highly disappointed.

6.title: It was like watching boring movie with batman in it
6.content:
After the second Batman movie I have lost my faith in batman movies and Nolan as director in general. This movie has been hyped well to do well in the box offices but not that many reviewers actually give their honest opinions towards it. Well here is my honest opinion of Batman Dark Knigh Rises: It sucked. It wasn't good enough to entertain. The characters were boring and even though I am fan of Bane as villain he was pretty much raped here. First of all the mask, looked cool in its own but for Bane it was like glitter on vampires. He also spoke with English accent and was member of Ras al Ghuls order? Okay... How about we stick a solid steel bar up Superman ass and call him Man of Steel because of that? There are things to do with origin stories and fcking it up this bad is one thing.

The story was also pretty boring. I almost fell asleep during the movie because there was not much happening. Lots of talk and mumbling but very little actual action. The whole idea that Batman has been just angsting in corner for 8years makes no sense. If the death of Robin did not shook Batman to stop his fighting crime why would death of Harvey Dent do that?

For what its worth, the previews of the movie was good and the soda kept itself cool almost whole movie but the overall movie was bad and i am happy to know that Nolan will not be doing anymore batman movies. Maybe the mantle will go to someone who actually does good Batman movie.

6.title: Has no right to be an average movie.
6.content:
How the hell is this this still in the 9's. It's beating like... Casablanca and stuff, what's going on? The story was tired, recycled from the first one; which didn't have that good a story in the first place, but is forgiven for being half origin.

The villain motives were poor; weren't interesting enough to be delved into; they didn't challenge the audience, there was intimidation but not intrigue.

Bataman was barely in it... which I have to convince people, isn't a nitpick... I like Batman! Generally character arcs were unsatisfying: What came of commissioner Gordon's storyline? What did he contribute? Why bother with all the Alfred afraid for Bruce's life stuff? We got that from the other two. Why did Bruce, a guy who's parents got shot, only go into solitary when Harvey (who put a gun to a kids head) died? Why was Bruce not Batman for so long? Where was Batman? (It's not a nitpick) And why so long in jail? The twist was bland... very bland.

The revelation or, the scene where we realise the title's relevance, had little relevance; it wasn't well developed and didn't resonate through the rest of the movie.

In another dumb action movie, the criticism's above wouldn't matter, but this film has no right to be a dumb action movie. Nolan has, by now, set the bar too high for dumb action movies, superhero movies, explosion blockbusters, to go now and make a film so shallow. A film so cold and un-moving, with innovation set to nought, with subtext dull or ridiculous. I want depth now, Nolan has inflamed that within me. My demands for blockbusters are low ones no longer; I want depth now, I want intelligence and awe found not in set pieces but in character, in story. In a post Dark Knight world, these are my demands. If you don't fulfil them, you are no longer excused.

Yeah, Bane was good, Catwoman was great, there were scenes of intimidation, scenes of dread, scenes with Batman in them, but overall, and it hurts to say this...

...meh, and that is all.

6.title: Disturbing but unfullfilling
6.content:
I thought this was a deeply disturbing but unfullfilling film. Right from the onset you sense the evil that permeates the story as it unfolds. The villain, Bane, is not as psychologically oppressing as the Joker, however, you sense that his pure determination and physical prowess will break and bend the world to his will. Against this is pitted a broken crusader in the from of a desolate Bruce Wayne isolated in his manor. We are being sold the premise that Commissioner Gordon has cleaned up Gotham under the cover of Harvey Dent's authority from beyond the grave. At this point we have already seen references to extraordinary rendition and now we learn that the methods of Gotham's PD has striking similarities to how the U.S. has fought the so-called War on Terror. Prisoners are being held at a Guantanamo-like facility without due recourse, and the sense that something is rotten at the core of government is tangible. A storm is brewing, and neither the people of Gotham, nor its guardians are prepared.

Batman, in my opinion does not even have center stage in his own movie. He is marginalized now, not really trusted by anyone except his life-time servant Alfred and, of course, Jim Gordon who owes him his life. When Batman returns to save the day, he does not rely particularly on his bodily strength and fortitude as he did before. What always made Batman the most special superhero for me, was that he was just a man. Now, half the time he is in a flying machine or on a motor bike which he later, rather handily gives over to the one person - the Catwoman - he chooses to trust despite plenty of warnings not to. Yes, Batman has always use gadgets, but they were wires to increase his velocity and to defy gravity in order to deliver the knock-out punch, by fist. Now, he's just an extension of a machine, firing explosives as he hovers between skyscrapers blowing up his own hardware that Bane's army has taken possession of. It is in the young police officer John Blake that we must look for a true moral conviction and desire to the right thing by simple means and true grit. A sham then, that Joseph Gordon-Leveitt is completely incapable of conveying these emotions.

As for the story, there are some twists and turns in the plot, trying to tie this whole epic together across 3 movies. I still do not know what the League of Shadows is supposed to reflect, or what purpose it has. Trying to place Gotham's fate into a macro context of a world-wide struggle between the established powers of capitalism and the monomaniacal, but still unclear, motivations of the secretive and elusive Ras Al' Gul falls short of delivering any kind of moral lesson or genuine emotion. It is the actions of the agents of madness and violence that make you uneasy, but truly what should scare you are the motivations behind them. In this regard, the League of Shadows is too quirky, too anarchist, and too unclear about its true ambition to be anything to get truly afraid of. What has always been most intriguing about Gotham has been its imperfections and the sense that it's a place that makes it own luck, independent and resolute.

To see the great city and its people become just a facade, a stage, filled with extras for a kind of great battle between forces that really has little to do with the city per se, just doesn't get to you in the way it did when the Joker terrorized the city. Perhaps most strange is the scene where the ragged band of just-freed cops storm against Bane's forces in medieval fashion, two army's face-to-face, clashing in hand-to-hand combat like androids despite the fact that both sides have plenty of fire arms and tactical training. I get a sense that Commissioner Gordon or the fine minds of the Gotham PD really would not have endeavored on such an ill-thought through maneuver. Fittingly then, the actions cuts away from this street mêlée to focus on Batman fighting Bane and we're left guessing how the fight ends.

This movie was designed to be a block-buster. The investment must be recouped, and that means Chris Nolan cannot use all the means required to truly deliver the sucker-punch. It has to be PG-12, and that means it simply does not deliver the graphical violence to really let you feel the inhumanity. Yes, some scenes of material destruction will get at you. A masterfully crafted serial bombing that cuts Gotham off from the world has eerie resonance to real world conflicts and most particularly that of 9/11. But being Norwegian and having endured our own encounter with the Devil on July 22 last year, I cannot but not take seriously the absence of bodily harm that the blows and bullets should have incurred on those who cross the path of Bane and his honchos' brutality. No blood. No screams. Not a gouged eye. It just doesn't get to you.

The way the real protagonist dies in the end is a whimper, just too stupid and far too convenient, uttering a few final words of destiny fulfilled before drawing last breath. No, I am sorry, this was just one movie too far. After the brilliance that was the Dark Knight, this picture fails to deliver the same emotion and to incur the same respect. A tighter manuscript with a shorter run time and a greater emphasis on the true horror that the evil of Bane shows us in flashes of would have made it better. Nothing could come close to the sheer psychological terror of the Joker and the existential questions left by the sheer lack of true meaning behind his actions. Certainly not the League of Shadows.

6.title: Very mixed bag but great ending
6.content:
Nolan is a fabulous director. But I felt like I was watching Batman/Bruce Wayne having a boring pity party and then pit against The Humungous Amongst Us from Mad Max, another orphanish pity party but his all insane rage that made absolutely no sense, even to the plot, even to the ending. And all a bit too darn cliché. And both Batman and Bain from the League of whatever? And Marion Cotillard, always gorgeous and competent. But I don't care whatsoever about that League and Liam Neeson and all of it. Total nonsense. So I would say I thought the plot/script quite weak while the acting was quite good.

Anne Hathaway is excellent and brings sophistication, beauty and much needed humor. I loved her take on Catwoman best because she is a woman, not a woman turned into a lunatic Catwoman.

I love Christian Bale. I just kept thinking, "I bet he wishes he was cast as Bain and had a juicy role." This is a role he can neither sink his teeth into nor save and it must kill him.

That being said, it is very difficult to wear a mask and have an altered voice, as Bain does, and be anything other than a big hunk of talking meat. I found him very boring. I mean come on, Heath Ledger as The Joker was entrancing. Who cares about the Wrestling TV Big Masked Freak?

Joseph Gordon Levitt was solid. Michael Caine wonderful. Morgan Freeman always great. Gary Oldman is good, having little to do.

I thought the gadgets were pretty cool. I thought the police being set up to be massacred over and over was just ridiculous. Please. Are we morons?

Okay - so I've gretched.

The last 40 minutes gets really good. From Batman in the prison on is great. The ending is a huge surprise and excellent. Worth it just to see it.

6.title: Only adequate
6.content:
The weakest of the 3 recent Batman movies

It starts very well. Nice new characters that are in-keeping with the comic books (as far as i know). The plot shows signs of being interesting and intricate, like it will twist and turn. But after Batman first meets Bane, it becomes rather dull, rather cheesy, something we've seen (executed better) a hundred times before.

So you have an hour settling in to a good movie, and then an hour sitting through an ordeal. It doesn't have much of the dark suspense "Batman" feel to it either. It feels like any old movie where the hero saves the day. I couldn't wait for it to end, and after all the anticipation of it's release, I felt rather disappointed.

6.title: Batman isn't even the star of his own movie!
6.content:
I know that this movie is commended by almost every poster on IMDb who has seen it, and not to say it was a bad film- it wasn't. But it did not hold as bright of a candle to "The Dark Knight." Not a die-hard fan of the comics, though I was pleased to read how faithful the brothers Nolan had remained with the comics when writing the scripts to these movies. What I have always liked about Nolan's approach to these films is that he never pushes it into extreme campiness in where it's hard to watch (I have Joel Schumacher in mind with his bastardization of the earlier Batman films). Harking back to the last movie, Heath Ledger doesn't prance around in silly clown make-up or don a permanent 'smile' for no apparent reason ("Why so sad?"): he explains as to why at one point. I liked how Anne Hathaway wore her get-up with the goggles that at first glance, appeared to be silly "cat ears"- but then wore them for what they were at times when the scenes called for it. Although everything about Bane was pretty implausible.

Is it my imagination, or did it feel as if Batman wasn't even the star of his own film after about 45 minutes into this? Reminded me of "Superman III" with how it became the Richard Pryor Show. It was tailored more for Gary Oldman and Joseph Gordon-Levitt. Batman and "The Cat" moved over while we dealt with the "suited villains," Matthew Modine, Morgan Freeman and supporting characters assuming command of the film (whom I think we were supposed to be shocked and awed by, but weren't). Christopher Nolan makes very ambitious films, no doubt- but I don't seem to share the same enthusiasm so many others have for his work. Personally, I'm an admirer of "Memento," but afterward, Nolan's films seem to fall into a predictable pattern with how the story is structured. At times, this felt like a continuing re-hash of "The Dark Knight," with some "Inception" and even "Batman Begins" peppered into it. But come to think of it, his films seem to always have a shocking beginning; followed by an hour or so of expository talk; and SO many characters that we don't know who we're supposed to keep focus on; followed up with a four to five layered climax in where it takes at least a half-hour to wrap up- that it all becomes pedestrian and boring. (Michael Mann follows a similar pattern to his films in terms of story- structure: Heat; Miami Vice; Public Enemies) And why is it that he always picks the same talent? With the exception of Bale reprising the title role, we have Cillian Murphy (4 films now); Michael Caine (EVERY film he does- there must be a clause in his contract to appear in every Nolan film, or vice-versa); Joseph Gordon-Levitt (two); Marion Cottliard (two); Tom Hardy (two)Oy vey! There are other actors out there, you know! I don't mean disrespect for Mr. Caine, but he is the same guy in every movie.

Sadly, this film never seemed to reach the emotional zenith I could tell it was trying to convey. If Nolan intends (or intended) to have Gordon-Levitt carry the torch- he isn't handsome nor charismatic enough to be a superhero. Not to say that that's a requirement these days, but for him to be Robin? Why? A previous poster stated that they didn't buy the love-story between Wayne and Kyle, but it made an interesting twist at the end. Not a believable one (since they never had any chemistry to begin with), but nevertheless- they looked good together. I think that was Nolan's desire.

6.title: A Subversive Achievement That Is Easy To Admire, But Hard To Like.
6.content:
"The Dark Knight Rises" sees trilogy director Christopher Nolan's thematic vision straight-through to its logical and supposed end, and if anything, it shows that Nolan is probably the director-to-beat for dramatic superhero storytelling.

After the candy-confectionery "The Avengers" earlier this summer with its equally huge crowd-pleasing mash-up of graphic novel heroes and heroines, this film is like a brutal poison-pill of apocalypse and anger.

It is certainly one of the most surprisingly subversive Big-Studio pictures ever to twist the nose of big targets like capitalism, socialism, the issue of police states and definition of law & order, as well as both sides of the environmental movement.

If the film is a success, it certainly is exciting that in this era of 'safe' cookie-cutter movie-making, director Nolan was given carte-blanche to create a sequel to a universally-beloved franchise with such an overarching, nihilistic scenario. Surely ticket buyers may not have had to factor into or wrestle with such counter-oppressive messages in their Batman popcorn entertainment before, but the film is a curious delivery system of unsettling real-world observations wrapped in the mythos of a cartoon character.

The picture's epic scope contains an abundance of dazzling technical achievements filtered through a fractured prism of comic-book storytelling coupled with plot elements ripped from today's headlines, such as the Occupy movement to the Wall Street meltdown. It's excessively violent, sometimes shockingly so.

Despite "The Dark Knight Rises" solid, illustrious pedigree in front of and behind the camera, as an entertainment, the film lacks the wit, creativity and viewer release of previous installments of the franchise. Perhaps sacrificed in a percussive effort to create a sinister tone that may play well to some, Nolan's "The Dark Knight Rises" amounts to a dizzying, bombastic 'big-ideas' canvas that - for better or worse - re-frames the overall thematic structure of his series.

The film's big caveat is that it recognizes that Bruce Wayne is an older, beaten man, and not a superhero of some amazing cosmic superpower. Despite of all of the possible gimmicks and technological frou-frou that the character of Wayne might have at his disposal to dispatch bad guys and save the world, Christian Bale's character is reduced to a physical human being who is pummeled endlessly at the mercy of the film's main villain, the confused patriot Bane (actor Tom Hardy) - whose expressive face is seen only in a flashback.

A good film is best with a good villain. The Bane character anchors the film as an intriguing - if enigmatic - adversary to Batman, with careful goals and an early devious Macguffin plot. However by the end Bane is reduced to an angry avatar with nothing but hate for all human race, and no way to beat him.

In the film's final reels, "The Dark Knight Rises" trades its expected superheroics in to revel in a non-stop onslaught of physical violence, humiliation and brutal force that is both indignant and mostly over the top. TDKR lacks the canny outplotting of previous entries in the series, and instead takes a leisurely 150+ minutes to reinforce that this is not a fantasy film, but in fact an unwinnable sturm un drang.

For the first time in a Batman entertainment, I found this picture's constant affront distressing and off-putting to the point of better judgment urging me to leave the theatre and do something happy and more enjoyable with my time. I stuck it out.

Easy to admire but very hard to like, "The Dark Knight Rises" is one of the most aggressively depressing, joyless movies I have ever sat through.

6.title: Over rated.
6.content: Yet another Nolan Batman movie about a crazy terrorist. Pretty sure we saw this in the previous movie. It would've been nice to have something different. The new movie with Robert Pattinson has highlighted the Nolan movies are definitely overrated - good for the time I guess - but now watching them back many years later - overrated. Also 3 movies of Bales flu voice is too much !!!

6.title: A great villain should never have an anti-climatic end because he/she becomes irrelevant and forgotten.
6.content: When I first saw the trailer of this movie I was very excited. The first two in the series are two of my favorite movies. I also find them to be much superior to the Tim Burton ones. I won't mention the Joel Schumacher ones especially Batman and Robin because those were just plain terrible. The Dark Knight in particular should be used as the Gold Standard when making comic book hero movies. When I went to watch the Dark Knight Rises I saw a movie that had it all. It had a great villain, BANE, who was amazingly portrayed by the gifted Tom Hardy. In fact, I like Bane almost as much as the Joker. In fact, as I read reviews I find it unfair to compare the two villains as they have almost nothing in common other than their wanting to create havoc. The way Bane was portrayed in Batman and Robin shouldn't serve as any comparison to Bane in The Dark Knight Rises. In the Dark Knight Rises Bane is articulate and calculating in his destruction of Gotham City. His manner of speech is that of a highly educated and intelligent person with a great scientific mind. In short he basically wants to create a new world order starting Gotham City. The Joker was just a madman who wanted to destroy just because he wanted to. I didn't mind the long pauses in the action. I didn't mind the extensive dialog because this is what made the Nolan series standout from the Tim Burton ones. Unfortunately, the Dark Knight Rises didn't live up to my expectations for several reasons. First, I found that Ann Hathaway was trying to hard to be seductive in her role. Her manner of speech when she was dancing with Wayne (i.e. there is a storm coming Mr. Wayne) was annoying and a big turn off for me. I am glad she didn't get so much screen time. I did like how her character played both sides. This gave her character complexity. I just wished she didn't act so seductive because she didn't have to. Secondly and most importantly, I felt that Bane's death was anti-climatic. His death happens so fast that if you turn your head for a moment you would miss his death scene. I expected a final battle between the hero and villain but it never materialized. In addition, the twist at the end effectively made Bane an irrelevant character. I kept hoping for Bane to appear during the end credits but to my disappointment it didn't happen. Also the manner of death of the true villain was also disappointing and anti-climatic. Bane deserved a better end than he got. In fact his end further reinforces my opinion that after the true bad guy is revealed that Bane is an irrelevant character in the movie. A great villain should never have an anti-climatic end because he/she becomes irrelevant and forgotten. This movie could have actually been made without Bane. By far my favorite characters in the movie were Miranda Tate, Luscious Fox, Commissioner Gordon and Detective Blake. I really liked the Miranda Tate and Detective Blake twists at the end. In fact, out of all the characters Detective Blake was the most developed and complex characters in the movie and I firmly believe his character really help the movie.

6.title: how could he survive that ???
6.content: In last scene, we all saw the hero alive somehow but to be honest I would like him to die to make it more epic end. Additionally, how he survived the atomic bomb?. In brief, his surviving is unreasonable and his death can serve the story.

6.title: A few things that did not work/add up for me...solid 6 stars
6.content:
**SPOILERS** There is a few things that just made NO sense or just basically left me {as the viewer}, feeling unsatisfied or worse yet, down-right confused! As much as I like Nolan and Tom Hardy with his portrayal of Bane, I have quite a few things that make this my least favorite of the series, with TDK being the best. Mostly because a few things either did not make much sense or were plot holes to me.

-Batman: Sure, all of his crime fighting and injuries took a toll on his body, but all you do is get these cool rings that tighten over your knees and suddenly it not only fixes your legs, it fixes all the rest of your injuries and bad limbs? This one is not such a big deal, but still I found it rather comical and ridiculous.

-Batman's "gruff voice": Sure, Batman disguises his voice like in Batman Begins and TDK, but did they really have to make it so over the top? Now even talking to people who are his allies, he speaks in a growl when he used to just speak in a husky voice. They should have left it like the first film, which was believable without being over the top.

-Bane: is physically the superior of Batman; in the opening fight scene he beats Batman easily and overpowers him. He is also in the majority of the film shown to be a criminal mastermind and seems to have all his bases covered, breaking necks and cashing checks. Then, in the end, he ends up doing all of this thanks to his puppy love for Talia al Ghul. He is a mere henchman and stooge for Talia. Then to add insult to injury, he is killed off like an afterthought by Catwoman on a Batpod. The man who broke Batman and took over the crime of Gotham, gets taken out with a gun as an afterthought?

Talia al Ghul: I can understand a love-interest with a hidden agenda, revenge. Why would she sleep with him when her ultimate goal was to just get revenge on him for her father and carry out his dream to destroy Gotham? Acting as a love interest is one thing, but that makes no sense. I know she had to get his trust but hard to believe she would want to do that considering her father fell because of Batman...

Surprised: Anne Hathaway is hot, and she surprised me with her portrayal of Catwoman without being over the top (Halle Berry much}. She pulled off the sexiness which I thought would be hard for her (or anyone for that matter} and was very good in the role. This was a positive thing and I was impressed because many thought she could never pull it off.

6/10: Has a lot of redeeming qualities, but falls short in a lot of areas. No where near as good as TDK and not as good as Batman Begins. Being realistic should not prevent things from making sense.

6.title: Decent movie, but ruined by plot holes and confusing ending.
6.content:
Don't get me wrong, I really liked "Batman Begins", and I LOVED "The Dark Knight". So naturally, I was super psyched for the epic conclusion, to this soon to be trilogy. But after watching it, I gotta say...It was just OK.

It was pretty disappointing, and I was really hoping for something more. I mean, the movie is over 2 and a half hours long, but it sure has a lot of "nothing" in it. Boring drawn out scenes without anything happening, instead of having character development or actually having BATMAN in the movie. Seriously, Batman appears only a couple of times in this film...this film about BATMAN! It also had a mediocre ending, with a lot of questions unanswered. And also...the plot holes. They really distracted from the main story, and there wore too many of them.

But the film has stuff I enjoy. I thought Bane (even though he had a odd voice) was pretty awesome, and when Batman appeared on screen, he was pretty cool. I also enjoyed the fight scenes, and the scenes with the whole city at war.

So really, if you liked the other films, you should watch this one too. Just don't expect too much.

In conclusion:

Pros:

+Bane

+Batman (when he appeared)

+Fight and war scenes

Cons:

-Not enough Batman

-Really rushed death scenes

-Batman's back problems

-Plotholes

-Ending

6/10

6.title: Bane vs. The Memory of Heath: Heath Wins
6.content:
I'm declaring The Dark Knight Rises to be a misfire, a confusing barrage of plot and speechifying without enough sticking to it. Nolan directs with very little of the stylistic energy of Inception or the propulsion of The Dark Knight. Easily one of the most anticipated films of the year, and despite an A-level cast, cutting edge special effects, and a terrifying villain, The Dark Knight Rises sinks.

For a minute, I'm going to focus on Bane, the villain of this third film in the Nolan Batman series. As played by Thomas Hardy, Bane resembles Darth Vader, Osama bin Laden, Sensei John Reese from the Cobra Kai in The Karate Kid with his trademark lapel-grabbing, and a He-Man Masters of the Universe character with swollen arms. Bane's spider-like mask robs us of seeing Hardy's full face, but his voice is wonderfully high-pitched and eerie, supposedly modeled on Eastern European voices recorded in the 1920's. However, I do have to complain if I cannot understand over 20% of the dialogue because of the way it was recorded. Frankly, I needed subtitles or Bane. I'm not saying do without the mask. Absolutely not. The mask ties Bane to Batman as well as the tradition of samurai, as well as it provides endless speculation about its functionality. How is it keeping him alive? Why does he need it? What happens when Batman punches it real, real hard? However, when the recording of a major character's voice is murky and indecipherable, Nolan has just undercut his own film. I lost threads of major speeches because of the sound quality. Bane's philosophies seem anarchic and revolutionary, and yet I'm not sure what drives him. Glimmers arrive in the last third of the film, far too late in my opinion.

I'm not a Batman scholar, and I can't rule definitively on the series. I've read that Nolan did not want to mention the character of The Joker in this film at all out of respect to Heath Ledger's memory, and that to me, again seems like a misfire and a miscalculation. The Joker's decision to kill Rachel Dawes rocked Bruce Wayne to his core; the open-ended decision to leave Heath Ledger's Joker hanging off the scaffolding of a building, tied up and ready for Arkham Asylum begs the question, What would have happened if Bane had united with the recently freed Joker in this film? At one moment, Bane calls the inmates of Blackgate, Gotham's most notorious prison, to join him in his revolution and they overwhelm the guards. Did this film need a slap of Ledger's brilliant, anarchic performance as The Joker? I say whole-heartedly, Yes! Bane seems content during the last third of the film to stand in the shadows, retreat and withdraw, in a way that is sadly disappointing and fails to develop him as a character. I'm endlessly impressed with his quick fighting style, Hardy's ferocious biceps, as well as his WWF-style, fur-coat wearing posture. I'm not at all satisfied by how Bane's story line was resolved as well. It felt like a cheat for a character of his mythos.

Nolan is reaching in the film, reaching for profundity, for connection to world that we live in with banks terrorizing homeowners, with Wall Street destroying Main Street, with the 1% vs. the 99%. Attempts are clumsily made to link the Dent Act to the overreach of the Patriot Act in our post-9-11 society. I admire the desire to be topical and cash in on some of the rage that has boiled over in America. However, beyond a few riotous crowds pushing the rich out onto the street, as well as some destruction, there is little sense of the chaos that has descended upon Gotham during the days of Bane's rule. I didn't get a sense of how the populace responded to the brazen act of terrorism or Bane's order to govern themselves. I was interested in how Commissioner Gordon and other police officers subverted Bane's rules and avoided the death squads, but not enough was ever made clear. Fall turns into winter, and the film boils down at moment to Gary Oldman jumping onto moving trucks which are simply not as guarded and secure as they should be. I'm still unclear who was holding the detonator. Nolan lost an opportunity to present a fully realized universe here, the hidden, cowering citizenry of Gotham with all of their naked ambition and desires unrestrained by police or common order.

In his pursuit of hyper-realism, has Nolan lost something in the telling of the Batman legend? Or, is this film just a minor step backwards from The Dark Knight, a high-watermark of comic book blockbusting entertainment, but still miles above the typical Hollywood dreck? As for this film's ending, Nolan had an opportunity to fully close a chapter forever with his sage and begin a new one. I'll say this; I liked the opening of the new chapter, and the penultimate sequence of shots in Italy robs the film of some of its pathos and power. There was a way to keep some open-ended qualities to that scene, and Nolan chose to avoid his ambiguous Inception spinning top. In this film, he shows us the top falling over which to me is not as enjoyable as the mystery. And, Heath Ledger's performance as The Joker and that character itself casts a shadow over The Dark Knight Rises in terms of performance and passion. It is hard to escape that shadow. But cheers to Tom Hardy for all that he did to make Bane indelible.

6.title: Exciting to watch, frustrating to think about
6.content:
This is a good movie. It has decent action, some well-developed character arcs and a few frightfully effective scenes. However, because of its pedigree (the director, budget, actors and predecessor), I expected more.

I wanted a brave thought-provoking finale that would have turned Nolan's Batman trilogy into an all-time masterpiece, on par with Star Wars and Indiana Jones trilogies. A lot of over-excited cool-aid drinkers think he pulled it off too, but I think, over time, the film's problems will become more and more apparent and eventually overshadow the initial positive reaction, the way it happened with The Episode One.

Problems such as:

NO BATMAN IN A BATMAN MOVIE


I'm not a big fan of batman character and superhero comics in general, but even I think the middle part, with Bruce out of the picture, was too long. This was a proper story arc for the first movie, not the ending of a trilogy.

TOO MANY SIDESHOWS


The movie tries to introduce both Catwoman (never called as such) and Robin. It definitely needed Robin, as Batman's successor, but Catwoman? Her arc was well executed, sure, but it didn't really tie into any of the major themes of the movie and trilogy, making it ultimately pointless.

This 45 minutes would have been better spent putting some more 'meat' on the whole 'Gotham under siege' situation, which brings us to...

SUPERFICIAL TREATMENT OF THE MAIN THEME


Batman and Gordon say Gotham is saved thanks to their lie. Bane says Gotham is a cesspool of corruption and that 99% is silently stirring with resentment. Bane takes over the city and gives it to the masses. What do they do? Revolution? Resistance? In between? Was Bane right? Was Batman right?

We just don't know. Other than a few contrived kangaroo court scenes (which seems to be under control of Bane's fanatics), we never really see how the ordinary people experienced the crisis. Think back to The Dark Knight and the two boats scene. This movie needed scenes like that. But whether because of political hot-potatitis or PG rating or simple lack of screen-time, we only see a few vague training-montage-like snapshots of what should have been the meat of the story.

And of course, this also brings into question...

BANE'S PLAN


Bane makes his move and brings down both Batman and Gotham City in one fell scoop. Brilliant! He takes Batman to his super prison, shows him a TV and gloats how he's going to torture Gotham before Batman's eyes. "You have't seen anything yet", he crows.

YES! Can't wait to see the rest of his plan! Will he turn the poor against the rich? Neighbor against neighbor? Will he trick one strata of the falling society to take out another, like Joker did with criminals in The Dark Knight's opening? Will he spread his madness to the society at large? The USA? The world?

.... or will he simply sit on his ass and wait for the bomb to explode, taking both him, his protégé and the last remnants of the secret society he claims to champion? WHAT!? Come on, what kind of nonsense is this? He didn't torture Batman. He didn't torture Gotham. He didn't seem to have a plan at all.

If he actually did something with the city he took over, he might have given more meat to another aspect that sorely needed more time, which is...

ROBIN'S ARC


Robin starts a perspective pro order cop. In the 2nd act, he starts losing faith in the system he is sworn to protect. In the big finale, he casts off the chains of ineffective government bureaucracy and steps in to take Batman's place as Gotham's reigning vigilante.

At least that was the plan. The problem is, we don't ever see the reasons behind his decision. Was cops blowing the bridge to prevent Bane from killing the entire city such an unreasonable decision, to push this law & order guy into vigilantism? Even though I knew they were grooming him for Batman's replacement/sidekick, it came as a real surprise for me when he threw his badge away.

Even worse, the cops in this movie aren't ineffective. They are the ones who take down Bane's army and stop the bomb from exploding. Batman is mostly just flying his little high-tech chopper around, which anyone could do (very over-used plot device, BTW). The cops here are the heroes! And Robin is somehow disillusioned by them? How? Why? This is another place where the minutes taken from Catwoman's pointless arc could have come in handy.

Of course, all this might not have mattered, as some of the movie's major problems lie outside Nolan's jurisdiction, the largest one of them being

REALISTIC BATMAN IN 21ST CENTURY


Batman was conceived a long time ago, when punching up obvious square- faces criminals and throwing them into jail seemed like a proper way for a vigilante to deal with crime. Nolan is aware how naïve this idea is. In his realistic take on Batman, he's constantly trying to appease this comic book background with modern reality. At times, he event succeeds.

And then, he has thousands of cops charge machine-gun-wielding paramilitaries with basically nightsticks. There's a rousing music and the good guys eventually win, of course, but in my mind, the whole time, I was like "Bullshit". It just doesn't work.

Nolan had stretched it too far and the thin line of believability has snapped. Even his major villain resolutions demonstrate the bankruptcy of Batman's ideas: both Bane and the girl are taken out by HE rockets, not handcuffs and the due process of the law.

Welcome to the 21st century, Batman fans. Take off your shoes and produce your biometric IDs in an orderly fashion.

Overall, a good film. Just not all it could have been.

6.title: One Big Montage
6.content:
I saw this opening night and paid $15 per ticket for a non 3d movie. I'm not going to go as far as to say this movie sucked. And I feel like it is over shadowed by the tragedy in Colorado, but the score to this movie, that was heard in the previous two movies, was played in almost every scene. Almost every scene was a montage, summarizing the passage of time, but in an expanded form. I don't know the technical term used for it, but each scene usually last just a few minutes before cutting to another scene. The longest scene was probably the opening one in the airplane or at bruce wayne's house; both were probably 5 min long before they cut to something else. There was very little character development and a few plot fallacies with the setting and environment. I did very much like the ending, but thought they could've gone about it a whole completely different way. The editing to this movie is non-logical, it does move the story and action forward, but it makes assumptions that the viewer won't connect, or at least to the more intelligent viewers. The plot tries to misdirect the viewer with a twist about the villain, but I feel cheapened because the character development of the head villain was never developed. The movie pretty much spends 5 mins in a montage explaining why and how the villain is who they are then expects the audience to accept it. Other characters too such as selina's, or soon to be catwomen,character was never developed either. She is a dynamic character who can't decide which side of the fence she wants to play on, but the movie never gives you reasons for her characteristics, it just expects you to accept this, which I feel is contrary to the previous two movies, where characters like bruce wayne, his ego batman, alfred, the joker, even fox's character is developed thoroughly; but not in this one.

In summary, weaker characters, inconsistent plot, but good special effects and action. I would only pay to see this in matinée.

6.title: Dark Knight Rises disappoints
6.content:
The movie is good on its own but do not provide you the same fast paced all action of Darkknight. The first half was really slow and the super hero was never there. Wayne Bruce was also not at his charming best. Caine produces another cameo touching upon the human side of Batman Gotham's struggles and fall along with Two face was not convincing enough.Bane, the villain had a great physical presence but was no match for the legendary Joker played by Heath Ledger.Selina kyle fits in but again the character cannot match Darkkinght's Harvey Dent. All in all, i felt the supporting cast was not as strong as the lineup we had for the prequel.

Maybe the brilliant prequels raised the expectation but sadly did not meet them. It saddens me to think that Christian Bale would not be playing another Batman

6.title: Highly Overrated Superhero Film
6.content:
After being told by friends that this was even better than 'The Dark Knight' I had high expectations. Unfortunately these expectations were not met. Being one of the few people who actually thought 'The Dark Knight' was good rather than great, perhaps that is an indication that I would not enjoy this as much, because Heath Ledger's Joker was really what made the previous film such a good watch.

As far as superhero films go I found this pretty average, hence my score. I thought it was too long, and although it ticked all the boxes, providing action and good acting there was really nothing that grabbed my attention. In all honesty I was waiting for it to finish, which is not the sign of a great film in my opinion. Perhaps this film would have more appeal if I had read the Batman comics, though I enjoyed most other superhero films without having read the comics (V for Vendetta being the exception - I love the film and comic). I found Bane to be a stock superhero villain, powerful but quite generic really. I also didn't really engage with his motives - the Joker was much easier to understand, as he had no remorse or morals, and was basically doing things for enjoyment.

By all means go and watch it, as it seems that most people consider it a truly groundbreaking masterpiece, but in no way does it warrant one of the highest scores on this website. It is far inferior to numerous films rated below it on IMDb, and personally I would not bother buying the DVD or re-watching it.

My 24 year old son calls this film epic..... I'm sorry the younger generation don't know what epic means. CGI's and explosions don't give films the right to be called epic.

6.title: Mixed emotions?
6.content:
This movie has definitely been one of the most anticipated movies of the year. The million dollar question, however, is whether it deserved the noise around and for it. The answer is not clear, I am afraid.

Trilogies are, by default, problematic. It quite scarce to produce three movies that stand at the same level and Nolan's trilogy poses no exception. As is well-known, the new Batman series has been stigmatized by the death of Heath Ledger, which has elevated the second part into an unreachable level. Fair? Perhaps not, but that is a fact to live with.

That said let's move to the movie in hand. The Dark Knight Rises (DKR) has its moments but, unfortunately, its bottleneck lies in the point where the vast majority of modern movies is, i.e. in the script. Indeed, acting is adequate, cinematography is fine, special effects are appropriate but the plot is simply not in accordance with our expectations. In fact, Mr Nolan had several years to work on the script and, therefore, trivial and obvious errors are not forgiven; such errors are not reported herein since other reviewers have made excellent work in pointing them out. One expects that more care would have been placed on the development of a decent script for this trilogy.

Summing up, the DKR is a good movie, with the potential to be much better, but cursed to live in the shadow of the Dark Knight. Probably this is not a good excuse for the sloppiness that we encountered but, nonetheless, can provide some justification. I think 6/10 is fair enough for the outcome that we experienced.

6.title: A disaster mitigated by production quality
6.content:
Surprisingly enough, The Dark Knight Rises does not live up to the first two installments of the trilogy.

There's too much story for one film and this heavily messes up the pacing and the overall structure of the film. There so much dialogue that is just exposition dumps for the viewers to understand what is going on. Some are so cringy it makes you wonder how it was even possible in a Nolan film. There are too many crutches that hold the story, everyone knows where everyone is, everything is always super convenient, there's just too many coincidences. Nothing besides basic symbolism is left to the viewer's interpretation, everything else is straight up delivered through bad dialogue. They did make sure that the viewer wouldn't have to do any thinking.

Bane is wasted and reduced to a mini-boss, Catwoman is passable, but Hathaway acting ruins what is left. There are too many side characters and the story desperately tries to give them meaningful filler missions to justify their existence.

The first half of the film is barely watchable if the viewer has somewhat of a critical mind and it completely crumbles if you start asking questions. This is especially painful after the greatness Nolan has delivered with The Dark Knight.

The prison segment and Batman's restoration is probably the best part of the film, but the climax is still underwhelming.

If you expect a deep dive into the characters after The Dark Knight you will not find those here, this is merely an action blockbuster with an overly complicated story that is barely held together by the writers taking some barely believable big stretches and assumptions.

The production quality helped with mitigating the disaster that this could've been, but the only good thing about this film I will remember is probably Michael Caine's acting.

6.title: In keeping with the series, a little too epic.
6.content: To take the same source material for the campy 1960's Adam West television show and give it the "Lawrence of Arabia" treatment takes some courage and Nolan is to be praised for his ambition. However, "Rises" like the Heath Ledger-fueled middle installment of the series suffers from somewhat from the over-inflation. Parts of the sumptuously shot tale of The Batman's redemption meander and drag and all but scream "something profound is happening in this scene". The grandiosity (the football game scene alone must have cost a fortune) of the production makes certain character interactions banal by comparison. At one point, The Batman and the somewhat campy Bain (at what point did you want him to just take off the goofy mask?) get into a straight-up fistfight and the schoolyard beatdown feels a little jejune and disappointing. The borrowed parts also feel a little beneath the film particularly the opening hijacking scene which is wholly lifted from a 1993 Sylvester Stallone film called "Cliffhanger". The sheer scale of Nolan's vision does a good job of masking some mediocre performances. Again, the angular Christian Bale seems more at sea in the part than Michael Keaton at point escaping from a foreign hell-hole, making it back to a Gotham on the bring of nuclear destruction and arriving in town grinning like a Spanish tourist come to see the latest Harry Connick, jr. musical. Anne Hathaway suffers from a similar illness - her good-nature and bright personality are far better suited to the tween fair ("The Princess Diaries") that made her name. Having said that, you have to go back to Eartha Kitt to find a decent Catwoman although Michelle Pfeiffer's tactic of infusing the character with a dollop of crazy was a good attempt. Poor Michael Caine looks like he is putting on an acting clinic for advanced students. Having said all that, like "Avatar" the film is a beautiful thing to behold despite the bad acting (Bale), dopey characters (Bane), borrowed ideas (the essence of the plot may have been written by Zaccotti Park protesters) and unrealistic ending. In short, rent it on pay per view.

6.title: Loved Prestige
6.content:
Loved Presige, but not thrilled with this film

Way too violent and kind of boring. It's not Nolan's fault. Superhero films are just idiotic overall I think.

Christopher Nolan & Jonathan Nolan's Screenplay is excellent in parts, but at times, it comes across as dragging & long. For example, the bad-guy, Bane, played by Tom Hardy, why does he hate Gotham so much & why he's being so god-damn heartless. There is proper reason, yet he's creating a chaos.
