So fans of Batman, Christopher Nolan, superheroes, video-game like special effects and Morgan Freeman in a spencer - will not be disappointed - thanks to the great production value - but in my opinion there are much better films out there that deserve the hype THE DARK KNIGHT RISES gets.

7.title: Not so "Dark" Knight
7.content:
I would like to start this review by highlighting that I am a fan of Batman, and also a fan of Christian Bale.

For me this was a very good film...... BUT - It was not a Batman film.

Before you shoot me down in flames - let me explain.

For me Batman is perfectly played out in the original Batman (Tim Burton version) Its Dark its gritty and yet it still has an element of fantasy and mystery) The Dark Knight rises is lacking the darkness that should be in a batman movie. There was far too much light! Whilst the film had some classic flash backs to his childhood etc, I think the point of Bruce Wayne being emotionally scared by the loss of his parents is missing.

Finally - For me Batman was not really in the film... He had less screen time than most of the other actors....

I also felt that by lowering the certificate to a 12A they have compromised on the realism, Shoot out scenes and bone breaking action seems cut or missing All in all it was a good film and worth a watch, But I would not put it in the same league as Batman / Batman Returns / Batman Begins / Dark Knight.

7.title: An impartial review
7.content:
I am not a fan of Nolan's Batman franchise. I think he made the superhero too emo and angsty in general and glamorizes the villains too much. I think his movies are lacking what makes comic books comic books- the grain of comedy that comes from clever one-liners and the heroes ability to laugh at themselves. In other words, this batman takes himself way to seriously for a man swinging around in a costume playing vigilante. That said, I am not a hater of the franchise low- balling the ratings just to hurt its standing. I am being fair and honest in my review of the title so those who read this review can decide for themselves whether they want to see it or not.

This movie is entertaining. I did find myself interested in what happened next. The action moved along at a good pace and the story unwound in a timely matter. There were only two places it dragged on a little. The first was Batman's first fist fight with Bane. It just lasted too long, the audience started to get restless and whisper and fidget. The same thing happened again when Batman was hauling the bomb out over the bay in his new flying machine. It was several minutes of watching him fly over the bay without any real tension to make us anxious. We knew he would make it away from the city or there would be no point to the movie. So why have us standing there gazing after him for so long. If the audience in theater gets restless enough to rustle, the timing is off.

There were far too many very dark scenes. Movie makers think it is artistic to shoot in full dark or dark lit only by a fireplace or a strategically placed blue light. It may be artistic but it is annoying to the watcher who is peering at the screen trying to make out what is happening. Hearing is not enough. Unless it is a monster movie and something is going to jump out of the darkness at us, we want to see what is going on. We have no way of knowing if the sex scene was hot or romantic or even boring because we didn't see anything but the occasional flash of fire lit skin.There were other places in the movie too where the screen was so dark we just had to guess what was going on.

Bane's diction was probably the worst problem with the movie. They made Bane talkative and gave him a rather cultured sounding way of speaking totally out of keeping with the comic book Bane. Then they slapped on the mask. Muffled is a kind way to put it. People were whispering and asking their seat mates what he just said. This was bad movie making. When Star Wars was filmed, they dubbed in Darth Vader's voice using a separate actor than the one in the mask. They could have spent the extra time to fix this problem in post production or just filmed and recorded the dialog separately then put them back together. It would have been easy since they didn't even have to worry about matching lip movement.

Characterization was good though there were way too many extra's without personalities. The main stay characters and the villains were well fleshed out.

Once again, Batman's motivation is saving Gotham City, though to be honest, seeing how the people behave when they are in a state of anarchy makes you wonder if anyone other than Robin and his bus load of orphans is worth saving.

This movie is grim, slower paced than its predecessors and has more moral ambiguity. The end twist on who the real villain is is good however the conclusion of the movie is not satisfying. I won't spoil it, but if you are a serious fan of this version of Batman it may let you down.

7.title: A satisfying conclusion to thrilling trilogy
7.content: Christopher Nolan has continuously provided us with intelligent, mature and original material with his blockbuster film-making, and after the dark knight and inceptions it was likely the dark knight rises would never truly live up to the monumental expectations placed upon its shoulders. The dark knight was a rare specimen, a comic book film that reflected modern society and raised deep questions in a way that never felt preachy or forced. The film was celebrated universally and went down with immense critical acclaim. Thus The dark knight rises has a lot to live up to. Not only does it have to compete with two modern greats in Christopher Nolan's previous batman films, but it also has to compete with Nolans more recent offering inception. The good news is, whether you think this matches the brilliance of begins, the thrills of the dark knight, or the professionalism of inception, TDKR does bring a satisfying conclusion the dark knight legend. The film is full of the intelligence and maturity you'd expect although it has to be said it never goes quite as dark as you might hope. Nolan once again has created a blockbuster that assumes the audience is as intelligent as he is, rather than patronising them and treating them like children who have only come to be dazzled by explosions and fist fights. Having said that when Nolan does bring in the pyrotechnics and the brawls they are stunning. High points include a jaw droppingly brutal fight between Bane and our hero mid way through the film where you can feel every single punch, and Banes escape from captivity in a plane that is unlike anything you've ever seen before. As usual the cast is all on top form. Bale brings us his most tragic and underplayed performance yet as a broken man following the events of the dark knight, Michael Cane provides reliable support as the true beating heart of the film in its more subtle small moments, Morgan Freeman injects some small humour in the film to counter act the sometimes overwhelming seriousness of the story, whilst Joseph Gordan Levitt proves to be a welcome presence as a newcomer to the trilogy. Other newcomers perhaps are not as impressive. Marion Cotillard's Miranda is a fairly uninteresting addition to the characters inhabiting Gotham, whilst Anne Hathaway amounts to little more than a waste of space, not that there's anything wrong with her performance, its just we'd gladly lose some time with her in favour of more time with Batman or our villain. Which brings us to Bane. You have to feel sorry for anyone following in the footsteps of Heath Ledgers unforgettable Joker, yet Tom Hardy proves he is more than up to the job as the hulking threatening legitimately believe Bane, who unlike previous incarnations of his character has real method, psychology and ideas behind his mask. The controversy over Banes verbal clarity has divided opinion but you will at least be able to make out most of his dialogue if not all of it and even if you don't, Hardy's physicality and facial expressions more than compensate in letting you know what the intelligent brute is thinking at all times. Bane allows us to really see Batman pushed to his physical limits as he faces an opponent stronger than ever before and as Batman is pushed to his physical limits he also pushed closer to his psychological limits too. Outside of the cast we have a visually stunning film, with brilliant cinema-photography, visual effects, and a brilliant (as usual) accompaniment from Hanz Zimmers score. The pacing of the film drags in places (particularily in an overlong 2nd act) but there's always a stunning moment just around the corner to inject life back into the narrative. And by the time the credits roll you really feel like you've not been cheated and have come to a dramatic conclusion to the batman story. The magnificent screenplay allows us to know then end is just around the corner (as Selina Kyle says "Theres a storm coming") and when it arrives it does so marvellously. The Dark Knight rises, may not be perfect. It has its pacing problems, too many characters, and a surprising lack of batman. But it more than makes up for all its flaws through its stunning set pieces, touching emotion, intelligent themes, and overall sense of event and power. Nolan has once again (and for the last time) delivered a batman film with true heart, brains, and excitement. Lets see what he does next

7.title: Good but...
7.content: Too much chat and not enough bat! I liked this film and i knew it was going to be a big story to tell and i think Nolan pulled it off. Maybe the hype was too much but being the concluding part i think Nolan could have given us more. It seemed to have a methodical pace which speeded up towards the end that in my opinion just seemed a bit rushed considering it took such a long time to layout the plot. Batman was as dark as he could have been but needed a few more silky moves. Michael Caine maybe a good luck charm for Nolan but in this case i didn't think he gave a particularly strong performance and his script just seemed a bit weak..its all very well trying to give words of wisdom (as Alfred always should) but when those words are..well..just a little bit pants, it just makes it harder for the actor to shine. All in all, i did enjoy it but was expecting maybe a little bit more.

7.title: A good movie, but not a Nolan film
7.content:
The Dark Knight Rises was the first Christopher Nolan movie I had seen since I became a fan of good film. So ever since that day I saw Inception, I had been anticipating this movie intensely. Unfortunately, it did disappoint. I was expecting a Christopher Nolan film, but what I got was a good action movie. It was like the most recent Pixar movies. Good, but lacking in the Pixar touch. The Dark Knight Rises was an entertaining and well made action movie, but fell short of the caliber of Christopher Nolan, falling to mediocrity, becoming a movie that any other director could have fabricated.

There are several reasons for my opinion, mostly stemming from one main deficiency that I find in no other Christopher Nolan movie. But I'll get to that later.

The acting was decent across the board with the shining beacon being Tom Hardy as Bane. Tom Hardy, in every role he has played, has hit the ball out of the park. In his role as Bane, he manages to be, in my opinion, scarier then the Joker (though overall not as quite as good). That's right folks, you heard that. He's the scariest villain I have ever viewed in film, and yet he goes farther, adding depth and emotion, all without using only his eyes and posture. His voice was also pretty awesome. Other than that, the rest of the cast, even the great Michael Cain performed only slightly above average. However, their average acting was not a result of their inability to act, but because of a uninspired dialogue.

The action scenes were well done with excellent special effects and some great shots during the final confrontations. This, combined with a score that stands as one of Hans Zimmer's greatest, made for some very intense scenes. However, they dragged a little long and after a while I tired of the constant explosions and gunfire.

But the root of the problem was not par acting or overextended action scenes, but Nolan's lack of efficiency in his writing. The Dark Knight Rises was 2 hours and 44 minutes, but probably should have been about 2 hours and 20 minutes. There were so many scenes that were used to developed character or to demonstrate the chaos in Gotham, but the were useless to the narrative. A mark of a good Christopher Nolan film such as The Dark Knight, is his ability to progress his characters using the storyline. Scenes that move along both the story of that world, not just the story of the individual characters. It was almost like side quests in a video game, except in a movie. By departing from the main story and creating these "side-scenes", Christopher Nolan worked with developing his characters, but sacrificed the flow of the movie, which in my opinion is one of the most important aspects of a movie. For an example of bad movie flow, I hated Wrath of the Titans, because it had really intense action sequences, then painfully boring dialogue which together whipped me back and forth like a rag doll until my brains flew out. Good directors such as Christopher Nolan, usually learn to use the events in the main narrative to develop their characters. Taking brakes and pausing the storyline to accommodate a scene to show something about the characters kept me from being immersed in his world and mentally exhausted me.

Christopher Nolan resorted to the "side-scenes" in order to juggle the many characters that he added (foolishly in some cases). The more main characters that are added to the story the harder it is to handle them all, and unfortunately, Christopher Nolan was unable to do that with his main narrative, and thus, resorted to sacrificing the flow of the movie with "side- scenes".

Don't get me wrong. This is a good movie and from what I've heard from other people they were entertained. But don't expect one of Christopher Nolan's signature immersive film experiences, cause you'll most likely be disappointed as I was. Expect a fun action flick with some emotion to back it up.

7.title: Good... But Unfortunately Not Great
7.content: I've gotten used to enter a Theater, and knowing that if it's a Nolan's movie, I will most likely see a highly engaging and intelligent scrip (for Hollywood standards), asides the overall good pace and direction. This movie has it's moments, very good moments, but unfortunately I felt several times along the 160m of TDKR, that it was just a regular Hollywood movie, not a "Nolan's Hollywood" special. All the acting is good, but I think the characters could have a better flown. What I mean is that certain scenes just seemed happen to get something out of the way or to get a scene going. Catwomen is the most at ease character, Bane was good (Hardy is a great actor), but it needed more time and insight. Many others, however, seemed to go a little on hiccups, and the one I felt most apart was the Batman himself, I didn't cared enough for him, and I was sad for this. It's not to like it's a bad movie, in fact it's better than the average, but when you compare it with the previous 2 entries, and Nolan's previous work, you know they should have got something more out of it. PS: I wished there was at least a small reference to Joker

7.title: in Nolen we trust no more
7.content: i've been expecting this movie for a year, each day more and more, my expectations were maybe a too high, maybe i made a mistake watching the dark night two days before, but i was disappointed. the movie was not only worse then the last two, it did not even hold up to the Nolen standards, it was worse then inception witch is the worst Nolen movie not to mention overrated, it was a good movie, but not nearly good enough, since i know everybody will give it a 10 I'm not afraid to give it a seven knowing it won't make a difference, it probably deserves a little more I'm writing from my emotions right now. just watched it last night.

7.title: Not great but solid entertainment
7.content: Having seen this newest installment of Nolans Batman Series I must say it is a hit-and-miss scenario. The hype for the movie was as always too big and it appears that mister Nolan has the most loyal audience who glorify his work. As for the movie itself, I must say the main antagonist is not scary at all even though he represents definite threat for our hero and Gotham City as well, but all Batmans foes are threat for the entire City. His motivations are not clear and his plans for the citizens of the City are fuzzy (Jokers plan from TDK is far scarier, forcing people to become more like him). He has no memorable lines and his diatribes about "giving the city to its people" while setting free worst criminals from the prison is beyond comprehension unless he means it as a cynical joke, but you can never tell. Bane's voice is very strange indeed and left me confused. It was like seeing Darth Vader speaks in a voice of Mickey Mouse. It was definitely not him. And as for his henchmen, it is beyond comprehension why are they so loyal to him. They are ready to die without question like they are dying for some great cause, but that is not so. Bane's cause is nothing but a destruction of a single city. As for Catwoman, I liked Anne Hathaway in that role. She showed she can act and change from shy to nasty in a second, and she is convincing as thug-beating-cat-burglar. Her main motivation for following Bane is fear (i believe) but it is never shown what caused it. She tries to start anew so that at least explains her change of spirit at the end. We see in this movie older and weaker version of Batman but it makes no sense to see him a mentally and physically broken man if he really retired after the episode with Two-face (or Half-face, to be correct). What happened in these eight years is also never shown. But his return as a crime fighter (the scene in the tunnels) is awesome. Police Officer Blake was welcome addition to the movie. At first he looked superficial but the character is really someone who we can imagine as Batmans heir. But not Batman. Bruce Wayne thinks that anyone can be Batman, but that is impossible. He was trained as a ninja and although John (Robin) Blake can kick some criminals a..ess he is no ninja. And no Batman. But still... All in all we have satisfying conclusion of Batmans battle for his City. Some parts of the movie are too long and implausible like Banes occupation of Gotham, but it's a superhero movie after all, it does not have to be always realistic or plausible. Enjoy!

7.title: What I think Nolan forgot how to do
7.content:
When Christopher Nolan went and made Batman Begins, I had no clue who Christian Bale was and my first reaction to the Tumbler was less than flattering. I thought it looked like something cartoony and hugely weird.

I was taken for a ride.

The Dark Knight Rises is no Nolan movie. He didn't think this through. It is either poorly written or poorly edited. Nolan is a brilliant visual artist and Tom Hardy does a respectable Bane. I loved the voice. And I stayed away from the first 6 minutes till the actual movie.

#SPOILERS#

But where he messed up. He forgot how to make the villain. Literally. You only forget what you had when you lose it. In Batman Begins, we find out Liam Neeson was Ra's. He spends a few minutes explaining it, and in a few seconds transforms the weight of villainy unto himself. Nolan executed that to perfection - thank you Liam Neeson, for a legendary performance - and managed to make the bad guy really scary and a worthy villain. He lost it here. Talia's backstory works beautifully into Banes life, but Banes death takes away every-thing he built up for 3 amazing hours right before.

Nolan needs to review his performance here. This was shoddy and not what I thought to see from the director of 'The Dark Knight' and 'Memento'.

#END SPOILERS#

Nevertheless, the movie is admirable. Bane is amazing as he is and the voice took me on a trip. Marion Cotillard was beautiful and Anne Hathaway was most interesting. Michael Caine, Liam Neeson and Morgan Freeman are just having some fun doing stuff they could in their sleep, and why Bale didn't ask Nolan what was wrong with him is beyond me. The movie is forgivable and as a friend said afterwards, 'Sure, it makes a good box set'.

7.title: Character Analysis
7.content:
Bruce Wayne / Batman:If you compare with other 2 films in series, batman has low profile, It couldn't dominate the film yet some logical problems in scenario about him. But in total it is as dark as it should be.

Bane:This man holds the movie on it's foot. Good performance...

Blake :Unnecessary character for this movie.A character happy to see how batman flies, fights and etc. A lot of cliché...Of course it's future's Robin. But i understand that why directors don't use Robin in Batman movies.Totally boring.

Selina : Physically attractive but very weak for this strong role.

Lastly, trilogy is a success and really a "must see". But that's all.

7.title: Beautiful, fast paced, but leaving something to be desired...
7.content:
The Dark Knight Rises was a summer blockbuster movie to be sure, but a bit weak. Despite the epic moneymaking it accomplished, its filmmaking achievements were smaller than its aspirations.

Bruce Wayne has been a recluse for eight years, hiding from the cape and cowl. When a new menace comes to town, Bane, the Dark Knight must come back.

STORY - 3 out of 5

There are too many inconsequential side characters that populate this film. They introduce exposition that could be gathered in one scene, versus the seven expositional scenes the film begins with.

Batman is in the backseat, while Catwoman becomes the most emotionally invested character. Bruce Wayne isn't emotionally invested in any one thing, so his tale is very messy. Additionally, there are two under-developed, flimsy romances in this film, both of which make the movie suffer further.

The plot has a dramatic twist midway that resembles Transformers Dark of the Moon. And luckily, there is enough time allowed for Batman to return from wounds that should take years to heal from, just to save the day at the last minute.

OVERALL This movie is overrated. I love Christopher Nolan's films, but this time he did not deliver. The writing does not stand up. The directing is exhausted. Making feature films is tough, and Nolan gave himself too much work to do, failing to make the main characters the most valuable part of the film.

'The Dark Knight Rises' will make more money than 'The Dark Knight', and many people will love it and cheer for it, but there is more emotional depth, and better storytelling in the movie 'Ted', which is also out in theaters. And I don't mean that as a joke. Ted is a really well-made, good film.

Perfect Batman movie: Blankman Worst Batman movie: Batman & Robin

7.title: Nolan's weakness resurfaced; TDK is still the best
7.content:
It is a huge undertaking to create a concluding movie meant to super cede TDK, which is still the best action film I have watched in a long time, and overall TDKR didn't disappoint, but it could have been better in my opinion.

The same fast-paced elements are there, and I liked the fact that this movie is an overall bird's eye view on all key characters rather than too much camera focus on the main heroes/ villains themselves. Also, in almost all superhero movies, the main characters are too one dimensional (1-D), in that they are either too cool or too depressed and never change across time, but in this film some of our beloved characters have 'changed', and therefore appeared to be more human.

One main problem is that I have realized that Nolan CANNOT excel in creating epic physical catastrophic effects as compared to psychological catastrophic effects. TDK (with the Joker) was the reason for the latter, and understandably Nolan have chosen two aspects for this movie to match up to TDK's ambitions - one is that if TDK was Batman in a crisis, TDKR is Batman in his downturn; another aspect is the villain this time, though far less brilliant than Joker, is more direct & devastating in terms of his aggression. The former aspect worked really well for the first 1.5 hours as we see that Batman/Wayne's reputations were no longer what they used to be, their lives were hell and Batman was ultimately a human like the rest, in that he had turned out to be tardy and useless as well.

However, Nolan's failure becomes more apparent in the second half of the movie when all of the COLLATERAL damage comes in - too much physical destruction going on but failed to cover up for too many unrealistic actions because the story had to go on at a pace way too fast. Also, I have yet to watch a movie with 'bombastic' actions going on and managed to escape all forms of cliché elements - Nolan has failed in Inception, and he failed again in this test too. Unlike TDK, TDKR has finally given in into convention in certain ways and that has cost a big rating penalty from me..for example, an injured, bankrupt and gadget-less Wayne apparently had no problem returning to a city where the villain had made extensive attempts to destroy all access points and maintained strict control over them.

Still, overall I liked this movie as it could have been much worse (according to almost all sequels historically) and manages to live up close to or on par with TDK, though sometimes I wonder if Inception was an audition process for Marion and Joseph's part in TDKR :)

7.title: Perhaps a little disappointing, though not detrimental
7.content:
Narrative; the most significant aspect of any format of storytelling (opinion). 'The Dark Knight Rises' embarks on an almost generic and chaotic plot that is maintained well within the 165 minutes, though feels too majestic and grand, causing it ironically to lose its dignity from four years ago. Nolan's trilogy has however, established a great deal of morality within justice and democracy that is fore grounded for the audience and is the catalyst for the actions of our heroes and villains in each of the 21st century Batman films. The problem with 'The Dark Knight Rises' is the villains appear to carry two motives, while our heroes lack any motive other than prevention, unlike the strive for justice we witnessed in 2005 and 2008. The first intention from Batman's adversary Bane, as an almost fascist leader, is to encompass economic equilibrium within Gotham City due to his, as well as many other characters's disgust of financial imbalance throughout western civilisation. As a contemporary issue, this works as a sensational purpose of the film, and Bane's actions to complete his goal are phenomenally written and represented. Meanwhile however, the character possesses a secondary goal, and all that can be said of this intent is it so disappointingly generic and cliché to the action genre.

The performances and casting are nothing short of spectacular, in fact, they are so far beyond spectacular that to describe Nolan's management of them all would result in one pondering for an inconceivable time. Tom Hardy expresses this dominant villain in Bane, whose voice engulfs the entire theatre each time his remarkable dialogue is heard. You feel his presence causing entrapment to your soul, and while menacing, is a beautiful sound that you may find trying to replicate yourself once at home. Though he does not quite exceed Heath Ledger's Joker as a motion picture comic book villain, in no way does the soon to be 35 year-old actor disappoint in what can only be described as an extraordinarily memorable role. Anne Hathaway also delivers a fantastic interpretation of Selina Kyle/Catwoman, with great qualities of an ambiguous anti-hero as she roams not in a pride, but as a lone creature within unique individual ideologies. At no point during the film does one find themselves questioning the importance or amount of screen time of any of the characters, they are managed with extreme care, and each provide the plot with a great distinctive personality and relevance. Furthermore, Nolan has once again ludicrously enabled his audience to adore the antagonists, primarily Bane "of course", to the extent of wanting to see more of them than our heroes. This is an unbelievable ability the Nolan brothers and David S. Goyer possess, as despite their pure malevolence, or in their view, "necessary evil", we continue to remember Nolan's Batman trilogy for the villains.

"Theatricality and deception" are quite modestly portrayed by Nolan in this picture. The modesty originates from almost taking for granted just how magnificent the overall cinematography is. You can almost create a mental list of aspects of the film which the entire production unit have impressively succeeded in delivering; tick off 99% of them while you are at it. One could probably close their eyes and simply listen for 165 minutes instead and still be astounded by the flawless dialogue and incredible score by Hans Zimmer. Simultaneously, the visual composition of each and every scene is impeccable; while particular scenes and camera shots leave you so engaged to the cinema screen that it is difficult to breakup your attention.

There are few negative components of the conclusion to a sensational trilogy. In my personal opinion, we are not likely to see another Batman trilogy, wait, superhero trilogy, no, just trilogy that embarks on such a phenomenal balance in all its characteristics. 'The Dark Knight Rises' is a satisfactory ending to a great character, but by no means perfect. The incorporation of both styles from its two predecessors is excellently conceived and executed with minor issues that can for the most part be ignored because of the film's, and trilogy's overall tremendousness.

7.title: The Weakest Movie of the Nolan Batman Trifecta is Still Good
7.content:
One of the strongest points about The Dark Knight was that it had a plot that was complex enough to be interesting, but not so much that you couldn't follow the story. The Dark Knight Rises pushes that boundary to its limits. Eventually things do come together, but it does require some heavy lifting to keep track of everything that's going on..and there's a lot going on.

Eight years have passed since the events of The Dark Knight, and Bruce Wayne has gone into self-imposed exile. The various injuries he's accumulated while chasing bad guys in his bat suit have caught up with him, and we find that he's blown most of his fortune. Early on, a petty thief named Selina (they don't call her "Catwoman" by name) robs Bruce's safe. It turns out that she wasn't after the contents; She was hired to get a piece of information that would be later used against Bruce. In spite of the inauspicious beginning, a weird romantic connection develops between the two. But never mind the complexities of the Bruce/Selina relationship. The real bad guy here is Bane.

And Bane (Tom Hardy) really is one bad dude, the most physically imposing villain Batman has ever faced. He demonstrates this by breaking Batman's back in the first part of the movie, then sending the unmasked Bruce Wayne to a sort of prison pit in some unknown foreign country, while he proceeds to all but destroy Gotham City and put certain residents "on trial" (the "judge" being Dr. Jonathan Crane aka Scarecrow). To make matters worse, Bane has found Batman's stash of toys (including three "tumbler" batmobiles), and he and his followers use them in wreaking havoc on Gotham. Part of what Bane is apparently attempting to do is expose Gotham's hypocrisy, specifically the secret that Batman and Commissioner Gordon kept in the wake of Harvey Dent's death, leading to a series of new anti-crime laws. He even refers to himself as "Gotham's reckoning." There's also another villain who is revealed late in the movie, who's really the one behind all the mayhem.

Some problems I have with this movie include the fact that Bane is an awful lot like a certain other iconic movie villain with a mask, with one exception: Bane's mask muffles half the stuff he says. Between that and the complexities of the story, this movie is really hard to follow in places. There are also some not-so-subtle references to the Occupy Wall Street movement made by Selina/Catwoman in particular, who uses the "haves and have-nots" argument to justify her criminal activities. I didn't like what they did with Catwoman in this. Catwoman has always oozed sexuality above all else, and you don't get that here. Part of it is the drab costume, but part of it is Anne Hathaway. She's pretty enough, but doesn't exactly have the sex appeal of, say Scarlet Johanssen as Black Widow in the Avengers. You actually don't see a lot of Batman in this movie..or at least not in his bat suit. What you do see a lot of is Bruce Wayne, who spends the majority of his screen time beaten and broken.

On the plus side, the effects and action sequences are superb (par for the course for Christopher Nolan). The scene where a football field is destroyed in the middle of the game is mind blowing. I don't generally like CGI, but Nolan uses it very effectively here. I also liked the way the movie ended, which left a good taste in my mouth, so to speak. Batman ultimately does save the day, and the surprise ending actually is a happier one than the Dark Knight, and neatly wraps up the third installment of the Nolan batman trilogy. 7.5.

7.title: It is only a movie...
7.content:
"Batman Begins" is the best batman movie ever taken. It re-introduced Batman on the big screen.

"The dark knight" as for me is fall, it portrayed the height of a mad villain. But Batman is ruthless and feared hero. Almost all the time he has something better under his sleeves to turn the tables.

7.title: The Dark Knight didn't quite Rise enough
7.content: Im probably the only person who isn't giving this movie more than 8 stars & will probably will be hated for it. Don't get me wrong I liked the movie a lot, but it just fell short of greatness when compared to The Dark Knight. I wanted TDKR to rise above TDK and fully expected it too. Maybee I wanted too much from a Threequel, lets face it how many 3rd movies have outdone their predecessor. Whilst it delivered in terms of spectacle & scale especially leading to the Climax, but the story & flow of the movie I felt didn't flow & fit like TDK did. TDKR at times suffered from some choppy scenes that didn't quite fit. This is what was wrong with the movie. There are also moments when you have to suspend your believe at some outcomes & although the ending was visually spectacular especially in IMAX some of the capers around the peril at the end of the movie seemed a bit tacky & obvious. O.K. thats enough about the bad points. Now what was good. The fights between Batman & Bane are awesome, thumping, crunching dramatic & thrilling stuff. The Bat is the type of thing that got me giddy, I loved it. I can remember actually bending to my right as I manouvered this beauty around the skyline. There is of course Zimmer's soundtrack which points out when something important is happening or accompanies the action scenes to lift them to another level, in a way only Zimmer can do. Oh and the Batpod does a couple of manouveres which were freaking awesome & again got me giddy too. On the whole when Batman is on screen the movie rocks & with some better more cohesive story telling this would be right up there with TDK. Having written all these points I've just realised I want to go see it again. That says it all, it didn't quite fulfill my expectations but still good enough to watch again, it is a Batman movie after all.

7.title: Token villains and reluctant heroes are out-shined by Anne Hathaway
7.content:
Bane is the main villain in this movie. He wears a mask to cover his mouth. His voice doesn't sound human.

While his outfit may look good on paper, it just doesn't work in the movie. Bane's character was one-dimensional. They could have basically put anyone in the Bane outfit and had the same results.

Anne Hathaway did a great job though. If she had a bigger part she would have stolen the show. Joseph Gordon-Levitt was also somewhat inspiring. He seems more mature in this movie.

But the Batman character in this movie was hardly inspiring at all.

And the stunts were forgettable. Comic book movies seem to be focusing more and more on CGI, and less and less on stunts.

7.title: A very sloppy, plot hole-filled, underwhelming followup to what has now grown on me enough to call a masterpiece.
7.content:
I have a love/like relationship with The Dark Knight. I remember the hype well, it was one of the most exciting experiences. I saw the film three times in the cinema, including IMAX and I'm not even a big fan. This film was huge. Although Heath Ledger's Joker was always the most compelling part, I found myself from viewing to viewing finding genius and then flaws and gaps of logic and confusion. Always a thrill though.

Only now do I see how truly valuable that film was.

I was excited for The Dark Knight Rises. Not the same hysteria as The Dark Knight, but I expected it to live up to its predecessors at least. Instead it's a completely different film from a completely different series. Though maybe The Dark Knight was the exception and not Rises as its roots are deep within Batman Begins, bringing everything cleverly full circle. It's certainly not the 'epic' film Nolan promised. The Dark Knight Rises is an ordinary blockbuster and not a Nolan blockbuster.

After the 2 and a half hours of relentless tension that The Dark Knight was, this film takes more time to breathe, savouring in moments of complete silence. It makes it a more intimate and visceral film but that comes at the dire expense of entertainment. The best moments are in the heartfelt monologues, particularly from Michael Caine and Joseph Gordon-Levitt in the first act. Those scenes are terrific and very fitting for the characters and the series. The film generally worked moment to moment but in the big picture, I have to question Nolan's attention to detail because it wasn't at work here. I'll get back to that in a moment.

It's a very gritty film, beating all the characters right down to the very bottom, particularly Gordon and literally for Bruce Wayne. So much so that it's disheartening for the audience, rather than thought-provoking. Bale's performance is probably the best it's been in the series here.

Pleasantly and surprisingly, Levitt's character had a big chunk of screen time and I really enjoyed his character. He's full of hope and always acts bravely, even making dire mistakes which are heart-breaking to see. Even if his character was more assumed than developed, I really liked him, though the twist at the end for his character was eye-rolling. Anne Hathaway was very good as the Catwoman, the highlights definitely being the shots with her expressions showing the act fading away and her sincerity melting in. Really touching, really subtle. Tom Hardy was mostly good, but it was hard to tell due to the mask. He was far away from any character I've seen him play that's for sure. His Sean Connery voice made me laugh at first but it grew on me and I looked forward to his later appearances.

However, one of my problems with the film is how the focus begins with Harvey Dent's influence on Gotham. It completely ignores the Joker's influence, even if negative, to society. Another disappointment is how this film really lacked the essential iconography that The Dark Knight had. That film had it in every single scene even at the expense of its coherency. All the iconography that this film had were used in the promotional material so I'd already seen it. I'm not sure why, but it seemed Wally Pfister's heart wasn't in this one. At least there was very little ambition with the action. There were a few shots that were great such as the big spectacle ones like the stadium collapse. It had a few jaw-dropping moments but no chills. There's a complete lack of consistent or rich atmosphere, especially in the very compact set decoration which now seem to overshadow the genuinely huge moments and make the film less epic. Although it lacked enough iconic moments, it was chockfull of iconic lines which were very effective.

There are two big fights between Batman and Bane. Both are exactly the same, just different sets, different winners. The lack of development in them is frustrating. Batman is known for his resourcefulness. Sure, it's revealed that his greatest weapon of darkness doesn't work on Bane and that is one of my favourite moments from that scene, but he could've used any of his gadgets on his utility belt to at least try to defeat him. Or even the power-kick he demonstrated in an earlier scene rather than just punching Bane repeatedly in the face. The first fight was brutal. The second one was extremely uninteresting. There are far too many missed opportunities in this film, mostly violent bits which are cut down due to censorship. But I really wanted to see Batman die in his suit which we didn't get. That would've been a brave move and this was not a brave film. Instead, we got two eye-rolling twists of who two characters really are.

I've only covered a few gripes I have with the film but none of them make me particularly angry, just disappointed. I know Nolan can do better. This film isn't even glossy enough to cover them up. The only scene that does anger me is how the climatic scene is something we've seen so many times before. We even saw it recently in both Captain America and The Avengers. Sure, that must mean it's a comic book staple, but it's not interesting in the slightest. The last 10 seconds saved the film. Not making it perfect, and it wasn't particularly brave. It just saved it from being completely depressing. Rises raises way more questions than it answers. Maybe Nolan is just a victim of his own shadow. There's an excellent film in here somewhere, those ideas are just buried deep within. This isn't a bad film, nor an average film. Just not a satisfying one.

I do feel like watching The Dark Knight again though.

6/10

7.title: Great Expectations...
7.content: In all honesty this movie was never going to be able to live up to and surpass the expectations set by 'The Dark Knight'. I was a little disappointed after viewing the movie but on reflection blame myself rather than Mr.Nolan. The unrealistic hype I had placed on the film in my own mind was entirely my own fault. Tom Hardy's performance as Bane, as great as a actor he is, was never going to match Heath Ledger's career defining moment. Don't get me wrong, this is still a great movie with many outstanding moments. But even with a running time nearing three hours I felt there was a lot of stuff left on the cutting room floor and dare I say it a little rushed. All in all I really enjoyed the movie and got a little emotional at the finale but in the end it was like 'Jedi' trying to improve on 'Empire'. Never gonna happen.

7.title: Really wanted to "love" this movie
7.content:
I really wanted to "love" this movie and I really tried. I went to see it twice simply because I thought I was crazy, during my first screening, for thinking it was anything but pure perfection, considering how amazing I thought the first two films were. What The Dark Knight Rises has going for it, are the incredible action sequences mixed with real characters thrown into another world of anarchy caused by the new villain in town: Bane. What it lacks, in my opinion, is the patience and depth of the original two.

Christopher Nolan is unarguably an incredible director. And his entire Batman trilogy succeeds in many ways. Rarely has a story about Batman, on film or in the comics, ever really understood the character of Bruce Wayne/Batman like his films have. By the end of The Dark Knight, Batman was far more than just a popular comic book figure, he became a modern tragic anti-hero. And The Dark Knight itself has become something of a modern day epic, on par with films of the past like Ben-Hur or Star Wars.

When we enter back into Batman's world, Gotham city is in good shape. The cops don't seem as dirty as they used to be. Other than the rare cat burglar and pick pocket-ers, citizens seem pretty clean. That is until a terrorist named Bane decides to come to Gotham bringing with him a whole league of minions, inspiring the corrupt of Gotham to have one more go at destroying the city. Which of course inspires Batman to return for one last time, to again ignore the needs of Bruce Wayne and only think of what Gotham and its citizens need. Batman is a great character, and Christian Bale does his best performance as the character in this film. He is also surrounded once again by an amazing cast, playing their own parts with equal realism, as if depicting nonfictional figures from the past.

This is the last in Nolan's series supposedly. I read in an interview with Christopher Nolan online before I saw the film that he was hesitant on making Dark Knight Rises. He realizes that there haven't been many great third films in other trilogies and he wanted to make sure that his series was perfect. And I can tell that they really tried to do this. If I go through the plot event by event, I have no complaints. But of course, that would just be a summary of a film, and film is not simply story. It is an emotional experience as well. And as an audience member, I felt as if the plot of Dark Knight Rises was forced upon me. There is so much going on in this story, and the film whips through it allowing little breathing space. Characters are given dialog, seemingly for the purpose of moving story even more quickly. Their lines are almost full of plot and character information rather than true human interactions. Where Batman Begins and The Dark Knight both seem to have their own tone and their stories exist in their own world, Dark Knight Rises seems to keep going back to the original films, afraid to exist completely on its own. I understand that this is an end to a series and reminding the audience of what happened in the past is important. But at times, it feels like we are being spoon fed new information.

The place where the story ends up is pretty satisfying for the characters and the series. We even get a twist similar to the one in Batman Begins, when an unexpected villain is revealed. As I was familiar with the comics, I saw this coming, but despite that it still felt shocking and unexpected. I suppose I may be being a little nit-picky considering other films in the genre of comic book movies. While disappointing to me as a fan of Batman, the film is far superior to your standard summer blockbuster film, especially comic book superhero summer blockbusters. It shows an intelligence that all of Nolan's previous films show. Also like his previous films, The Dark Knight Rises is thoroughly entertaining, and I am sure that I will watch it again. I would certainly suggest it to anyone as a pretty great action/drama. The fact that it falls short of the original two is perhaps unavoidable, considering how tough of an act it must be to follow a masterpiece like The Dark Knight. Whether or not you "love" The Dark Knight Rises, Christopher Nolan's Batman series is one of the best trilogies ever made. And if you are like me and felt a little let down as a fan by The Dark Knight Rises, at least we still have the other two to keep watching for years to come.

7.title: The Dark Knight Rises.... but not above it's predecessors
7.content:
What made the first two batman films in Nolan's trilogy great, was due to the well paced storytelling. Another aspect was the great character development, and the clear motivations that each character had with one another. This is where the previous films succeeded and where TDKR struggles the most. It's not that this isn't a decent film, but these two major issues keep it from reaching the same level as Batman Begins and TDK.

The Dark Knight Rises however has many things that work well. Just like the previous batman films the movie itself looks great, and sounds great, so no complaints there. The stock market scene was good, and showed off Bane's brutality quite well. The masquerade scene between Selina and Bruce showed the audience the dynamic between the two, as well as their screen chemistry. The sewer scene where Bane and Batman first brawl is well done for the most part, and Alfred and Bruce share a scene that reveals a long overdue discussion. The casting of TDKR is also good, and I will briefly go over the characters old and new.

Anne Hathaway as Selina Kyle aka Catwoman is very good for that part. Although changed in appearance, this is the closest she has ever been to her comic book counterpart. Hathaway and Bale also have pretty good screen chemistry, which in my opinion never really happened much with Rachel in the prior movies. The romance between these two sadly, never really evolves into anything special. Bane played by Tom Hardy does the best he can with the part. Bane is one tough dude there's no denying that, but he isn't as clever, or as interesting, as I believed Nolan wanted him to be. I am however happy that Nolan didn't play it safe, and had Batman get broken by Bane. It's what Bane is most iconic for, and would have been seen as a missed opportunity, had he not broke batman. It does put the batman out of commission, which in turn doesn't allow for as much screen time for Batman.

The most developed new character is John Blake played by Joseph Gordon Levitt, who acts as the film's moral center, and Levitt and Bale both work good together on screen, which is important considering the ending. Jim Gordon, Alfred, and Lucius Fox all return, and do their roles just as well as in the previous films, but with less to do.

The biggest problem with TDKR, besides being rushed, is that it has too many unnecessary characters, which manages to do nothing, but take away screen time from the important ones. Miranda Tate aka Talia Al Ghul's

could've been cut in my opinion. She is meant to be a plot twist, which I know many others saw coming a mile away including myself. Maybe its due to the fact that I'm not a big Marion Cotillard fan, but this character irritated me the most. She steals Bane's prison back story, and manages to makes Bane seem much less imposing, which is a mistake. The pointless and awkward relationship is so forced between Talia and Bruce, that it borders on ridiculous. For me that was time that could have been better spent on Selina and Bruce's relationship, which could have made the ending with them more meaningful.

Christian Bale's Bruce Wayne/ Batman is still interesting, and emotional. Bruce has plenty of hurdles to overcome in this last chapter, both physically, and emotionally. People complain about Bale's Batman voice, which I'll admit is too much at times. He is however, the best all around Bruce Wayne/Batman, because he plays each one so differently. He plays three roles basically, the "real" tormented Bruce, the cocky fake Bruce, and the angry but heroic Batman. That is no easy task for any actor, so I appreciate his commitment to the role, as well as keeping it interesting.

Despite TDKR long runtime of 165 minutes the movie does move along pretty well. The plot is different from the last two movies, in the sense that it's less of a crime film, and more of a war film. The only real problem is that Nolan tried to go too big with it. The whole city under siege thing was too over the top, and unbelievable. The plot is interesting enough, but requires too much suspension of disbelief, which sorry, I'm not willing to do. The ticking time bomb was very cliché considering the interesting ferry boat dilemma from TDK, or the unique, and thrilling fear gas climax from Batman Begins. I'm not saying that this isn't a valid threat to a city, its just the fact that it has been so overdone.

The most disappointing thing to me in TDKR is the anti-climatic, and abrupt conclusions to the films antagonists. The lead up to Batman, and Bane's final fight was what everyone was waiting for, and the end result is a relatively quick fight, followed by Bane getting blown away by Catwoman. Talia's death is no better really, expect the manner in how she dies is very similar to Ra's Al Ghul's death, which was a nice touch. I give credit to whoever didn't laugh when Talia dies in the most poorly acted death I've seen in a while, Nolan really should have demanded a more believable performance out of Cotillard.

The most redeeming quality this film has to offer is the last five minutes of the ending. The music starts somber, and tragic, then slowly becomes the triumphant score the fan's know, and love. I am glad that Bruce wasn't killed off, even though some fans argued that would be more definitive. The ending wraps up everything pretty well but, could have been more meaningful, if the character development was a bit stronger. TDKR may not be as streamlined as the prior films, but is decent conclusion to a great series.

7/10

7.title: Matthew Modine's Greatest Role since "Vision Quest"
7.content:
Just kidding. But seriously, TDKR is a bit of a mess. So, like the movie, this review will just be a hodgepodge of non-sequiturs.

Spoilers ahead, possibly for the whole trilogy, but you know you've already seen it.

I wish the role of "picture of Rachel Dawes" had been played by a picture of Katie Holmes rather than a picture of Maggie Gyllenhall.


Was Bane supposed to be a sympathetic character at the end because he turned out to be a mass murderer who once was kind to the young daughter of a mass murderer who herself grew up to be a wanna-be mass murderer?


On the other hand, thank you, Bane, for outing Harvey Dent as a two-face. His legacy was way overrated. Still, I'm not quite sure why every criminal locked up in Gotham should be released from jail just because Dent crossed over to the dark side for all of two days.


What should have been the coolest scene in the movie - the collapse of Heinz Field - was totally boring because everyone had already seen it dozens of times in the trailer. I guess they had to cut that scene short because Hines Ward is known to smile after every play, no matter how brutal, and that wouldn't have been appropriate here.


I thought the big surprise ending was gonna be that Batman died. Once he inexplicably survived that shanking from Marion Cotillard, I knew a little thing like a nuclear bomb wouldn't stop him.


OK, so the Tumblers are cool but those new guns on them looked like they were made by Hasbro. The Bat(wing) took a direct hit from them at point-blank range and didn't miss a beat.


Any particular reason that police officials wouldn't believe Commissioner Gordon's reports of terrorists in the sewers? I'd believe any random stranger who reported that.


Bane, you are one ominous dude. I like your style and your long hours at the gym have really paid off. But you're a bit of a mushmouth.


If I ever get sent to prison I wanna go to that hellhole. Unlimited free escape attempts with your fellow cons holding the rope and rooting you on. Plus free chiropractic.


OK, so Michael Keaton, Val Kilmer, and especially George Clooney may all be totally unbelievable as Batman, but I realized watching this movie that Christian Bale is simply unlikeable as Batman. And that's worse.


Why are regular citizens and city officials in Nolan's Batman movies always more cartoonish and unbelievable than the superheroes and supervillains?


Cillian Murphy had a pointless, disappointing cameo in this movie. Just like in "Batman Begins".


The extended boxing matches in TDKR were more interesting than the choppily edited fight scenes in "Batman Begins". But just barely.


Pretty much every bad thing that happened to Bruce Wayne and Gotham City in this movie is Catwoman's fault. But she looks fly in her outfit so all is forgiven.


Who would have thought that all these years later, "Memento" would still be Christopher Nolan's least ridiculous film?

7.title: Immense, Empowering, Psychological, Groundbreaking, Legendary.
7.content:
"The Dark Knight" was my favorite movie of the 2 last decades, up until yesterday, when I watched "The Dark Knight Rises".

This movie delivers a cinematic experience like I've never watched before. Photography is absolutely genius and the sense of scale is unreal. The casting is a collection of hand picked professional actors who do their job perfectly, it is simply brilliant.

Christian Bale, as always, does not disappoint as Bruce Wayne nor as Batman and manages to keep the 2 characters separated while portraying Wayne as a very fragile, sentimental person who lost the love of his life on the one hand and a patriotic, cunning, powerful Batman on the other, great performance.

Anne Hathaway is golden, as said. Her physical capabilities are impressing but her ability to catch the viewer's eye is even better, her facial expressions, gestures and slick tongue make her an absolute joy to watch.

Tom Hardy as Bane is, hands down, one of the best villains ever seen on the screen. (I will avoid comparing his appearance to Ledger's legendary Joker as the 2 are very different)

Immediately when appearing on the screen, Bane induces a sense of chaos, terror and brutality while keeping an absolute crisp, logical and articulate tongue, it was just an experience to watch him bend everything to his advantage, not always having to use his terrifying physique, but also his brilliant mind and intelligence. Just wonderful.

Michael Cane is simply one of the best actors alive today and should be nominated for an academy award for his outstanding appearance in this film, nothing more is needed to be said.

The plot of this film is just brilliant and although Bane and the Joker are very different, it feels like at some points Bane actually tries to fulfill the Joker's vision in spreading chaos everywhere, but in a much more intelligent way.

The texts are brilliant, saturated with philosophical and psychological meanings and it truly feels like every scene is extremely important to understand the entire trilogy and the chronicles of Batman and Gotham.

This movie strikes a perfect balance between hi-tech, fast paced, precise action scenes and engrossing, deep, meaningful events and texts.

The Photography and the sense of scale this movie provides left me in awe, the soundtrack was impeccable and the editing was spot on.

I am running out of adjectives to commend this movie enough.

To summarize, I will recommend everyone to watch this movie, even twice in order to absorb the entire experience to its fullest.

"The Dark Knight Rises" is a huge collision between a deep, intelligent, psychological plot to stunning photography, brilliant editing and outstanding acting performance who together create a legendary cinematic experience.

Without a shred of doubt, this is Nolan's best work to date and it absolutely deserves the title "Best Film of the year"

10/10

7.title: It's about pain
7.content:
Batman Begins was about fear, TDK was about chaos....here Nolan completes his Batman trilogy with a tightly themed disaster movie about pain.

Considering this was never planned as a trilogy, the links back to the previous films are set up perfectly. Bale and Caine give their best performances to date, Tom Hardy conveys the brutality and intellect of Bane brilliantly, but the big surprise for me is Anne Hathaway- who nails the character of Selina Kyle.

The film isn't without its flaws (a product of too many characters), but the last 30mins took me on a roller-coaster of emotions- a fitting end to the definitive Batman story.

7.title: A fitting finale.
7.content: The Dark Knight Rises was probably the most hyped film of the summer but my oh my did it deliver. After The Dark Knight it seemed clear that this film tried to make epic in every way and for the most part it succeeds. The film starts as a huge downer with Batman out of the game and an impending attack on Gotham unbeknown to the people of the city, being in peace time supposedly. At a massive 164 minutes the film was always going to be a slow burner but it did very well in its first act. New characters Bane and Selina Kyle are introduced brilliantly and instantly at that. Bane works brilliantly as a villain, becoming intimidating as soon as he appeared on screen. This carried on throughout the film and we saw a genuine villain that is capable of physically challenging Batman in a way that we have not seen in the series before. Much has been said of Bane's voice being difficult to understand but personally I didn't find any trouble. Anne Hathaway as Selina Kyle gave a memorable performance, they did not succumb to the 'thief with a heart of gold' and turned out to be more ruthless than I expected her to be. If the film has a flaw, its that it lags slightly in the second act where we are in some parts waiting for the climax. This is made up however in the fact that the action scenes are brilliantly shot with many fight scenes being well shot as well. Past films in the series, specifically Batman Begins made the fight scenes in particular difficult to decipher what is going on. This film practically eradicates that and it becomes clear from the scenes with Batman and Bane this was intended. Elsewhere performances were strong from the likes of Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman and Joseph Gordon-Levitt, and managed to convey the emotion when they needed to. Overall the film was a very fitting finale to a fantastic series which for want of a better phrase redefined the Batman character.

7.title: Satisfied but not overawed!!!
7.content: It is surprising what hype can do to a movie. The dark Knight rises never really got the kind of hype that its prequel "The dark knight" did and that too for obvious reasons. There was no Heath Ledger here who had rather conveniently outsmarted even the performance of Jack Nicholson's take on Joker. His sudden demise had initiated a kind of morbid interest in "The dark Knight". The dark knight rises on the other hand, irrespective of the fact that it was the third and final installment of the Batman Saga by the supremely talented Christopher Nolan knew that it could not possibly overshadow the box office sales and the critical acclaim received by "The dark knight". They decided to tone down the publicity gimmicks this time because they knew that they had a good product at their hands which however in no way was superior to the earlier flick. The villain was an eyesore due to its unabashed projection of its brute strength rather than its cunning which has always been a prerequisite for a typical Batman movie villain. The limited hype ensured that the audience was not over expecting from this production and they came out satisfied. They got what they expected. A product well made and garnished accordingly without superciliously fibbing on its achievements.

7.title: Fantastic conclusion to the Batman trilogy
7.content:
I had very high expectations for this film. I'm happy to say, this film has surpassed all of them. While I won't give the story away, I will say it's very well written and takes several twists and turns. Tom Hardy gives a fantastic performance as Bane, Jospeh Gordon-Levitt gives a brilliant performance as officer John Blake and Anne Hathaway gives an outstanding performance as Selina Kyle. All of them deserve at least Oscar nominations. The big question is though, is it better than Dark Knight? That all comes to preference. Personally, I can't decide between the two. The film is fantastic and brings a satisfying conclusion to the trilogy and would very much recommend to everyone.

10/10

7.title: Just a notch below expectation.
7.content:
Initially deprived of this screening, audiences in the UAE had to wait an agonizingly long month more than most other parts of the world. But was it worth the wait? That depends. Batman fanboys will find this movie has the most intricately woven plot structure of the trilogy. The dialogue heavy first hour is questionable, yet makes for concrete character build-up with perfectly punctuated throwbacks to the preceding films as well as Gotham City's DC origins.

It is eight years since our caped crusader was framed by The Joker. Slain district attorney Harvey Dent is a revered hero for eradicating organized crime. Bruce Wayne is now a recluse with his alter ego a fading memory. Wayne Enterprises is on the verge of bankruptcy having invested in a sustainable energy source with disastrous potential. During all this, Gotham's underbelly rises from the shadows, led by a new and powerful insurgent known only as Bane.

This second half, with Bane literally in explosive control, is when returning director Christopher Nolan gives this finale an epic, full-bodied, and raw closure. While "The Avengers" is still fresh in memory, it now seems like popcorn entertainment in comparison to Nolan's colossus here. That being said, this difference in scale is also the jarring disparity between entertainment, satisfaction and disappointment. And believe me, any way you look at it, there are disproportionate amounts of all three, all through the movie. To begin with, a lot relies on bringing the audience up to speed with Wayne's need to vanquish crime. Why he does it, the manner in which he does it, and the whole ethos of hiding behind a mask. In a brutally painful illustration, it dawns on Wayne (and the audience) that Batman is less of a superhero than he is a livid vigilante with endless pocket money. For good measure, Bane also goes to the extent of proving that Batman is after all, an aging mortal. But just as Bruce Wayne has his reasons in doing what he does, so does Bane. This, in my opinion, is where Nolan's co-scripting philosophies hit the mark. Unlike previous antagonists, Bane is not a maniacal villain or even a super-criminal, but as brilliantly depicted by Tom Hardy (and voiced), an oppressed terrorist whose precarious nature would have given Osama bin Laden nightmares!

Cinematically speaking, there are some spectacular moments but refurbished if you will, off Nolan's fantastic action sequences from "The Dark Knight", essentially making this finale an intense action-drama, where drama has the lion's share of the plot. New to the series is over an hour of original IMAX format shot over various locales in UK, USA and India, making this an obvious IMAX choice for maximum viewing pleasure. As expected, aiding supporting roles are a plethora of top talents returning, but with less screen time in favor of new characters, including police officer John 'Robin' Blake (Joseph Gordon-Levitt in a breakthrough performance), Anne Hathaway as jewel thief Selina Kyle aka Catwoman, and a pivotal character revealed to be a direct descendant of Ra's al Ghul.

"The Dark Knight Rises" could have been a genre defining finale for Nolan and the team had it not been for the low-beat first half. When the pace does pick up, the story catapults at breakneck speed but results in a rushed ending. Does this say something about a muddled effort in editing the plot's time compression? Probably; how else can you compact bits and pieces borrowed from DC's countless volumes and then present it without any of the original humor. Another personal disappointment is the underdeveloped Catwoman. Hathaway's Kyle is a super thief with a conscience but not one with a curvy catwalk. No purr either. Finally, last minute plot-twists and a butter-finger countdown cliché reiterate the fact that the Hollywood strain is inherent, no matter how you mask it.

All considered, Chris Nolan has closed this chapter on a high note, albeit with subtle opening for an off-shoot, should the next director rise to the challenge. Until next summer, when Nolan's ingenuity is fused with Zack Snyder's visual aplomb in "Man of Steel", we accept the fact that Marvel and "The Avengers" remain undisputed with a definitive edge in all-rounded entertainment for the masses.

7.title: Mixed Feelings at most
7.content:
First off I'd like to say that the casting for this movie was fantastic. Everyone fit their roles perfectly, and no one felt out of place. Bane was probably the most vicious, intelligent villain to hit any superhero movie. His decisions were tactical, he did not treat anyone differently, and he was vicious, violent, and malevolent as all hell. He was literally Gotham's Reckoning. Fantastic job done by Tom Hardy. Batman/Christian Bale was great as well. He made the audience really feel for him as a human being rather than as a superhero. Anne Hathaway's Catwoman was very sexy, and simple, but that did not take away from her role. She was easily the best Catwoman to date. Gordon- Levitt as John Blake was a great addition as well. Now here comes the bad news...

My issue with movie was with the plot. While the movie was overall fantastic, it shouldn't be considered as an epic ending to the Batman franchise, because it left more questions than anything. There's many parts in the film where you feel bad for Bruce Wayne, and frightened for the fate of Gotham, and terrified of how malevolent Bane was and what his next move would do to the lives of the citizens. But for a movie that's almost 3 hours long, there were too many portions of the film which felt rushed, others unnecessarily drawn out, and some which just left you scratching your head.

Overall, as a movie, The Dark Knight Rises is a must-see, but do not expect to be amazed, or surprised with the action you see, and expect some questions to arise. I was personally more confused, and angry with the ending, rather than satisfied. Great movie, sub-par superhero film. Sorry Nolan, but this is your best Bruce Wayne movie, and second best Batman movie. Sad to say, Avengers was a better superhero movie overall.

7.title: It was a good movie, but not great or legendary
7.content:
Hi All,

I watched this movie at the cinemas on the weekend.
